en: The Garland of the Bodhisattva’s Previous Births (Jātakamālā), Fascicle One.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Āryaśūra and others.
Translated during the Song Dynasty by the Imperially Appointed Grand Master for Dispelling Dust, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Translator of the Scriptures.

Translated by the Great Master Fancai (Shao Dehui and Hui Xun) et al., by Imperial Decree: I prostrate to the Omniscient One, whose wondrous, profound, and perfectly integrated virtues, And whose sacred limbs and marks are unconditioned and identical with the ultimate reality.
My mind is tranquil and free from strife; I have forgotten the praise of giving.
Taking the four great elements as its basis, the pure and white arises without change.
In former times, among human beings, I constantly cultivated the practice of tranquility.
With *kusuma* flowers, they join their palms and scatter them as an offering.
Far removed from all evils and liberated from all afflictions,
they are loved and revered by humans and devas, as they proclaim the unsurpassed path.
Because the mind is tranquil, one attains the pure Dharma;
the characteristics of the world are eternally abiding—exhaustless and beyond cultivation.
Those sentient beings of the world hear of these corresponding merits.
Arisen with resolute faith and understanding, Abiding in the Tathāgata’s secret treasury;
Cessation of continuous movement and change, The extinction of delusion and inversion;
The power of that supreme wisdom Constantly shines everywhere like a lamp.
These classes of sentient beings, whose intrinsic nature is fundamentally stainless,
rely upon the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and delight in cultivating truly pure deeds.
This refers to hearing the names of the Triple Gem and receiving the instructions of their teachers.
Following and practicing wholesome conduct, He eliminated the mind of self-conceit.
In the past, the Teacher of Men diligently cultivated the Bodhisattva path;
Relying upon generosity, kind speech, Beneficial action, and cooperation.
Having grasped supreme wisdom, one is liberated from the entanglements of defilement;
bringing benefit and happiness to sentient beings, one increases all wholesome dharmas.
Through the perfection of the power of giving, one is born into the lineage of the Brahmā heavens.
Exclusively supreme pure karma serves as its foundation;
yet if one gives rise to self-conceit and lacks the power of superior wisdom,
one will produce many forms of pride within one's own kind.
Regarding the hundreds of thousands of kinds of joy and bliss born of seclusion,
because they grasp them through inversion, those people cannot realize them.
Furthermore, that state of tranquility possesses the most supreme merit.
Possessing vast physical marks, these cannot be attained through minor causes.
Only by renouncing the home and leaving the household life can that bodhisattva,
endowed with great wisdom, be capable of bearing this burden.
In past lives, he long cultivated the practice of the six perfections;
having already severed all obscurations and defilements, he has reached the final limit of transcendence.
Possessing a vast heart of loving-kindness, he feels compassion for all classes of sentient beings.
His self-nature is true and real, Without any cause for defilement.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, Observed the world And came to test the man’s conduct; Yet his mind remained unshaken.
And he spoke these words:
"Now this son of good family has appeared in the world as one most preeminent;
regarding the impermanence of change and transformation, his mind remains as firm and stable as this."
With pure and exquisite food and drink, they extend offerings and respect;
thus all devas and worldly beings alike obtain wholesome benefit.
Recalling and cultivating pure causes, they accord with signless, true wisdom.
A practitioner who trains in this way can cure the disease of afflictions;
abiding in the pure precepts, upright and without hypocrisy,
they contemplate the ultimate truth, free from defilement and without contrived effort.
Opening the compassionate gate of skillful means, bestowing impartial peace and happiness,
generating resolute conviction, and being free from the pursuit of wrong livelihood;
turning one's back on all conditioned phenomena, one ascends directly to the limit of reality.
Having accomplished the pure path and being endowed with all corresponding virtues,
one utterly eradicates all causes and conditions of defilement.
One should always revere and faithfully trust the secret treasury of the Tathāgata.
Free from deluded grasping and discrimination, one quiets and eliminates anger and affliction;
following along with the supreme lineage, one gives rise to habitual tendencies,
just as a shadow follows its form, or as a mother gives birth to her child.
By the power of the Bodhisattva’s compassionate vows, he takes pity on all living beings;
with valor, he sacrifices his own body without giving rise to thoughts of sorrow or suffering.
Now, through these slight merits, I take refuge and offer this praise.
May all the holy ones secretly bestow their grace, and may we pray for the accomplishment of *siddhi*.
1. The Account of Offering One’s Body to Feed the Tiger. At that time, the World-Honored One, leading the great assembly, went to the village of Pañcāla and arrived at a certain forest.
He said to Ānanda: "Spread a seat for me here."
The Buddha sat upon it and addressed the bhikṣus:
"Do you wish to see the relics from my past practice of asceticism?
They replied: [“We do.”]
“I wish to see it.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One pressed the earth with his hand, and it shook in six ways; a stupa made of the seven treasures emerged before him, and the World-Honored One immediately rose, paid homage, and circumambulated it to the right.
“Ānanda! You may open the door of this stūpa.
Inside, he saw a casket made of the seven precious gems, adorned with various rare and wonderful ornaments.
“Ānanda! You may open this casket once more.
Inside, he saw relics as white as jade or snow.
"Bring these bones of the Great Being here.
Having accepted them, the World-Honored One had the assembly observe them closely and spoke in verse:
"The supreme merit of the Bodhisattva, Diligently cultivated through the practice of the six perfections;..."
"Bravely seeking bodhi, with a heart of great renunciation, he never grew weary.
You bhikṣus, all extend your salutations; these śarīras have been perfumed and cultivated by immeasurable fragrances of precept, concentration, and wisdom."
At that time, the assembly prostrated and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“The Great Teacher, the Tathāgata, has transcended the three realms; for what reason and by what causal conditions do you pay homage to these skeletal remains?
The Buddha said, “Ānanda!
It is because of this that I attained Buddhahood; to repay my past kindness, I now offer this salutation.
I shall now sever your doubts by recounting these ancient causes and conditions; listen with a sincere and attentive mind.
Ānanda! In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a king named Mahāratha.
The king had three sons: Mahāpāla, Mahādeva, and Mahāsattva.
At that time, the Great King went hunting in the mountain valleys, and his three sons followed him; they reached a great bamboo grove where they rested.
Continuing further on their way, they saw a tigress who had given birth to seven cubs seven days prior.
The first prince spoke these words:
"Surrounded by seven sons, he will have no leisure to seek food; driven by hunger and thirst, he will surely devour his own children.
Having heard this, the second prince said:
"Alas! This tiger will not live much longer; what ability do I have to save its life?
The third prince thought to himself:
"Throughout hundreds of thousands of lifetimes, this body of mine has been wasted and ruined in vain without providing even the slightest benefit; why then can I not give it up today?"
After the princes had deliberated thus, they wandered about for a long time and then all departed together.
Prince Sattva then thought to himself:
"I must cause my own body to accomplish great wholesome karma and become a great vessel for those in the ocean of birth and death."

If one abandons this, one discards immeasurable abscesses, malignant diseases, and hundreds of thousands of fears; for this body consists only of excrement and impurities, held together by sinews and bones, and is utterly loathsome.

Therefore, I should now renounce it in order to seek unsurpassed, ultimate *nirvāṇa*, to be forever free from sorrow, lamentation, impermanence, and suffering, to be adorned with a hundred merits, to attain all-knowledge, and to bestow immeasurable Dharma-joy upon all sentient beings.

At that time, the prince aroused great courage and, strengthening his resolve through the power of his compassionate vow, feared that his two elder brothers might create obstacles; he therefore requested to return to the palace first, saying, "I shall arrive later."

At that time, Prince Mahāsattva hurriedly entered the bamboo grove and went to where the tigress was. He stripped off his clothes and placed them upon a bamboo branch; then, before the tigress, he threw himself down and lay there.
Because of the Bodhisattva’s compassionate forbearance, the tigress could do him no harm.
He immediately climbed a high mountain and threw himself to the ground; thinking that the tiger was now too weak to devour him, he took dry bamboo and pierced his own neck to draw blood.

At that time, the great earth shook in six ways, surging and subsiding uneasily like water stirred by a gale; the sun lost its brilliance as if eclipsed by Rāhu; the heavens rained down various flowers and exquisite powdered incense, which fell in profusion and filled the grove; and the devas in the void all joined in praise.
At that time, the starving tigress immediately licked the blood from his neck and devoured the flesh until it was entirely gone, leaving nothing but the remaining bones.

Then the two princes were overcome with great sorrow and suffering; they went together to the place where the tigress was, unable to sustain themselves, and threw themselves upon the bones. Only after a long time did they regain consciousness, and weeping bitterly in distress, they gradually departed.
At that time, the King’s consort was sleeping on a high tower when she suddenly saw an inauspicious event in a dream:
her two breasts were cut off, her teeth fell out, and she obtained three young pigeons, one of which was snatched away by a hawk.
The lady then noticed that milk was flowing from both her breasts.
At that time, a handmaid overheard people outside saying:
"We have been searching for the prince, but have not yet found him."
He immediately entered the palace and informed the Queen.
Having heard this, she was filled with grief and distress, her eyes brimming with tears; she went at once to the King’s presence and said:
"Great King!..."
"I have lost my youngest and most beloved son.
Upon hearing this, the king spoke with choked sobs:
"Alas! How bitter!"
"Today I have lost my beloved son.
He then consoled the lady, saying:
"Do not grieve; I shall now assemble the great ministers and the people, and we shall immediately go out of the city together to search for him in all directions."
Before long, a high minister came forward and addressed the king, saying:
"I have heard that the princes are here; however, the youngest one has not yet been seen."
Next, the second minister came to the king’s presence, weeping in distress, and reported in full detail to the king the matter of the prince’s self-sacrifice.

The king and his consort were overcome with grief beyond measure; together they went to the place where the Bodhisattva had sacrificed himself. Seeing his remains strewn about in every direction, they fainted and fell to the ground, unconscious of anything. Water was sprinkled over them everywhere until they regained their senses.

At that time, the queen’s hair was disheveled as she rolled upon the ground like a fish cast up on dry land; and the king and his two sons, wailing in grief, together gathered the relics of the Bodhisattva’s remains, making offerings to them by enshrining them within a precious stupa.
“Ānanda, you should know!
These are the relics of that sattva.

At that time, although I was possessed of afflictions such as greed, hatred, and delusion, I was able to rescue and provide relief to those within the evil realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals according to their circumstances, enabling them to attain liberation.”

How much more so now, when his afflictions are entirely exhausted and no residual habits remain, and he is titled the Teacher of Gods and Humans, endowed with all-knowledge—could he not, for the sake of each and every sentient being, undergo various sufferings on their behalf amidst perilous difficulties?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Was the Prince Mahāsattva of old anyone else?
He is none other than my own self within this assembly."
The king of that former time was none other than the present King Śuddhodana;
the queen of that former time was Queen Māyā;
and the eldest son of that former time was Maitreya.
The second son of former times was Mañjuśrī;
the tiger of former times is now my maternal aunt;
and the seven tiger cubs are Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, and the five bhikṣus.

At that time, as the World-Honored One was speaking of these past causes and conditions, an immeasurable asaṃkhyeya of the great assembly of humans and devas were all filled with both sorrow and joy, and together they resolved to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The wondrous stupa made of the seven precious gems that had previously emerged suddenly vanished when the Buddha withdrew his supernormal power.
**The Second Account of King Śibi Saving the Life of a Pigeon.** The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:

"I recall that in the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a great king in Jambudvīpa named Śibi. The city where he resided was called Devavatī; its soil was fertile and rich, and its people were prosperous and joyful. He ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kingdoms, with twenty thousand queens, concubines, and handmaidens, five hundred crown princes, and ten thousand ministers."
The King’s conduct was imbued with compassion, benevolence, forbearance, and peace; he cherished the common people as if they were his own infants.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, perceived the five signs of decline and feared he was about to fall from his station.
He had a close attendant, the devaputra Viśvāmitra, who, having witnessed this, addressed the Lord of Devas, saying:
"For what reason does your honored countenance suddenly bear a look of sorrow? Śakra replied:
"I am about to depart; I reflect that the Buddha-dharma has already perished in this world, and the great Bodhisattvas no longer appear. I do not know where my heart shall turn for refuge."
Then Viśvadeva again addressed the Lord of Devas:

"In Jambudvīpa there is now King Śibi, whose will is firm and who practices with diligence, seeking the path of the Buddha; you should go to him for refuge, and he will surely deliver you from this peril."
Having heard this, the Lord of Devas thought, "Is this truly so?
If he is indeed a Bodhisattva, I shall now test him.

He then dispatched Viśvakarman to transform himself into a pigeon, while he himself manifested as a hawk; pursuing them to the king's presence, he sought his protection to verify the king's sincerity.
Viśvakarman addressed him, saying:
"Now one should properly offer worship to the Bodhisattva; it is not fitting to inflict suffering upon him, nor should he be distressed by difficult tasks.
Then Śakra, Lord of Devas, spoke in verse:
"I originally had no ill intent, like fire testing true gold;
by this means I examine the Bodhisattva to know whether he is genuine or not."
Having spoken these verses, the Devaputra Viśvāmitra transformed himself into a pigeon, while Śakra became a hawk, swiftly pursuing him from behind with the intent to seize him;
the pigeon, filled with extreme terror, flew beneath the King’s armpit seeking a place of refuge.
The hawk stood before the king and spoke in human speech:
"This dove is my food; I am extremely hungry and distressed. I pray that Your Majesty will return her to me."
The King said:
"It was my original vow that I would deliver all beings; since this pigeon has come to me for refuge, I shall never give it to you.
The hawk said:
"Great King, you now cherish all beings; yet if my food is cut off, my life will not be sustained.
The King said, "If I were to give you other meat, would you be able to eat it?"
The hawk said,
"I eat only fresh flesh and blood.
The king thought to himself:
"It is contrary to principle to harm one to save another; only my own body can serve as a substitute for his. As for all other living beings, they must each preserve their own lives.
Having said this, he took a sharp knife and cut the flesh from his own thigh, holding the meat to trade for the life of this pigeon.
The hawk said, "The King is the donor; now that he offers his own flesh in exchange for the pigeon, it may be called sufficient.
The King ordered the scales to be brought, with two pans suspended from a hook in the center, so that they might be made equal.

The dove and the meat were each placed in a separate location; though the flesh of his thighs was completely cut away and the body of the dove still weighed more, even when the flesh of his arms, sides, and entire body had vanished, the weight of his own flesh was still not equal to that of the dove’s form.

The King raised his entire body, intending to ascend onto the scale-pan; however, his strength was insufficient to support him, and he lost his footing, falling to the ground. He fainted and remained unconscious for a long while before regaining consciousness.
With his courageous power, he rebuked his own mind:

"For vast eons, I have been burdened by this body, cycling through the six realms of existence and enduring every kind of suffering, yet I have never once performed acts of merit or benefit for sentient beings. Now is precisely the time—why do I succumb to indolence?"

At that time, having formed this thought, the Great King exerted himself to stand up and place his body upon the platter; his heart was filled with joy and contentment, experiencing something he had never known before.

At that time, the great earth shook in six ways, and all the celestial palaces trembled and swayed. The gods of the Form Realm, dwelling in the void, offered praise; beholding this Bodhisattva’s ascetic practices and austerities, they were each moved with compassion and their tears fell like rain, as they further rained down celestial flowers to present as an offering.
Then Śakra and the others returned to their original forms and stood before the king, saying:

"The merit of the King’s cultivation of ascetic practices is immeasurable. Since you seek the rank of a Wheel-Turning King, a Śakra, or a Brahmā, what do you intend to accomplish within the three realms?"
The King then replied:
"As for my aspiration, I do not require the rewards of worldly honor and glory; by means of these roots of goodness, I vow to seek the path of the Buddha."
The Heavenly Lord spoke again:
"O King, now that this body of yours suffers pain that penetrates to the very marrow of your bones, do you have any regrets?
The King replied:
"No! [The King replied.
"I observe that your body is in extreme suffering, yet you say you have no regrets; by what can this be demonstrated?
The King then made a vow, saying:
"From the moment I first resolved my mind until now, I have not felt even a hair’s breadth of regret.
If what I seek is certain to result in Buddhahood, and if it is truly not in vain so that I may obtain my wish, then let my limbs be restored to their former state immediately."
“Having made this vow, it was restored to its former state in an instant.
All the devas and people of the world praised it as rare, leaping for joy and unable to contain themselves.
The Buddha told the great assembly:
"Was the King Śibi of old anyone other than myself? It was I.
When the assembly heard these words, they all, with one voice and in unison, extended their request:

"In the past, when the World-Honored One was saving and delivering all beings, he did not spare his own life in his quest for the Great Dharma. Now that the ocean of Dharma is full, the banner of Dharma has been raised, the drum of Dharma has been struck, and the torch of Dharma has been lit; since the faculties of beings have matured and conditions have harmonized so that they have rightly attained their place, why would you abandon all sentient beings and enter nirvana without preaching the Dharma?"
At that time, Brahmā Śakra praised the Tathāgata, saying that for the sake of seeking the Dharma, he had once sacrificed a thousand heads.

Having accepted the invitation, the Buddha immediately proceeded to the Deer Park at Vārāṇasī, where he turned the Wheel of Dharma three times, causing the four noble truths to be perceived. Thereupon, the Three Jewels appeared in the world.

3. The Origin of the Tathāgata’s Almsround. Third: At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Multi-storied Lecture Hall of the Bamboo Grove Monastery in the kingdom of Magadha. Together with Ānanda, he donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
He saw an elderly couple, both of whom were blind and further impoverished; they had only a son, seven years of age, who constantly went out to beg in order to support his parents.
Whenever he obtained fresh, fine fruits or food and drink, he first offered them to his parents, while he himself ate whatever was hard, coarse, or leftover.

At that time, Ānanda thought to himself: "Although this child is still in his youth, he practices profound filial piety; with diligent devotion morning and evening, he never fails to provide what is required.

When the Buddha had finished his almsround and returned to the vihāra, he sat down after finishing his meal, washing his feet and spreading out his seat, intending to expound the Dharma for the great assembly.
Ānanda joined his palms, stepped forward, and addressed the Buddha:

"Just now, while attending upon the World-Honored One as we entered the city for alms, I saw a young boy leading his blind parents about, begging from door to door and serving them with filial piety; he does this daily, which is truly rare to encounter."
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!
Not only for those living at home and those who have gone forth, but for all, filial conduct must be made the foremost; its merit is beyond measure."

Why is this so? I recall that in the past, immeasurable kalpas ago, when I was a youth also seven years of age, I once cut flesh from my own body out of a heart of filial piety and obedience to save my parents from a life-threatening crisis. From that time forward, I have relied upon this merit to constantly serve as a Lord of Devas and as a human king; even until my attainment of Buddhahood, it has all been due to this blessing.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“I wish to hear of the past causes for saving his relative’s life; what were the circumstances?
The Buddha said:
“Ānanda! You should listen attentively; I shall now explain this to you in detail for you.

In ages past, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great kingdom named Takṣaśilā. At that time, the king’s name was Deva, who had ten crown princes, each ruling over a separate kingdom. The youngest was named Sunetra (Good Abiding); his realm was peaceful and prosperous, and its population was flourishing.”
At that time, there was an evil king in a neighboring realm named Rāhu, who desired to invade and plunder; he gathered a band of fierce partisans and raised an army to attack.
King Supratiṣṭhita’s military forces were no match for them, so he fled to his father’s kingdom to escape the calamity.

The king had a beloved son named Sujāta, who was still in his early childhood; unable to bear the thought of abandoning him, the king took his wife and child and hurriedly crossed the border. After seven days on the road, they reached their own kingdom; yet another fourteen stages through desolate and remote lands followed. Carrying seven days’ provisions with great effort, they set out in a state of panic and mistakenly took a circuitous route. When they had traveled only halfway, their food supplies were exhausted, and for many days they remained so emaciated from hunger that they could barely look upon one another.
The king thought to himself:
"The situation is desperate and all means are exhausted; it is necessary to sacrifice one person so that two lives may be preserved.
He then instructed his consort to take their son and move forward, while he drew his blade behind them, intending to strike the woman's body in order to save the infant and thereby sustain himself.
Sujāta looked back and saw his father raising a blade; he quickly addressed the king, saying, "Do not kill my mother!
It would be better to cut my own flesh to serve as provisions for him; I have never heard of a son eating the flesh of his own mother."
Through diligent sincerity and weeping entreaty, he saved his mother’s life.
At that time, Śaṅkhapāla addressed the king, saying:

“I wish to offer my own flesh to save my parents; when you cut the flesh, do not let it be exhausted all at once, but take small portions gradually so that they may sustain themselves for several stages of the journey.”
"If his life were to end, his flesh would surely rot and stink, and he would inevitably be cast aside, with no success in his undertaking.
At that time, his parents said to Sujāta, "Now you are committing a sinful act against our original intention; how could we bear to raise a blade and personally cut off your own flesh?"
Thereupon, the prince first took a sharp blade and cut the flesh from his own body, kneeling to offer it to them.
When the king and the queen saw this, they wept and were filled with grief; only after a long time were they able to eat.
After several days had passed, the flesh of his body was entirely exhausted; before reaching another country, his hunger and distress became unbearable.
From between the joints of his bones, he obtained a small amount of flesh, which he carried along the road to sustain his remaining life.
At that time, King Suvikrānta and his consort each comforted their son with kind words; they gathered their heads together in sorrowful affection and finally let him go as he departed.
Then the prince thought to himself:

"I have saved my parents' lives with the flesh of my own body. May I reach my home country in safety and well-being. By this root of goodness, may I swiftly attain Bodhi, deliver all beings throughout the ten directions, cause them to leave behind all suffering, and realize true, eternal bliss."

When he made this vow, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways, and the devas of the desire and form realms were all struck with amazement; they immediately observed the world with their divine eyes and beheld the Bodhisattva practicing such filial conduct.
These sons of the gods, in the midst of the sky, joined their palms in praise, their tears falling like rain.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, manifested as tigers and wolves to test the Bodhisattva, intending to come and devour him.
The prince thought to himself:
"These fierce beasts are now coming to devour me; I shall give them even my remaining bones, and with a heart of joy, I will feel no regret or distress."
At that time, Śakra returned to his original form and praised the prince, saying:
"This is truly rare! To be able to save and sustain one's parents with the flesh of one's own body—such filial devotion is beyond compare."
"What wish do you require? Speak it now. [The youth replied:
"I seek only the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.
The Lord of Devas spoke again:
"I now see that the flesh of your body is entirely exhausted; your exhaustion and suffering are unbearable. Do you perhaps harbor regrets toward your parents?
The prince replied, "If my heart is sincere and free from regret, and if it is certain that I shall attain Buddhahood in the future, may the flesh of my body suddenly return to its former state."
Having made this vow, he was immediately restored to health.
Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and all the devas and humans praised him with one voice, saying: "Excellent!"
"Excellent! The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Was the King Supratiṣṭhita of long ago anyone other than this person?"
The King, Śuddhodana, was my father; the Queen was the present Lady Māyā;
and the Prince Sujāta was none other than myself.
The Garland of the Previous Births of the Bodhisattva, Volume One.
The Garland of the Previous Births of the Bodhisattva, Volume Two.
Composed by the Noble Vīrasena and others.

Translated by the Imperial Decree by the *Sō-sansai-dai* (Court Rank of Sagely Virtue), Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Great Master of Sanskrit Scholarship for the Translation of Scriptures, Shōtoku Eikon and others. 4. The Origin of the Supreme Divine Transformation. At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha in the kingdom of Magadha, wandering and teaching, accompanied by his disciples, one thousand two hundred and fifty great *arhats*.

At that time, there was a king named Bimbisāra, who was by nature benevolent and virtuous, having long planted the roots of merit. He had already realized the first fruit of the path and attained indestructible faith; his devotion to the Buddha grew ever more profound, and he constantly provided the Tathāgata and the assembly of bhikṣus with the most excellent food and drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine.

At that time, there were within the kingdom the followers of the six heretical teachers, such as Pūraṇa and others, who had long resided within the king’s domain propagating their false teachings; they deluded and confused the common people, and many believed in them. The king had a younger brother who venerated their school, honoring and supporting them with the four requisites, claiming that they possessed the Way.

When the Sun of the Buddha first rose and the Jewel of the Dharma began to flourish, the King’s intent was earnest in making them turn toward it; yet they stubbornly clung to their heterodox doctrines and refused his exhortations. Thereupon, they addressed the King, saying:
"We already have our own teachers and shall no longer pay homage to that Gautama."
The king spoke again, saying, "A field of merit is difficult to encounter; you may prepare exquisite delicacies to make offerings to the Tathāgata.
[The other replied,] "I shall not dare to disobey what Your Majesty has instructed. I shall arrange a great feast for all who come, and if they arrive of their own accord, I shall welcome them."

Having prepared the food and drink and arranged the seats, he then secretly dispatched his attendants to summon the six teachers; they arrived at his command and sat in positions of honor, while the Buddha and the assembly of monks did not come in person.
The King said to his younger brother, "Although you cannot go in person to invite the Buddha, dispatch one man specifically to announce that the time has arrived.

Once the Buddha had accepted the invitation, he led the great assembly, their deportment solemn and dignified, to the place of the gathering. Seeing that the various non-Buddhists were already seated in the high seats, he used his supernormal powers to move those six teachers and their followers, placing them all in the lower rows.

They all looked at one another as their names were called and moved their seats; once seated, they saw that he was already beneath them. This occurred three times, after which they sat with a mixture of deference and embarrassment.
Next, when the pure water was being distributed, the Buddha said to the donor, "First give the mouth-cork of your teacher’s water-pitcher."
Water then flowed down starting from the Buddha.
Next, food was to be offered; the Buddha said to the donor, "You should invite your teacher to receive this food."

The six masters’ mouths were clenched and they could utter no word; they could only point toward the Buddha. The Buddha offered a blessing in a pure and resonant Brahma-voice, which those who heard it delighted in.
Next, as the food was about to be served, the Buddha said to the donor, “First offer it to your teacher.”
The food then stayed suspended in mid-air as he carried it to the Buddha’s location, whereupon the food descended once more.
After the Buddha and the assembly of monks had finished their meal, they rinsed their mouths, used tooth-sticks, and sat upon prepared seats; it was now time for the Buddha to preach the Dharma.
The Buddha said to the donor,
"Let your teacher speak. As before,
he remained mute, merely pointing toward the Buddha to indicate that he should speak.
At that time, the Tathāgata, with a Brahma-like voice, extensively expounded the subtle and wondrous Dharma for the great assembly; having heard it, the multitude all attained complete understanding.
The younger brother of King Bimbisāra, his mind pure and filled with faith and resolve, took refuge in the Triple Gem and realized the first fruit of the path.
Among the remaining assembly, some attained the two fruits [of stream-entry and once-returning], while others reached the fruit of the exhaustion of outflows and non-arising.

At that time, the followers of external paths suffered losses in their endeavors; they harbored intense resentment and distress, finding no moment of peace in their minds, and each sought to learn extraordinary arts in secluded places.

The celestial Māra Pāpīyān, fearing that [the disciples] were timid and weak and thus unable to protect the Dharma previously bestowed upon them, descended and manifested the appearances of the six heretical teachers. Before each individual, he displayed the arts of the five men, flying through the air, emitting water and fire from his body, and performing various transformations by dividing his form and dispersing his limbs.

Consequently, these heretics relied upon one another; remembering their previous humiliation and how the multitude’s hearts had been scattered, they now observed that they were capable of surely defeating their opponents. They immediately went before the king and boasted of their own supernatural powers, requesting a contest to demonstrate their relative superiority.
At that time, King Bimbisāra laughed and said to him:

"Behold, you heretics are exceptionally foolish and deluded. The Buddha’s virtue is so vast that words cannot fully proclaim it; yet you wish to compete with the sun for its brilliance using a firefly, compare the water in a hoof-print to the great ocean, equate an anthill to Mount Sumeru, and set the humble body of a jackal against a lion. The disparity between the small and the great is thus clearly revealed."
The six teachers said: "Great King!
You have not yet fathomed our extraordinary transformations; for what reason do you treat us with such partiality and disregard?"
"Seven days after the appointed time, please establish a place for the trial.
The King went to the Buddha’s dwelling and related the matter in detail:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to manifest his majestic power for a moment, to subdue and eliminate the faction of the heterodox, so that they all return to the Right Path."
The Buddha said, "Great King!
I myself know the proper time."

Upon hearing these words, the king took it to mean that the Buddha had granted his permission; he immediately commanded his ministers and officials to select a spacious location, to level and smooth the ground until it was pure and clean, and to erect banners and streamers and arrange seats and thrones.
On the day of the assembly, the people looked forward to it with great anticipation.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata, accompanied by the great multitude, traveled from Rājagṛha to the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
At that time, the great king named Licchavi led his ministers and subjects to welcome the Buddha.
The six heretical teachers all proclaimed these words:
"We have long known that Gautama’s wisdom and arts are shallow; it was only because we were pressed to compete for victory that we feared and fled.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, hearing that the Buddha was advancing, prepared various offerings filling five hundred carts. The king, his ministers, and the common people, numbering about one hundred thousand, provided whatever was required and followed after the Buddha.
The non-Buddhist practitioner then said to King Aḷaka,
"I request to compete with the śramaṇa in a contest of supernatural transformations.
The king then said to him:
"Alas, you foolish men!
You claim yourselves to possess the Way, yet I fear only that you will bring disgrace and humiliation upon yourselves.
The King addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The six teachers are in disarray, desiring to compete with their extraordinary arts; we only pray that the Tathāgata will subdue their wickedness.
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
"I shall know the time myself.

Having heard this, they took it to mean that the Buddha had granted his permission; they made elaborate preparations as King Bimbisāra had done, and the common people waited expectantly, anticipating the event for the following day.

At that time, the Tathāgata, leading a great assembly, traveled from Vaiśālī to the kingdom of Kauśāmbī. Then the great king there, named Udayana, gathered his ministers and citizens, all of whom came to welcome him. On the following morning, the people of Vaiśālī asked the Buddha:

"How is it that you have already gone to the kingdom of Kauśāmbī? Because of this, the six heretical teachers became even more arrogant; they said to their followers: "Once we see him, he will surely be brought to ruin."
At that time, when King Roca heard that the Buddha was proceeding forward, he also prepared provisions filling five hundred carts to await the offering.

The king, his ministers, and the common people, numbering seventy thousand, provided all that was required and followed behind the Buddha as they went from the kingdom of Kauśāmbī to the kingdom of Vaiśālī, from the kingdom of Vaiśālī to the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, and so on until they reached the kingdoms of Vārāṇasī, Kapilavastu, Śrāvastī, and others.
At that time, wherever the World-Honored One traveled, kings, ministers, and subjects—countless thousands of myriads of kotis—all came forth to welcome, make offerings to, and revere him.

Whenever he arrived in a kingdom, those six teachers would invariably follow behind him, seeking to challenge the Buddha to a contest and extensively displaying their own abilities, all as previously described.
At that time, the kings and their subjects—countless hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis in number—filled the rivers, fields, and wildernesses as they gathered in the kingdom of Śrāvastī.
Among them was a great king named Jayasena, who possessed a vast reputation and was preeminent in majestic virtue.
At that time, the six teachers came forward and said to the king:

"We request to compete with the śramaṇa to determine who is superior or inferior; he has secretly fled to various kingdoms, intending to seek refuge there, and we, along with our disciples, have now pursued him until we arrived here."
Then King Jayasena said to the non-Buddhists, "The noble virtue of the Tathāgata is inconceivable; you common and ignorant folk have rashly debated matters of victory and defeat.
The king went to the Buddha’s dwelling and related the preceding events in detail.

“I only pray that the World-Honored One will briefly manifest a divine transformation, so that all the deluded multitudes throughout the various kingdoms may behold the Buddha’s supernormal powers and distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.
The Buddha said,
“Great King!...”
"This is no small matter; now is precisely the right time, just as you have requested.

The King commanded his ministers and officials to strictly prepare the assembly hall, accumulating vast quantities of incense and flowers and arranging seats and thrones, until the great multitude who had come gathered there like clouds.
On the first day of that month, at the time of dawn, the Buddha and the great assembly first arrived at the site of the debate.
On this day, King Vijayin prepared a meal and, with a pure mind, personally offered a tooth-stick with his own hands.

After the Buddha had finished chewing it, he threw the remains upon the ground; in an instant, roots and stalks sprouted and grew lush green, gradually reaching a height of three hundred *yojanas*. Its branches spread out to two hundred *yojanas*, and its twigs, leaves, flowers, and fruits were composed of the seven treasures. They possessed various colors, each emitting light according to its hue, and those who ate the fruit found its taste to be like nectar.
When all the people witnessed this supernatural transformation, they all conceived faith and reverence, exclaiming in praise, "How rare!
The Buddha, according to their individual capacities and needs, expounded the sublime Dharma for them; upon hearing the Dharma, they attained realization and reached the stage of non-retrogression.

On the second day, King Udayana of the kingdom of Kauśāmbī invited the Buddha for a meal offering. The Buddha manifested two great mountains on either side, lofty, vast, and magnificent, composed of the seven precious gems and radiant with manifold colors. From atop one mountain emerged rice porridge, fragrant, smooth, sweet, and delicious like the taste of *sudhā*; beings from immeasurable lands gathered together to eat it, and all were fully satisfied.

On one mountain there grew fine, tender, fragrant herbs; eating them caused no bitterness or astringency, yet they were sufficient to satisfy, so that elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and all other classes of animals were fully satiated.
The people of the various kingdoms, beholding these supernatural transformations, all conceived faith and reverence, exclaiming in praise, "How rare!
The Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained awakening and understanding, realizing the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

On the third day thereafter, King Cūḍāmaṇi of the country of Mahācīna invited the Buddha for a meal and offered him pure water. As he washed his mouth and discarded the water upon the ground, it formed a pool of seven precious jewels; in each direction, extending two hundred li, the pool was filled with water possessing the eight virtues, and fragrant four-colored lotuses spread their scent afar.

At that time, the entire assembly, beholding this miraculous manifestation, all gave rise to faith and reverence; the Buddha preached the Dharma for them, and their minds were opened and their intentions liberated, so that they distanced themselves from dust and left behind defilement, all attaining the first fruit of the path.
On the fourth day, King Dabhami of the kingdom of Takṣaśilā invited the Buddha for a meal offering.

At that time, the Tathāgata manifested eight channels of flowing water on the four sides of the pond; the clear ripples surged and intermingled in a continuous cascade. The sound of the flowing water proclaimed the Dharma of the eight liberations and the various pāramitās, and all who heard it gave rise to the mind of great bodhicitta.
On the fifth day thereafter, King Brahmadatta of Vārāṇasī invited the Buddha for a meal offering.

From the mouth of the Tathāgata, golden light was emitted, illuminating the entire trichiliocosm. Those who were touched by this light felt their bodies and minds become serene and at ease, as if they had attained the bliss of the third dhyāna. The Buddha then preached the Dharma for them, and they attained the purity of the Dharma-eye.
On the sixth day thereafter, King Roca of the kingdom of Vaiśālī invited the Buddha for a meal offering.

Through the Tathāgata’s compassionate power and impartial empowerment, he caused all sentient beings in the assembly to mutually understand the distinctions in their mental activities and the wholesome or unwholesome karmic retributions resulting from their mental movements. All were filled with wonder and joy, praising the Buddha’s merit; as the Buddha preached the Dharma for them, each attained understanding, gave rise to a pure mind, and dwelt in the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
On the seventh day thereafter, the Śākya clansmen of the kingdom of Kapilavastu invited the Buddha for a meal offering.

By means of his supernatural power, the Buddha caused everyone present in the assembly to see themselves as universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), fully endowed with the seven treasures and surrounded by a thousand sons; minor kings, ministers, and subjects served them with reverent solemnity. Each person rejoiced and praised the Buddha’s merits, and as the Buddha preached the Dharma for them, they all joyfully sought the unsurpassed path of the Buddha.

On the eighth day thereafter, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had subdued the faction of the heterodox, descended to the human realm to invite the Buddha for an offering and constructed for the Buddha a lion throne adorned with the seven precious gems.
The Buddha sat upon it, his radiance blazing brilliantly; Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas stood in attendance at his left and right, while the entire assembly sat in silent tranquility.
At that time, the Tathāgata extended his golden arm and pressed his hand down upon the seat; suddenly there was a sound like the roar of a king of elephants.

At that very moment, five great yakṣas appeared and violently overturned and dragged away the seats of the six heretical teachers. As fire erupted from the head of Guhyapada’s vajra, he raised it in a threatening gesture toward the six teachers; struck with terror, they fled in haste, and feeling such profound shame at this heavy humiliation, they drowned themselves to death. The ninety thousand followers of the six teachers all took refuge in the Buddha, vowing to become his disciples.
The Buddha said,
"Welcome! His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, he assumed the appearance of a śramaṇa, and he realized the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, King Bimbisāra again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Although these six disciples encountered the Buddha in this life, they have not received deliverance. I pray that you will explain their past causes.”
The Buddha said:
"Great King! Listen well and reflect carefully!"

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a king in this Jambudvīpa named Śākyu-li. Having long occupied the precious throne, he had no noble heir; reflecting on this matter, his heart sank into an ocean of sorrow, and he extensively performed meritorious deeds to pray for the fulfillment of this wish.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, transformed himself into a physician and approached the king, asking him about the cause of his distress.
The king then answered him in full detail regarding the aforementioned matter.
The physician said:
"To enter the Snowy Mountains on behalf of Your Majesty to gather numinous herbs, which, once administered to the queens and consorts,
shall result in the birth of children. The King said, "Excellent."
Later, the physician returned to the palace with the gathered medicine; he prepared it by boiling it with milk and presented it for the King to take.
When the Queen saw it, she avoided it because of its odor and refused to take it, further refusing to believe in it. Consequently, the physician was transformed and departed.
The other palace ladies vied with one another to share and drink the medicine; before long, they all perceived that they were pregnant.

At that time, the Queen was filled with regret, distress, and lamentation; she searched everywhere for the original medicine and found only a small amount of dregs, which she boiled with milk and drank, after which she too conceived a child.
When the months were complete, the other queens each gave birth to sons who were all handsome and dignified; the king was greatly delighted.

Finally, the principal queen gave birth to a son whose face was exceedingly ugly and whose form resembled a stump. When the king and his queen saw him, they were displeased, and for this reason he was named Prince Khaṇḍa (Stump).
As he gradually grew up, his martial prowess became preeminent in the world.
At that time, when a band of rebels from a neighboring state invaded the borders, the prince was dispatched to strike them down, causing them to retreat and disperse.
The King’s affection and care for him increased, and he sought a suitable match for him.
In a distant land there was a king named Liṣevatsa; he had a daughter of upright and beautiful appearance. He dispatched an envoy to seek her hand in marriage and received a favorable response.
When the six kingdoms heard of this, each harbored a longing for her, and they vied with one another to send envoys for her hand, launching military expeditions against each other.
The king then said, "If you grant me one [head], the others will harbor resentment; only if you can repel the enemy forces shall I give my daughter to you in marriage.

At that time, having heard these words, Śuṇḍaka realized they were indeed true. He sharpened his weapons, and being still in the prime of his youth, he fought and achieved victory. He then took six heads and presented them to King Batsa, who was filled with great joy and accepted him as a son-in-law. He seized the enemy soldiers and returned to his own country with his wife.
The wife, beholding his hideous appearance, was constantly filled with fear;
the prince, overcome with shame, could find no peace of mind and went into the forest intending to take his own life.

Śakra, knowing this from afar, descended to his location and comforted him with kind words, granting him a precious jewel and secretly instructing him: "Place this upon the crown of your head, and you shall possess a countenance and deportment no different from mine."
Having knelt and received it, he returned home with joy. When his wife saw him and did not recognize him, she asked, "Who are you?
The husband then explained in detail the circumstances of how he had obtained the pearl; from that time on, the name Zhulu (Stump-Leg) ceased to be used.
"Therefore, change its name to Sudarśana.
The Buddha said, "Great King!"
At that time, King Śākyamuni was the present Father-King Śuddhodana;
the King’s consort was the present Māyā;
and the Prince Virūpa was my own self.
The beautiful woman of former times was none other than the lady Yaśodharā today;
the six kings of former times were none other than the six teachers, including Pūraṇa, today.

5. The Discourse on the Tathāgata Not Being Harmed by Poison: The Fifth At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha while traveling for the sake of conversion. Then the king of that country, Ajātaśatru, first gave rise to pure faith and took refuge in the Buddha. He provided the four types of requisites for his support without ever lacking anything. His ministers, the populace, and the fourfold assembly all drew near to the Tathāgata with reverence. With a Brahma-voice, he preached the subtle and wondrous Dharma, instructing his disciples to sever the ten unwholesome karmas: not to kill living beings, not to steal the wealth of others, not to engage in unchaste conduct, and not to speak falsehoods, frivolous words, divisive speech, or harsh words; nor to harbor greed, anger, or wrong views.
These sentient beings, having received the Buddha’s instruction and practicing the ten wholesome paths of action, dwell in purity within the Buddha-dharma.

At that time, there was an elder named Shenri (Sunakṣatra), whose wealth was immeasurable and who possessed great power; from the past until now, he had served non-Buddhist teachers and was deeply attached to the false views of the Brahmanical dharma.

At that time, the followers of external paths saw that King Ajātaśatru, his ministers, and the people were largely turning to and honoring the Tathāgata, while their own group received no offerings; harboring hatred and jealousy, they desired to cause him harm.
They went to the householder’s place and deliberated together, saying:
"The śramaṇa constantly claims to have mastered the three periods of time and to know in advance what others are thinking in their hearts; we should now test whether this is indeed true."
The elder said, "Indeed. How shall we test this?"
The non-Buddhist practitioner said:

"The elder must feign taking refuge in the Buddha and invite him to his home for a modest offering. If he perceives this from afar, he will likely not grant the request; however, if he accepts the invitation, he will surely fall into our trap."

He then ordered the elder to first dig a large, deep pit inside the gate and fill it with a great quantity of blazing fire; he had iron beams laid across it precariously and covered them with a thin layer of earth. He waited for the śramaṇa and his disciples to arrive there, then, bowing and leading him by the side, he invited him to walk upon it. If the śramaṇa remained unharmed and uninjured, he was to be commanded to proceed to the meal, at which point he would serve him rice mixed with poison.
Shenri said, “Excellent.
Following the instructions exactly as given, he immediately ordered the ground to be dug and that the task be swiftly completed.
He immediately went to invite the Buddha and fully expressed his devout intentions;
knowing that [the Buddha's] faculties were ripe, the Buddha silently granted his consent.
At that time, all the non-Buddhists were filled with great joy.

The elder had a son named Candraprabha, who was sixteen years old, possessed of the marks of excellence, and was intelligent and sharp-witted. Having long planted the roots of merit, he had attained the knowledge of past lives and addressed his father, saying:
"The Tathāgata’s divine discernment knows all as soon as a thought arises; you must be careful not to trust those foolish outsiders."
At that time, Shenri did not follow his son’s words; he dug a pit, placed fire within it, and mixed poison into the rice. When dawn approached, he sent a messenger to invite the Buddha to visit him.
The Tathāgata, knowing this, commanded the bhikṣus:
"Take up your alms bowls and follow behind me."
The Four Great Heavenly Kings, Śakra, Brahmā, and other devas, nāgas, spirits, and ghosts all attended upon him.

At that time, the Tathāgata manifested various supernatural transformations and emitted golden light that illuminated Shenri’s house; accompanied by the great assembly, he approached with serene composure, his majestic physical form towering like the moon among the stars.

As he approached the gate, the earth shook in six ways; all sentient beings suffering from illness were healed, the blind regained their sight, the deaf could hear, and the poisoned were cured. The insane returned to their right minds, while all kinds of music spontaneously resounded, and rare birds and auspicious beasts danced together in harmony.
The fire pit that had covered it was, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, transformed into a vast and pure pond, within which appeared a thousand-petaled lotus flower;
the Tathāgata walked slowly forward and entered it, while the great disciples each stepped upon a hundred-petaled lotus flower as they proceeded in a procession.

Thereupon, Shenri beheld the Buddha’s supernatural transformations; reflecting on his own ignorance, he was seized with great anxiety and fear, prostrating himself with his head to the ground to repent and reproach himself.
As the time for the meal approached, he hurriedly wished to cook exquisite fragrant rice to offer to the Tathāgata, but the Buddha immediately stopped him, saying:
"Simply bring the rice mixed with poison; there is no need to prepare any more."
The Buddha said to the great assembly:
"Having received this food, set it aside in your bowls; you must not eat yet.
Ordinary worldlings possess the three poisons: [lust, hatred, and delusion]."
The first is greed, the second is hatred, and the third is delusion.

Having now, throughout vast eons, extinguished the fires of affliction, my mind has attained cool serenity; these three poisons are forever exhausted within me without remainder. Even if poison were as large as Mount Sumeru, or the fiery pit it pierced were as wide as the great ocean, it could not harm my body.
By the power of the actual practice of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, all evil poisons naturally dissipate.
Having spoken thus, he invited them to eat the rice from his bowl; yet the Buddha and the great assembly suffered not the slightest harm, while those heretics fled in secret, their traces vanishing.
Shenri knelt with his head bowed at the Buddha’s feet and said:
“World-Honored One!

I am greatly deluded and ignorant, having followed that false teacher to commit these evil deeds; I only pray that you, in your great compassion, will take pity on me and accept me, granting me the means for repentance so that I may be freed from sorrow and fear.
The Tathāgata taught him the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths: suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.
Having heard this, the householder’s mind attained pure faith and understanding, and he realized the first fruit of the path; he paid homage and withdrew.

6. The Story of the Rabbit King Sacrificing His Body to Offer to a Brahmin The sixth story concerns the origin of the rabbit king sacrificing his body to offer to a brahmin. In a past life, the Bodhisattva once served as a rabbit king. Due to the causal conditions of residual karma from previous lives, although he received this rebirth as an animal, he was able to speak human language. He was pure, sincere, and straightforward, never having been false or deceptive; he had accumulated wisdom and cultivated compassion, never giving rise to even a single thought of killing or harm.

Among those countless hundreds of thousands of hares, he was by nature gentle and served as their leader; for his followers, he expounded the Dharma, urging them to listen attentively and reflect upon it well:
"From beginningless kalpas, you and I have failed to cultivate right conduct and have followed along with the evil currents; due to four causes, we have fallen into the three miserable realms."
The so-called four are:
greed, hatred, delusion, and pride.

Alternatively, by committing the ten unwholesome karmas out of stinginess and greed, one falls among the hungry ghosts due to these causes and conditions. Because stinginess is predominant, their throats are like needles; for long eons they do not even hear the names of liquids or water. Even if they obtain a small amount of food, it turns into a mass of fire, and with skin and bones standing together, they endure the suffering of hunger and thirst.

Or, having committed the ten unwholesome karmas out of malice, they fall among the animals (*tiryagyoni*) due to these causes and conditions. They may become predatory beasts, tigers, rhinoceroses, venomous snakes, or creatures with no feet or many feet, devouring one another; or they receive the retribution of camels or oxen, carrying heavy loads to distant places, their necks and jaws pierced and torn as they repay the debts of their past lives.

Alternatively, due to ignorance they may commit the ten non-virtuous actions; by these causes and conditions, they fall into hell. Lacking pure wisdom, they deny cause and effect, disparage the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and sever their study of Prajñāpāramitā. Thus they enter places of suffering, where they undergo various punishments such as the eight cold hells, the eight hot hells, the mountain of blades, and the forest of swords.

Alternatively, due to committing the ten unwholesome karmas out of self-conceit (*asmimāna*), one falls among the asuras by reason of these causes and conditions. Their minds are constantly crooked and deceitful, arrogant and haughty; they distance themselves from virtuous friends and do not believe in the Triple Gem. Although they receive fortunate retributions similar to those in the heavens, they suffer constantly from fighting and the maiming of their limbs.
I now briefly describe the manifold sufferings experienced in these various realms of existence; were I to speak of them in detail, they would not be exhausted even at the end of an eon.

Furthermore, because we are blind and lack the eye of wisdom, and because our delusion is so predominant, we have taken this body of a rabbit. We constantly endure hunger and thirst, lacking water and grass; dwelling in the forests and wilds, we are filled with anxiety and terror. Sometimes we are trapped by snares, nets, or mechanical pitfalls, and are harmed by hunters. To undergo such present suffering is deeply loathsome; therefore, each of you should rouse a heart of diligent vigor, cultivate the ten virtuous actions, and proceed upon the path of deliverance to seek birth in a superior realm.
At that time, the hare king constantly expounded the essential points of the corresponding Dharma for his fellow kind.

There was a brahmin of a certain lineage who, weary of the world, left the household life to cultivate the path of a rishi. He remained far removed from sensual desires and gave rise to no anger; he drank water and ate fruit, delighting in dwelling in solitude and silence. He maintained long nails and hair as the mark of a brahmacārin.
Suddenly, at one time, he heard from afar the rabbit king preaching the Dharma to his herd of rabbits. He sighed to himself and spoke these words:
"Although I have now been born among humans, I am foolish and lacking in wisdom; I do not equal that rabbit who thoroughly understands the wholesome Dharma and awakens others."

"This must surely have been transformed by a great powerful sage or a holy one, or perhaps by a Brahmā or Maheśvara; because I have heard the Dharma they preached, my body and mind are at ease, free from all feverish afflictions."

Now this King of Hares is by nature benevolent and virtuous; he is well able to elucidate the Way of the former sages and discern the principles of the retribution of good and evil. Since ancient times, I have dwelt in the mountain valleys, wearing clothes of grass and eating food from trees while seeking the path of liberation, yet I have never encountered a teacher or friend who could instruct me as you do. Having now finally met you, my joy is immeasurable.
At that time, the rishi immediately rose, joined his palms, and approached the king of the hares, speaking with calm composure:
"How marvelous, O Great Being!
You have manifested this provisional body to extensively proclaim the essentials of the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."
"You are now truly a bearer of the Great Dharma; you must surely possess the treasury of the True Dharma. I pray that you will now reveal and expound for me the supreme, ultimate path of liberation."

"I previously practiced the dharma of the brahmins and endured diligent austerities for a long time, yet it was of no benefit whatsoever. It is like a person who, following the example of a fool, drills ice in search of fire—it cannot be obtained. I pray that you will accept me as one who seeks refuge in you."
The hare then replied, “Great Brahmin!

The Dharma of liberation that I am now about to explain can bring an end to the limits of suffering. If it accords with your capacity, you should simply ask whatever questions you wish, without any hesitation.”

"I have long since removed the defilement of stinginess and greed; for the sake of benefiting sentient beings, I joyfully dwell within the cycle of birth and death to transform those of their own kind and cause them to receive this rabbit body.
When the rishi heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy at such an unprecedented occurrence:

"I am now fortunate to have come into close proximity with your compassionate transformation. I pray that you will grant me your instruction without sparing yourself the toil; for many years we have shared a deep bond as friends, grazing on grass and drinking from springs no different from a rabbit."

At that time, the people of the world practiced unrighteousness and became habituated to evil; their power of merit declined, and benevolent deities abandoned them. Calamities arose in competition, summoned by their collective karma, causing the heavens to suffer a drought for several years without a drop of sweet rain falling. Grasses and trees withered, and springs and sources ran dry.
At that time, the brahmin thought to himself:
"I am now advanced in years and lack sustenance; if I remain here alone, my hunger and emaciation will only increase.
He then spoke to the hare:
"Now, please excuse me for a moment as I go elsewhere; I hope you will not take offense.
The rabbit then said, "Great Sage!..."

"Now that I no longer find joy in this place, I truly fear I have committed some offense; I beg for your forgiveness. These words of long-standing commitment have suddenly turned into a light parting. The Brahmin said: "This place is secluded and free from all afflictions;

the rabbits are well-behaved and do not harm one another. However, I am of meager merit and lack the food I require. Having long relied upon the Great Being, I have obtained the flavor of the Dharma, which I must keep within my heart for the rest of my life. I pray you will propagate it widely to save all beings. Yet, having gone without water and food for ten days, I fear I cannot preserve my life and would thus vainly waste my previous efforts."
Having heard this, the hare spoke with choked sobs:
"Now that we are separated, when shall we meet again?
I pray you stay for one night so that I may respectfully present my humble offering."
At that time, the hare king said to the herd of hares:

"This great seer possesses firm power of the Path; he is a virtuous friend and the supreme field of merit. You all must exert yourselves to gather a great quantity of dry firewood to assist him in preparing his morning meal."
He then went to the place where the seer was and spoke again, saying:
"I pray that you will certainly accept my invitation for tomorrow morning.
The seer immediately granted his request.
That brahmin stood still and reflected with careful scrutiny: "What could this rabbit possess?
Has it obtained a slain deer, or encountered some leftover meat, that its heart is so filled with joy as to urge me with such persistence?"
At that time, the king of the rabbits said to his followers:

"Now this great seer wishes to abandon me and depart; such is the nature of impermanent separation in the world. The life-span of sentient beings is like a magical illusion; once the fruit of karma arrives, none can escape it. Therefore, you all should apply yourselves with diligent effort to seek the path of liberation and reach the end of suffering."
At that time, the hare king did not sleep throughout the entire night, preaching this Dharma for his fellow kindred.
When the clear dawn arrived, he went to the place where the firewood was piled and set it ablaze; its flames gradually grew fierce.
He addressed him, saying: "Great Seer!
Regarding the modest offering I previously requested to present to you, it is now fully prepared; I pray that you will partake of it with vigor."

Why is this? Because the wise person accumulates wealth and is able to give it away, while the recipient, out of compassion, must certainly accept it. I am now impoverished, and thus the power to give is difficult for me to exercise; I only pray that you, O Benevolent One, will definitely accept [this]. I desire to cause others to obtain peaceful happiness, and having relinquished my own body without any greed or regret, I shall together with all sentient beings realize unsurpassed enlightenment.
Having spoken these words, he threw himself into the fire.
When the seer beheld this, he scrambled toward the mass of flames in haste to rescue him; but the fragile body suddenly perished, and he took it onto his lap, overcome by grief, crying out:
"Alas, Great Being! How bitter!"
In such a sudden manner, he has sacrificed his own life for the sake of saving another’s body.
I now pay homage to him as my refuge-master; may I always be his disciple in future lives.
Having made this vow, he placed the rabbit on the ground, prostrated with his head at its feet, and then embraced it; immediately, he and the rabbit king both cast themselves into the blazing flames.
At that time, Śakra, observing from afar with his divine eye, went to that place and performed a great offering, constructing a stūpa out of various precious gems.
The Buddha said to the bhikṣus:
"The seer of old was Maitreya;
that rabbit king was none other than myself."
The Garland of the Previous Births of the Bodhisattva, Fascicle Two;
The Garland of the Previous Births of the Bodhisattva, Fascicle Three.
Composed by the Noble Vīrasena and others.

Translated by the Imperial Decree by Śāstrin Śīladeva-Hui-xun, Great Master of Sanskrit Talent, concurrently serving as Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial and *Sōng-sǎn-dà-fū* of the Song Dynasty.

7. The Origin Story of the Nāga King Maitrīcitta Subduing Hostility and Harm. The Origin Story of the Nāga King Maitrīcitta Subduing Hostility and Harm, the Seventh. In the past, due to the causal conditions of anger, a Bodhisattva fell among the nāgas and possessed three kinds of poison, namely:

Possessing the poisons of breath, the eyes, and touch, yet by the power of other karmic fruits of merit, his body is endowed with manifold colors like a heap of the seven treasures; he does not rely on the illumination of the sun or moon, and is constantly surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of nāgas as his retinue. Manifesting in human form with upright and handsome features, he dwells in the secluded regions of Mount Vaidūrya, where trees and forests abound and flowers and fruits flourish, and where pure ponds and marshes are most delightful. There, together with various nāga maidens, he performs songs and dances for their mutual enjoyment, remaining therein for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of myriads of years.
At that time, there was a king of the garuḍas who soared and gathered from the sky, descending to seize various nāgas as food.
As he approached, he gored the winds and beat his wings, shattering mountains and pulverizing rocks, until the rivers, streams, and sources were all completely dried up.

At that time, when those nāgas and nāga maidens saw this occurrence, their hearts were filled with great terror. The necklaces and ornaments adorning their bodies trembled uncontrollably and all fell to the ground, as they all spoke these words:
"This great enemy has a beak like a vajra; whatever it touches is shattered. It is coming here to devour us—what are we to do?"
At that time, when the Nāga King first heard these words, he was deeply distressed; yet, by the power of his past roots of merit, he further reflected:
"My mind is indeed fearless, but this Garuḍa possesses great majesty and power; only I alone am capable of resisting him."
He said to the nāgas:
"You need only follow behind me, and you will certainly suffer no harm.
If I am unable to act as a protector for my companions and kin, what is the use of possessing such a massive body?"
At that time, the Dragon King went to the place where the Golden-Winged Bird was and, with a heart free from fear or weakness, addressed him, saying:

"I pray you will deign to pause for a moment to deliberate on this matter together. You have always harbored thoughts of enmity and harm toward my body, yet I have never entertained such thoughts toward you, O Benevolent One. This great body of mine has been summoned by past evil karma; although it possesses the three kinds of poison—of breath, eyes, and touch—I have never once given rise to injury or harm against another. If my own power were sufficient to resist you, I could also depart far away so that you would no longer see me."
The reason I do not depart now is that there are many nāgas who rely upon me; for this reason, I do not wish for a battle between the two of us, and therefore I harbor no resentment toward you.
The Golden-Winged Bird spoke again:
"Do you truly have no heart of enmity toward me?
The Dragon replied:

"Although I have the body of a beast, I am well-versed in the retribution of karma; I know with certainty that even a small evil brings about a particularly heavy result, just as a shadow follows a form and never departs from it.
That both you and I have now fallen into this evil realm is entirely due to the causes of sin we created in previous lives."

You should remember what the Tathāgata has taught: enmity cannot be resolved through a heart of resentment; only by giving rise to loving-kindness and patience can it be extinguished. It is like throwing dry wood into a mass of fire—the flames increase all the more, without end. To repay anger with anger follows this same principle.
At that time, having heard these words, the garuḍa’s resentment immediately subsided and a wholesome mind arose within him.
He then spoke thus to the nāga king:

"You have now been able to quell my anger through the power of loving-kindness and forbearance, like drawing water from a spring to extinguish a blazing fire, causing the ground of my heart to suddenly attain clarity and coolness."
The Dragon King spoke again:

"In the past, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, you and I both previously received the precepts from a Buddha; yet our minds were not pure and we did not uphold them steadfastly. Out of a desire for fame and reputation, we harbored mutual hatred and jealousy. Due to these causes and conditions, we fell into the evil realms."

Because I previously confessed my faults, I am able to remember and maintain [the precepts]; because you have concealed yours, you have now forgotten them all. You should now recollect your original right mindfulness, give rise to a mind of loving-kindness and forbearance, and purely cultivate the holy life.
The Golden-Winged Bird spoke again:
"From this day forth, I shall universally bestow peace and fearlessness upon all the dragons.
Having said this, he departed from the dragon palace and returned to his own abode.
The Dragon King then comforted his dragon retinue and asked them again,
"Did you feel terror upon seeing the Golden-Winged Bird?
Each of them replied as follows:
"Extremely terrifying!
The dragon said,
"If the sentient beings of the world were to see you, they would give rise to great terror just as this."

"You nāgas, cherish your own lives no differently than you do those of all other sentient beings; you should observe your own bodies as a means to understand the bodies of others. Therefore, you ought to give rise to a mind of great compassion. Through the causal conditions of my cultivation of loving-kindness, may your adversaries return to their original abodes."
For all sentient beings wandering through birth and death, there is no refuge superior to the mind of loving-kindness (*maitrīcitta*).
The great mind of loving-kindness is like excellent medicine, capable of curing the grave illnesses of the afflictions (*kleśa*) of sentient beings;
the great mind of loving-kindness is like a bright lamp, capable of dispelling the darkness of the three poisons (*triviṣa*) of sentient beings.
The mind of great compassion is like a boat or raft, capable of ferrying sentient beings across the ocean of suffering of the three realms of existence;
the mind of great compassion is like a companion, capable of leading one beyond the perilous and evil paths of birth and death;
the mind of great compassion is like a *maṇi* jewel, capable of fulfilling the virtuous aspirations of sentient beings.
Because I lost my mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) in the past, I have fallen into this state as a nāga and cannot attain liberation.

If all sentient beings establish the gateway of loving-kindness, they will be able to give rise to immeasurable wholesome dharmas; they will block all the darkness of ignorance and delusion, so that the conditions for the various afflictions (*kleśa*) cannot enter, and they will constantly be born among humans and devas in the peace and bliss of liberation.
When the retinues of the nāgas heard these words, they all abandoned their anger and gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness.
At that time, the Nāga King, seeing his fellow beings transformed by his own influence, spoke in self-congratulation: "Excellent!"
"What I have now accomplished is already done; I have caused you to eliminate immeasurable evil poisons and have replaced them with the wholesome and pure Dharma.
Furthermore, for your sake, I establish this pure Eightfold Precept Fast (aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa), which you should uphold."

The sentient beings of Jambudvīpa wash their bodies and minds with the water of the eight precepts, thereby attaining purity; they sever the immeasurable stains of greed, hatred, and delusion, and gather the provisions for the path of humans and devas.
If one can uphold this eightfold precept fast, know that although such a person may lack exquisite garments, they have already donned the robes of shame and remorse;
know that although such a person may lack walls and enclosures, they are able to repel the enemy thieves of the six sense faculties;
know that although such a person may not belong to a noble lineage, they have already taken their place within the lineage of the sages.
One should know that although such a person lacks necklaces and ornaments, they adorn their body with manifold virtues;
one should know that although such a person lacks precious jewels, they have accumulated the seven kinds of Dharma-wealth of humans and devas;
and without relying on bridges, they cross over dangerous paths.
"The merit of one who observes the eight precepts is such as this.
At that time, those nāgas each spoke these words:
"We now wish to hear the names of the eight precepts; we shall receive them upon our heads and practice them with diligence."
The Dragon King said: "As for those eight precepts: first, not killing; second, not stealing;

third, not engaging in sexual misconduct; fourth, not speaking falsehoods; fifth, not drinking intoxicants; sixth, not eating past midday; seventh, not sitting on high or broad beds; eighth, not engaging in singing, dancing, music, or anointing the body with fragrant oils. These are called the Eight Precepts of the Pure Fast."
"You must distance yourselves from clamor and distraction; in a place of tranquility, attend to the teachings with correct mental application and uphold them with focused devotion. The nāgas replied:

"For those such as us, even a brief separation from the King causes our minds to be restless. By relying on the King’s majestic power, we are spared from decline and affliction, dwelling in peace and security at all times. Since the efficacy of the Buddha-dharma has no place where it cannot reach, why must you necessarily seek a place of solitude?"
Then that dragon king replied to the dragons, saying:
