"If one does not observe what is desired, then thoughts do not arise; yet when one is habituated to grasping at objects, they arise again upon encountering them. It is like damp ground where mud easily forms, whereas in a secluded place, the defiled mind remains unmoved."

At that time, the Dragon King, accompanied by his retinue, went to a secluded and vast place within the mountain forests. There, he distanced himself from thoughts of greed and anger, constantly cultivating his person through compassion and patience. He observed the precepts of the fast for many days; as his food was restricted, his body grew emaciated and he became further exhausted.
When certain wicked people arrived at that dwelling, the nāga, hearing the sound of their voices, immediately woke up.
Upon seeing this, the wicked people were all struck with terror and said:
"What mass of jewels is this that has surged forth from the earth?"
The dragon thought to himself:
"If I were to let those people see my true form, they would die of terror instantly, which would ruin my current practice of the precepts.
These people have come here now; they will surely covet my body and take my life."
Then those wicked men said to one another again:

"We have been in the mountains for many years, yet we have never before seen such a form as this. Its various colors are intermingled and brilliant, dazzling the eyes. If we obtain this hide and present it to the King, we shall surely receive a heavy reward; would that not be most gratifying!"
He immediately took a sharp blade and began to flay and tear [the dragon] apart to seize it.

At that moment, by the power of his compassion and patience, the Dragon King gave rise to no resentment and felt no pain or distress; he instead conceived a thought of embracing this man, and his three poisons were instantly extinguished.
He consoled himself, thinking:
"I should not be stingy; for when an adversary arrives suddenly, one cannot escape.
These people are now killing me out of greed for my wealth and goods."
"I would rather die myself than return harm to them, so as not to cause this person to suffer in the present life.
At that time, the wicked men exerted their strength with fierce vigor; seizing sharp knives, they cut [the child] into pieces and departed.
At that time, the Dragon King further reflected to himself:

"If a person, though innocent, is dismembered by another yet endures it without retaliation and harbors no resentment, one should know that such a person is a true gentleman (*satpuruṣa*). However, if one can remain silent and patient toward one's parents, brothers, wife, or children, this is not particularly praiseworthy; but if one can endure silently without returning harm for the injuries of an enemy, this is truly difficult."
Nevertheless, for the sake of benefiting others, I ought now to endure this in silence.

Since beginningless saṃsāra, how many times have I recklessly sacrificed my life and body? Yet I have never once bestowed them specifically upon another person. I vow that in future lives, I shall grant this person immeasurable Dharma-wealth so that their wishes may be fulfilled.

At that time, having been flayed, the dragon king’s entire body was covered in blood; his suffering was unbearable, and his whole body trembled so violently that he could not support himself. Furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of small insects, upon smelling the blood of his body, all came to swarm and devour him.
The Dragon King then said,
"As for these small insects that eat my food, I vow to bestow upon them the food of the Dharma in a future life.
At that time, the Dragon King’s body was afflicted by agonizing pain, and when the other dragons witnessed this, they were all filled with sorrow and distress.
The king then made this vow:
"If I shall attain Buddhahood in the future, let the skin of my body be restored to its former state.
Having made this aspiration, his body was naturally restored.
Those various dragon species were filled with great joy.
This is how a bodhisattva, while amidst the evil realms, abides in the power of loving-kindness and patience, firmly upholding the pure precepts in such a manner.

8. The Account of King Maitrībala Piercing His Own Body to Give Blood to Five Yakṣas. At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at the Jeta Grove Monastery in Śrāvastī for the summer retreat. During the middle part of the day, after Ānanda had finished his meal and put away his bowl, he went with the bhikṣus into the forest to walk back and forth, sit in meditation, and rest.

There they deliberated among themselves, saying: "Now the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has appeared in the world; this is most extraordinary and unprecedented, bringing great benefit to all sentient beings."

Now these five great bhikṣus, led by the preeminent Kauṇḍinya, were the first to encounter the Buddha after he attained equal and perfect enlightenment; they went to the Deer Park and heard the teaching on the Four Noble Truths, being the first to achieve awakening and understanding.
What roots of goodness have been planted?

What causes and conditions exist such that one is able to awaken and enter [the Dharma] as soon as the Wheel of Dharma is first turned, and hears it for the very first time when the drum of Dharma is struck? The Earth Deities emerge and report to the Space Deities; this has already reached all the heavens, who act as witnesses, declaring that Kauṇḍinya has attained understanding.
Having formed this thought, he immediately rose from his seat and reported all that had occurred to the World-Honored One.
At that time, the Tathāgata said to Ānanda:
"That which you have asked was not without cause or condition."

In the past, out of compassion for him, I once pierced my own body to draw blood and save his life, relieving his hunger and thirst and granting him peace and happiness. By virtue of these causes and conditions, within this present life, he was the first among those who heard the Dharma from me to attain realization and understanding.
The Venerable Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I pray that you will reveal this matter which has not yet been heard, so that the minds of those in this assembly may attain tranquility.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"In the distant past, throughout immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there was a king of this Jambudvīpa named Maitrībala. He possessed great renown, with merit and wisdom profound and vast; his appearance was dignified and majestic, and his spiritual power was peerless. He ruled over eighty-four thousand minor kingdoms, with tens of thousands of queens and retinues, and twenty thousand ministers who assisted him in governing the affairs of state."

That King Maitrībala had long encountered former Buddhas and planted many roots of goodness; he delighted in cultivating the practice of loving-kindness, being benevolent, forgiving, harmonious, and peaceful. He bestowed happiness upon all sentient beings and further gave rise to a heart of compassion, taking pity on the poor and destitute, so that all suffering beings were rescued and delivered.
Furthermore, he gave rise to a heart of sympathetic joy, honoring and respecting the virtuous, and constantly using words of affection to cause universal delight.

Finally, he gave rise to a heart of equanimity, free from both joy and anger, possessing no stinginess regarding internal or external wealth, and viewing all sentient beings equally as if they were his only son.
Thus he cultivated these four equal practices, never flagging or abandoning them for many kalpas.

Furthermore, he exhorted and guided his ministers and subjects with the ten wholesome paths; each of them respectfully followed and strictly maintained purity, so that the land was peaceful and stable, and all shared in the joy.

There were various pestilential spirits and five yakṣas who constantly devoured blood and vital energy to harass and disturb people; however, because they all practiced the ten virtuous deeds, their physical, verbal, and mental impurities were purified and their manifold calamities were extinguished. Thus, the devas and benevolent deities constantly provided them with protection, so that even if malevolent demons and evil spirits harbored intentions to cause harm, they could find no opportunity to do so.
At that time, five yakṣas came to the king’s presence and all spoke thus:

“We and our followers depend upon the blood and breath of others to sustain our lives. Because of your majesty’s instruction, all the people have come to practice the ten wholesome paths; consequently, we can no longer obtain food. We are suddenly exhausted by hunger and thirst, and there is no way for us to survive.”
"Great King, your compassionate virtue rescues all from suffering and distress, yet you alone have not bestowed your grace upon us.
When the king heard these words, he was deeply moved with pity and immediately reflected:
"The yaksas drink only human blood; by what means can I fulfill their request?"
"Only by breaking my own body can I possibly save them.
He then pierced five places on his body, and blood immediately gushed forth.
At that time, the five yakṣas each brought a vessel, arrived to take it and drink; having drunk their fill, they were both satiated and joyful.
The King then spoke, saying:

"I have saved your life with the blood of my own body; if this has sufficed for you, I have no further desire. My only hope is that by practicing the ten wholesome deeds, you may repay my kindness. I vow that in a future age, when I attain Buddhahood, I shall be the first to preach the Dharma and deliver you all, using the flavor of the nectar of immortality to eliminate your three poisons and purify you from the hunger and thirst of all desires."
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who that King Maitrībala was in the past, could he have been anyone else?
It was I myself."
As for the five yakṣas, they are the five bhikṣus, including Kauṇḍinya and the others, present in this assembly.

By virtue of the power of my original vows made in former times, I have now attained Buddhahood; and when I first turned the wheel of Dharma in the Deer Park, they were the very first to realize and understand it, attaining the end of suffering and becoming arhats. It was at that time that the distinct names of the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha first appeared in the world.
When the great assembly heard what the Buddha had spoken, they were all greatly rejoiced; they paid their respects and withdrew.

9. The Ninth Chapter: Revealing the Causes, Conditions, and Efficacy of Even Small Offerings. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, at the Anāthapiṇḍada Monastery, together with a great community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, there was a merchant leader in the kingdom who, together with five hundred men, intended to launch a great ship into the vast ocean to gather various precious gems.

Then that merchant leader, having conceived pure faith, desired to provide a meal for the Buddha and the Sangha to pray for blessings and protection; he went before the Buddhas of the past and made a sincere and diligent invitation.
The Tathāgata, knowing this, granted his consent by remaining silent.
At their dwelling place, they prepared a meal at dawn and offered it with all their sweet delicacies and devout reverence.

When the meal was finished, they spread out seats; the Buddha then preached the Dharma for them, praising the practice of giving, explaining how its influence accords with one's aspirations, such that the field of merit is superior and the cause, though small, yields abundant fruit.
Upon hearing the Dharma, the merchant leader’s mind was opened and he attained realization; he paid homage, circumambulated the Buddha to the right, and stood to one side.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the merchant leader:

"If you wish to enter the great ocean, it is full of many perils and hardships. You must take refuge in and keep the Three Jewels in mind, receive and uphold the five precepts to become an upāsaka, and then you may fulfill your aspirations and return in safety."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma, the merchant leader reverently received it with devotion and requested to receive the five precepts.
The Buddha told him to listen attentively and reflect upon them well: “What are these five?”

First, abstaining from killing; second, abstaining from stealing; third, abstaining from sexual misconduct; fourth, abstaining from false speech; fifth, abstaining from intoxicants. These are called the five precepts; you should uphold them throughout your entire life and must not violate them. One who does so is called an upāsaka.

Because that merchant leader had planted roots of virtue in the past, was wise and discerning, and was able to observe the auspicious or inauspicious signs of wind and waves, the assembly of merchants requested him to serve as their guide; they held him in high esteem and addressed him as "the Wise One."
They then selected an auspicious day, gathered provisions and piled up firewood, and assembled the merchants to enter the great ocean together.

After traveling for several days, a violent wind and surging waves arose; the Sea God transformed himself into a yakṣa, his form hideous and his complexion dark blue-black, with sharp fangs protruding from his mouth and flames appearing at their tips. Emerging from the waves, he pulled the ship so that it could not move forward, and asked the merchants:
"Have you ever seen anything in this world more terrifying than I?"

At that time, the Venerable One beheld its monstrous form; yet, with single-minded devotion, he took refuge in the Triple Gem. Through the Buddha’s empowerment, his terror was immediately dispelled, and he replied in a stern voice:
"I have seen such things before, even more wicked and many times worse than you."
The deity asked,
"Who are you? The wise man replied:

"In this world there are foolish people who constantly practice unwholesome deeds, committing the ten non-virtues and sinking into false views. Later, they fall into hell and undergo myriad forms of suffering. The hell-wardens and rākṣasas seize these sinners and inflict various punishments upon them—some by hacking, some by chopping, some by pounding, and some by grinding. They tear their bodies apart into hundreds of thousands of pieces. They must endure everything: the mountain of knives, the forest of swords, the flaming chariots, the pit of hot embers, the freezing ice, and the boiling excrement. Such agonies last for thousands of millions of kalpas; this dreadfulness is far more intense than yours."
The deity then remained silent, vanished from sight, and departed.

After proceeding further for several more days, the sea deity again transformed himself into the body of a man who was extremely emaciated, his skin and bones joined together, and his breath gasping and labored;
drawing close to the ship, he asked the merchants, "Have you ever seen anyone in this world as thin as I?"
The wise man replied,
"There are others who are even more withered and emaciated than you.
The spirit said:
"Who are you? the wise man replied:

"There was a foolish person whose nature was wicked, who was stingy, greedy, and envious, not knowing how to practice generosity. Afterward, he fell among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), with a head as large as Mount Tai and a throat like a needle; his hair was disheveled and his form was scorched black. For long eons he has not even heard the names of food or drink—such emaciation is far more extreme than yours."
The sea deity released the ship and vanished.

After traveling forward for several more days, the sea deity again transformed himself into a man, youthful in appearance and exceedingly handsome; he surged forth, hauled upon the ship, and asked the merchants:
"Have you ever seen anyone as young and possessed of such physical strength as I?"
The worthy one replied:
“In terms of physical form, you are surpassed by a hundred thousand million times.
The spirit asked:
"Who is it? the wise man replied:

"In this world there are wise people who practice the ten wholesome deeds, keeping the actions of body, speech, and mind constantly pure; they have profound faith in the Triple Gem and make offerings to them at all times. When such a person's life ends, they attain rebirth in the heavens, where their countenance is upright and handsome, peerless in the world. To compare your appearance with theirs would be like comparing a blind monkey to a celestial nymph."
When the sea deity heard these words, he was silent with self-reproach and thought to himself:

"This merchant leader possesses vast and penetrating wisdom; his skill in discoursing on cause and effect and his eloquence are such as this. I shall test him with a single question concerning a lay follower (*upāsaka*)."
He then took a handful of water with his right hand and asked him:
"Is the water in my hand more,
or is the water in the ocean more?"
The wise man replied, “The water in my cupped hands is more; the water of the ocean is less.
The deity questioned him again:
"It is directly perceptible; what you have just said is truly difficult to believe.
The worthy one replied, "These words are true and certainly not erroneous; this is not something that can be understood by worldly wisdom."
How is this clarified?

Although the waters of the ocean are vast, they must eventually dry up; when the kalpa is about to end, the great trichiliocosm is destroyed together with it, and Mount Sumeru and the great oceans are worn away until nothing remains. By this, one knows for certain that the ocean waters must be exhausted.

Furthermore, if there is a person who, with pure faith, takes a single handful of water to make an offering to the Buddha, or bestows it upon sentient beings, or presents it to their parents, or even gives it to beggars and down to the class of birds and beasts—the power of this small root of goodness and correct cause cannot be exhausted even after passing through kalpas as numerous as atoms.
"Therefore, you should know that the water of the great ocean is but little, while the water held in a single handful is much.

At that time, the sea deity was filled with great joy in his heart; he immediately presented various rare and wondrous treasures to the worthy man, entrusting these precious ornaments to be offered to the Buddha and the Sangha.

At that time, the merchants each returned to their own country. They all went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet in salutation, and presenting the goods entrusted to them by the sea deity as well as their own offerings, they knelt on both knees with palms joined and said:
"World-Honored One!..."

"By the great fortune of being protected from afar by the Tathāgata’s compassionate care, we have entered the sea, avoided disaster, obtained treasures, and returned home. We all bear the Buddha's grace;
we wish to become his disciples. The Buddha said, "Welcome!"
Possessing the marks of a bhikṣu, he exhausted all fetters of existence and became an arhat.

10. The Tenth Chapter: The Origin of the Tathāgata’s Possession of Wisdom and His Lack of Envy Toward the Goodness of Others. At that time, the World-Honored One, together with his disciples—the great assembly of bhikṣus—was wandering and teaching while residing in the great city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, the Tathāgata rose from his seat and stepped into the void, manifesting a rare and wondrous event: beneath his feet appeared the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel, and from between each spoke emerged eighty-four thousand lotus flowers made of various jewels;
from each flower issued eighty-four thousand exquisite filaments and petals, arranged in successive tiers of adornment, covering immeasurable worlds throughout the ten directions.
Upon each of these flowers sat immeasurable and subtle Buddhas, and beneath their feet were all manifested the marks of thousand-spoked wheels.

At that time, King Śuddhodana, the father of the Buddha, having witnessed this event, was filled with great joy; prostrating himself with his five limbs toward the Buddha, he immediately realized the fruit of Anāgāmin.
At that time, the great assembly, beholding the Buddha’s supernatural transformations, all joined their palms together and said:
“World-Honored One!
We now see countless Buddhas of the ten directions; having observed them closely, we cannot discern which one is the true Buddha.”
"What is a transformation Buddha?
At that time, the Tathāgata, out of great compassion and pity for the assembled multitude, spoke to them, saying:

"The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, enter the state of empty stillness; through liberation and samādhi, they exercise sovereign mastery at will. The characteristics of the true and the transformed are summoned from within your own minds."

Why is this so? Because the Buddha-mind is fundamentally serene, empty, and quiescent; furthermore, by relying on the Samādhi of the King of the Radiance of Liberation, he manifests infinite bodies through the power of this samādhi. These infinite bodies are *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge);
*sarvajñā* is called the Samādhi of Non-attachment.
The concentration of non-attachment is that which is practiced by the Tathāgata;
he may manifest as begging for alms or practicing walking meditation, benefiting sentient beings through these two methods.

Furthermore, while the Buddha was in the world, if there were sons or daughters of good family who beheld the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the Buddha’s feet, and with a profound mind prostrated, made offerings, and offered praise, they would be able to extinguish the most grievous evil karma of a thousand kalpas.

If, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, the disciples of the four assemblies dwell in right concentration (*samādhi*) and, recollecting the Buddha’s gait, pay him respectful homage and offerings, they will likewise be able to extinguish the sins of a thousand kalpas;

even if they do not practice such recollection, yet behold the Buddha’s footprints or images of his walking, and according to their capacity offer worship and give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy, the meritorious retribution they obtain shall be inexhaustible.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"Since the vast eons of the past, I have venerated all beings with pure faith. Seeing their cultivation of sublime and wondrous practices, I have always offered praise to cause them to increase in merit; even regarding a minute amount of virtue, such as a single hair’s breadth, I have never once conceived a mind of envy toward the goodness of others. For this reason, I have now obtained this supreme retribution."
Furthermore, Ānanda!

After my parinirvāṇa, if any disciples wish to create images of the Buddha, they should ensure that the bodily marks are complete and perfect, manifesting the body’s radiance surrounded by transformation Buddhas, and painting the thousand-spoked wheel design beneath the feet. This will cause all sentient beings of future ages, upon beholding these signs, to obtain vast and auspicious accumulations of merit and wisdom, such that their heavy karmic obstructions are extinguished without remainder.
"O you bhikṣus! You should diligently contemplate and act in accordance with the Dharma.
Having spoken thus, the Buddha returned to his original seat.
Then King Śuddhodana rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Now that the Buddha has appeared in the world, what beneficial matters are there that can enable sentient beings to attain peace and happiness?"
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke to the King, his father:

“In the city of Śrāvastī, there is an elder named Sudatta who has an old servant woman named Viḍūra. She is diligent and prudent in her household duties and is always trusted; all matters of income and expenditure, receiving and giving, are entrusted to her.”

One day, the elder invited the Buddha and the bhikṣus to his home for a meal offering. There were many sick bhikṣus who made numerous requests, and the old mother, being stingy and miserly, became filled with resentment. Unwilling to give anything, she spoke these words:
"This great elder has adopted the ways of the śramaṇas; those mendicants beg insatiably. What kind of path is this?"
He further uttered evil words:
"When shall I reach a time when I no longer hear the name of the Buddha, no longer hear the name of the Dharma, and no longer see those who have shaved their hair and donned dyed robes?"
"Thus, this evil report was heard by one person and passed on to another until it spread throughout the city of Śrāvastī.
At that time, Queen Mallikā, hearing this slander, was deeply struck with astonishment and said:
'How is it that Sudatta, whose benevolence is universal—like a beautiful lotus that all people delight to behold—is instead guarded over by a venomous serpent?'"
Having spoken thus, he then commanded the householder:
"Send your wife here; I wish to speak with her.
When the wife arrived, he bade her sit and immediately said to her:
"The old servant girl of your household constantly slanders the Triple Gem with evil words; I do not wish to hear even her name.
Why do you not expel her?
Would that not be a source of joy?"
Then the elder’s wife said to the lady:

“The Buddha-Sun has appeared in the world to dispel the darkness of ignorance and to bring great benefit and moisture to all sentient beings. Even a person of great evil like Aṅgulimāla, who killed a thousand people to take their fingers for a garland, the Buddha was able to subdue and cause him to resolve upon the path;
why then should one worry about this old slave girl?”
Upon hearing these words, the lady was greatly delighted in her heart and said:
"I shall invite the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus; I will adorn the palace and provide offerings tomorrow.
You may verify this by sending a maidservant here."
At that time, the elder immediately filled a precious vase with various rare *maṇi* jewels and other treasures, and sent a maidservant to present them as an offering to support the ceremony.
From afar, Queen Mallikā saw the maidservant approaching and thought:
"This person of wrong views shall receive the Buddha’s transformation; if I see this person being transformed by the Buddha, I will surely obtain vast spiritual benefit."
At that time, the Tathāgata entered through the main gate, with Nanda on his left and Ānanda on his right, while Rāhula and others followed behind him.

When the old woman saw the Buddha, her heart was struck with alarm and her hair stood on end; she immediately sought to retreat and exit through a dog-hole. As the old woman covered her face with a fan, the Buddha stood before her so that the fan appeared like a mirror. She turned her head to look east, and there was a Buddha in the eastern direction; she then looked throughout the south, west, and north, and in all four intermediate directions, as well as above and below, and everywhere there was a Buddha.
She covered her face with her hands, and between each of her ten fingers there were transformed Buddhas.
When the old woman closed her eyes and opened them again, she saw that the worlds of the ten directions were entirely filled with transformed Buddhas.

When this sign was manifested, there were twenty-five Caṇḍāla women, fifty Brahmin women of heterodox views, and five hundred women of other castes in the city of Śrāvastī who had previously adhered to false doctrines and lacked faith in the Buddha-dharma. Upon seeing the Tathāgata manifesting countless bodies from his feet as he walked through the air for the sake of that old woman, their hearts were filled with great joy; they tore apart the net of heterodox views and prostrated themselves, bowing their heads to the feet of the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the women with a Brahma-voice, saying:
"You may now invoke my name: 'Namo Śākyamuni Buddha!'"
"Homage to Śākyamuni Buddha!

By reciting my name and contemplating my physical form, one shall immediately attain liberation from the sins of birth and death accumulated over eight billion kalpas, and shall be inspired to give rise to the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, the old woman, having caught a brief glimpse of the Buddha, hurried back to her home and said to her mistress:

"Today I encountered a most wretched sight. The śramaṇa Gautama stood at the gate of the royal palace before a great multitude and displayed various sorcerous arts. His body was like a mountain of gold and his eyes surpassed the blue lotus; he possessed ten billion rays of light beyond full description. This śramaṇa is a master of illusions, peerless in the world, and your young son will not find him pleasing to behold."
Having spoken thus, she entered a wooden cage, covered its top with many ox-hide skins, and lay hidden in a dark place.
At that time, as the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was about to return to the vihāra, Queen Mallikā came forward and said to the Buddha:
"I beg you to deign to extend your compassionate light to convert this old mother."
The Buddha said:
"That man’s roots of sin are deep and heavy; he has no affinity with me, yet he was a good friend to Rāhula in the past.
Today, the Tathāgata shall travel through the air to extinguish his heavy obstacles accumulated over many kalpas."
He then returned to the Jeta Grove and summoned Rāhula, saying:
"Go to the house of the upāsaka Sudatta and ordain that old woman.
All one thousand two hundred great disciples felt sympathetic joy and wished to go along with him.

At that time, the Venerable Rāhula, empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, entered the *ṛddhi-samādhi*. Having paid homage to the Buddha and circumambulated him seven times to the right, he immediately transformed his body into that of a Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*);
the one thousand bhikṣus were transformed into a thousand sons, and the seven treasures and the fourfold army were all fully provided.
At that time, the precious golden wheel, mounted upon a lotus pedestal, traveled through the air and came to rest above the house of Sudatta.
Then the yakṣa guardian of the residence and the local spirits cried out in a loud voice:
"A Holy King has appeared in the world! He banishes all evil people and proclaims the sublime Dharma."
Upon hearing this, the old woman was filled with great joy and thought:
"Now that a Holy King has appeared, I have nothing further to seek; my only wish is to obtain the wish-fulfilling jewel.

At that time, the Holy King, riding in a great precious palanquin and sounding bells and drums, arrived at the elder’s house. Hearing him, the old woman emerged from her wooden cage, prostrated herself with her head to the ground, and praised his meritorious virtues.
"Now that she has encountered the Holy King who transforms others through the Good Dharma, she will certainly not be deluded by the śramaṇas.
The king then immediately dispatched his minister in charge of the treasury to the woman’s location, saying: "Sister!..."
"You possess the merit from past lives and the auspicious signs of one destined for kingship; I now wish to honor you as the Jewel of the Jade Maiden.

The old woman replied, "My body is lowly and base, like excrement and filth. Though I am filled with boundless joy at being briefly questioned by Your Majesty, how could I possibly be fit to serve as the Jewel of the Jade Maiden?"
At that time, the Holy King said to Sudatta:
"The old woman of your house possesses all the auspicious marks; I now wish to take her as my 'Jewel of the Woman' (Strīratna).
The Elder replied:
"Your command shall be obeyed.
Hearing this, the old maidservant was filled with uncontrollable joy.
The king had her look at her face in a jewel; she was as beautiful as he had wished, and feeling only increased shame and gratitude, she immediately thought to herself:

"These various śramaṇas claim for themselves that they possess the Way, yet they pride themselves on their eloquence while achieving not a single effective result. Now that the Sage King has appeared in the world, his benefit to sentient beings is vast and great; he has caused my withered appearance to become that of a jade maiden treasure."
Prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they reverently offered their thanks.
At that time, the Minister in Charge of the Treasury proclaimed the King’s decree, instructing them to cultivate the ten wholesome dharmas to subdue their minds.
Thereupon, the Venerable One resumed his original form. The old woman attained awakening; seeing the great assembly, she wept with grief and said:
"The Buddha-dharma is pure and does not abandon sentient beings; even one as debased and evil as I am still deserves to be saved.
Thus he repented and reproached himself, purifying his former transgressions through confession, and sought to receive the five precepts.

Then that Venerable One expounded for her the Dharma of the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts; the old woman understood and her mind became peaceful and composed, and before she had even raised her head, she realized the fruit of Srotāpanna.
The earth deity emerged from the ground and said to Sudatta: "Excellent,
O Householder!"
"To tear asunder the net of false views—for this alone is the purpose for which the Tathāgata appears in the world!
At that time, Rāhula took the old woman and went to the Jeta Grove.

Having arrived, he beheld the Buddha; filled with joy, he prostrated himself, confessed his transgressions, and revealed them, vowing to leave the household life in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching.
The Buddha commanded him to go to Kautamī and practice with diligence, never flagging. Like fine white cotton that is easily dyed, he realized the path of Arhatship at that very moment.

11. The Origin Story of the Buddha Bestowing the Consecration upon a Sick Bhikṣu and His Attainment of Peace. The Origin Story of the Buddha Bestowing the Consecration upon a Sick Bhikṣu and His Attainment of Peace, Number Eleven. At that time, the World-Honored One was dwelling at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha.

There was a bhikṣu who suffered from a malignant ulcer; his entire body was covered with flowing pus and blood, such that he was loathsome to behold and people would not approach him. He was moved to dwell beneath a dilapidated, low, and small room.

The World-Honored One, having known this, immediately employed his supernormal powers to obscure the great assembly so that none would know; the Tathāgata went alone to where the sick bhikṣu was, comforted him with kind words, and washed him with water.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the sons of the gods, was deliberating on state affairs in the Sudharmā Hall. The Buddha, through his majestic spiritual power, caused him to become aware of this; he then took immeasurable hundreds of thousands of attendants and, surrounded by celestial music before and behind, descended from the sky to the place where the Buddha was. He inquired after his well-being and offered greetings, prostrating his head at the Buddha’s feet. Holding a precious pitcher filled with fragrant water, he welcomed the World-Honored One and stood to one side.

At that time, the Tathāgata extended his arm, adorned with the marks of a hundred merits, and from the tips of his five fingers emitted a great radiance, summoning all the devas from afar so that they gathered like clouds. Furthermore, from the crown of his head, he again emitted pure light that shone upon the sick bhikṣu. When the light touched his body, his suffering was immediately healed; the ulcer burst open, and the pus and blood were entirely purified. He joined his palms in homage, sought refuge, and cried out in lamentation and confession: "I pray that the Buddha, out of compassion, will extinguish my grave offenses."

Then Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knelt on his right knee and offered the precious vase; having accepted it, the World-Honored One poured water from his right hand over the bhikṣu’s head and massaged his body with his left hand.
At that time, the chronic illness afflicting the sick bhikṣu was immediately cured by the touch of the Tathāgata’s hand.
Having been restored to health, he felt immeasurable joy and with a sincere heart called out: “Namo Śākyamuni!”
Homage to the Great Compassionate Father!
Homage to the Supreme King of Physicians!
May my bodily illness be healed this very day.

I only pray that the Tathāgata, by the power of his original vows, will compassionately take me into his care and bestow the medicine of the Dharma to eliminate the ailments of my mind, so that all my heavy obscurations may be extinguished without remainder.
At that time, the Buddha said to that bhikṣu:
"I shall now repay the profound kindness you showed me in the past.

He then further expounded for him the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths—suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path—demonstrating their characteristics, exhorting him to practice, and bringing his realization to full perfection.
Immediately, he attained the path of Arhatship, endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, and the great assembly, having heard this account, all fell into a web of doubt, thinking:
"Now the Tathāgata has needlessly exhausted his spiritual merit to wash the sores of this sick bhikṣu, which are festering with pus and blood."
He spoke again, saying:
"I now wish to repay the profound kindness you showed me in the past;
I pray that you will analyze and explain this for the sake of those gathered here."
The Buddha said, "Lord of Devas!

In the distant past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a village named Vardhana. Its soil was exclusively fertile, and its people were mostly wealthy and happy; those who resided therein were all of noble lineage, and they honored a certain elder as their judge."

Not long ago, there was an elderly upāsaka who was suddenly and unjustly plotted against by evil men and brought before the authorities for imprisonment. The public, considering him innocent, went before the court of justice to seek a clear investigation and his release. In the midst of that perilous crisis, he was immediately set free; therefore, I now speak these words.
"Lord of Devas, you should know: was the one who adjudicated the case in the past anyone else?
It was none other than this sick bhikṣu.
As for that upāsaka who narrowly escaped the calamity, he is my very self within this assembly."
Therefore, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, a bodhisattva constantly contemplates repaying even small kindnesses with great rewards, never forgetting them until the attainment of Buddhahood.

When Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had heard the Buddha’s teaching, his heart was filled with great joy; the assembled multitude performed celestial music and each returned to their respective abodes, prostrating before the Buddha and withdrawing.

12. The Origin of the Merit of Reciting the Names of the Triple Gem The twelfth chapter, "The Origin of the Merit of Reciting the Names of the Triple Gem," begins thus: In the past, when the Tathāgata appeared in the world, he expounded for his father, the King, and the great assembly the Dharma-gate of the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha. The Tathāgata was endowed with the thirty-two primary marks and eighty secondary characteristics, manifesting a golden hue and immeasurable radiance.

At that time, five hundred members of the Śākya clan within the assembly beheld the Buddha’s physical marks as being like those of a withered man or a gaunt Brahmin; having seen this, they wailed aloud, tore out their hair, threw their entire bodies to the ground, and vomited blood from their mouths and noses.
The Tathāgata saw this and comforted him, saying:
"Do not wail! I shall speak for you."

In the past, there was a Buddha named Vipaśyin. After he had entered nirvana, during the period of the Semblance Dharma, there was an elder named Candravat who had five hundred sons. They were intelligent and possessed great wisdom, being thoroughly versed in all the secular scriptures and treatises of the world. Their father, the elder, placed his faith in the Triple Gem and constantly expounded the meaning of the Buddha-dharma to his sons; however, the sons held heterodox views and lacked faith.
Later, when his sons were all stricken with a serious illness, the father went before them, wept, joined his palms, and said to his sons:

"You all held wrong views and did not believe in the Buddha-dharma; now you are being cut and sliced by the sharp blade of impermanence. Your lives are but a moment—upon what can you rely for refuge?"
"Now there is a Tathāgata named Vipaśyin; you should single-mindedly recite his name.
Having heard this, the sons immediately followed the instruction, chanting "Namo Buddha," and chanting the names of the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Having announced that he had passed away, because of his mindfulness of the Buddha, he was immediately reborn in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings;
when his lifespan there ended, due to the causes and conditions of his former wrong views, he fell back into hell.

The rakshasa wardens of hell pierced his eyes with hot iron forks; while undergoing this agony, he remembered his father’s instruction and invoked "Namo Buddha. By virtue of this, he was spared from the hell and emerged, taking birth among humans as one who is poor and lowly.

"Later, when the Tathāgata Śikhin appeared in the world, I encountered him as well; yet I only heard his name and did not behold the Buddha's form. This continued through the successive appearances of the six Buddhas—Viśvabhū Buddha, Krakucchanda Buddha, Kanakamuni Buddha, and Kāśyapa Buddha—wherein I only heard their names and failed to see them all."
Because you have heard the names of the six Buddhas, you are now born into the Śākya clan together with me.

My body is the color of Jāmbūnada gold, whereas you see me as a greyish and emaciated Brahmin; all this is due to your past slighting and disparaging of the Buddhas, and your deep attachment to false views, which have brought about these heavy obstacles.

Now you should recite the names of the Buddhas of the past, as well as my name, the name of Maitreya Buddha, and the name of your father; having recited them, prostrate yourself and, before the great assembly and the virtuous Saṃgha, cast down your body with its five limbs to confess and repent for the sin of your wrong views.

Having received these instructions, the people completed their repentance; their past calamities were dissipated and their three karmas became pure. They beheld the Buddha’s physical form as golden in color, majestic and sublime like Mount Sumeru, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics and immeasurable radiance. Overjoyed and leaping for gladness, they attained the first fruit of the path. Seeking ordination under the Buddha, they gradually realized the fruit of Arhatship, becoming possessed of the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"After my parinirvāṇa, if one invokes my name and the names of the various Buddhas, the merit and reward obtained will be immeasurable and boundless. Ānanda!"

Observe the Tathāgata as he travels along the road: he causes the high places of the great earth to become low and the low places to become high, making all uneven terrain perfectly level. Once the Buddha has passed through, the features of the ground return to their original state.

All the trees and forests lean toward the Buddha; the tree spirits manifest their forms and bow in reverent salutation. After the Buddha has journeyed through them, the trees and forests return to their former positions.

All hills, ravines, pits, mounds, foul impurities, tiles, gravel, thorns, and brambles are entirely cleared away and swept clean; various flowers are strewn upon the ground, emitting a most fragrant and exquisite scent.

Furthermore, when the Tathāgata treads upon a long path, even insentient things such as earth and wood all incline themselves in reverence; how much more so should sentient beings not always show respect? Why is this?

When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I did not give rise to arrogance toward any sentient beings; rather, I humbled myself to welcome them and cause them joy. By virtue of these wholesome karmas, having attained buddhahood, both sentient and insentient beings alike incline and bow their heads in reverent salutation whenever the Buddha walks.

In the past, I once offered my vast assets with a pure mind to the Sangha of the ten directions; by virtue of these causes and conditions, I have now attained Buddhahood, and wherever I go, the land is expansive, majestic, and pure.

Furthermore, in the past, toward my noble and holy companions in the holy life, I leveled and swept the roads and fully provided dwellings and requisites with plastered decorations; at all times, I joyfully sought the Buddha-way to benefit and bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, so that wherever I went, the place naturally became pure.

Furthermore, Mount Sumeru is eighty-four thousand yojanas in height and breadth, and its depth within the great ocean is equal to that measure. As for Mount Cakravāḍa, it is one hundred twenty-eight thousand yojanas in height and is as firm as vajra, indestructible; yet when the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa, there is nothing that does not lean toward the Buddha to pay homage. Were it to attempt to avoid leaning and remain upright, such a thing would be impossible.
Furthermore, the mind of the Buddha-Tathāgata is pure and free from defilement; wherever he walks, his feet remain unstained and are not harmed by insects or ants.
There are three reasons why the Buddha does not wear sandals:

first, to cause those who walk behind him to give rise to few desires; second, to manifest the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of his feet; and third, to cause those who see him to feel joy in their hearts.
Furthermore, when the Buddha walks, his feet remain four inches above the ground for three reasons:
first, out of compassion for the insects and ants on the ground; second, to protect the living plants upon the earth; and third, to manifest the Buddha’s supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*).
"You monks, you should practice in accordance with the Buddha’s words and follow the teachings; thus you shall reach the end of suffering.
**Chapter Thirteen: The Origin of the Superior Reward of Building Stūpas** The Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"I shall now briefly explain, before this great assembly, the merit obtained from building stūpas. You should listen attentively and reflect upon it well."

Suppose that all the grasses, trees, and forests filling the four continents were transformed into human bodies, and each of those individuals resolved their minds to practice, attaining according to their realization either the fruit of a *srotāpanna*, a *sakṛdāgāmin*, an *anāgāmin*, an *arhat*, or the fruit of a *pratyekabuddha*.

At that time, there was an elder who, with a mind of pure giving, provided food, drink, clothing, bedding, and medicine for a long period; throughout the rest of his life, he ensured they lacked nothing. Furthermore, after their parinirvāṇa, he erected stūpas and shrines for each one, adorned them extensively with silk canopies, banners, and streamers, and made various offerings of incense, flowers, lamps, and ointments.
"Ānanda! Is the merit and reward obtained by this person not great?
"It is very great, World-Honored One!"
The Buddha said,
“Ānanda! Although this great householder has obtained merit, it is still limited.”

It is not as good as if someone, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, with a heart of veneration and longing, were to seek even a single relic as minute as a mustard seed and construct a stūpa to enshrine it for worship, the size of which is exactly equal to an *āmra* fruit.

The central wooden pillar of the stupa is as straight and firm as a needle; atop it is placed a dew-dish (āmalaka) shaped like a jujube leaf. Within it is installed a Buddha image the size of a grain of barley, to which one may offer worship according to one's means with either incense or lamps.
Ānanda! The meritorious deeds performed by that householder cannot be compared to the cultivation of a Buddhist stūpa. To speak in brief:

even if the superior rewards resulting from the construction of a stūpa were divided into a hundred parts, the former would not equal even one; it would not equal one part in ten million, nor one part in a hundred billion, nor indeed could it be known through calculation or analogy.

Ānanda! You should know that the Tathāgata, through the accumulation of practice and cultivation over kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, has brought forth the merits of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañca-dharmakāya*): namely, the constituent of morality (*śīla-bhāga*), the constituent of concentration (*samādhi-bhāga*), the constituent of wisdom (*prajñā-bhāga*), the constituent of liberation (*vimukti-bhāga*), and the constituent of the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimukti-jñāna-darśana-bhāga*). Furthermore, his four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), difficult practices and ascetic austerities for the benefit of self and others, and his inconceivable supernormal powers and power of vows are such that none in the mundane or supramundane realms can surpass them.
Why is this? It is because the Buddha has attained immeasurable and boundless true wisdom. Ānanda!
In the past, when all Tathāgatas were on the stage of practice, they knew that the nature of the realm of sentient beings is intrinsically pure, yet it is shrouded by adventitious afflictions;
nevertheless, it is ultimately beyond being defiled.
"For this reason, the Tathāgata has appeared in the world to preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma for all sentient beings, removing all defilements and impurities so that they may attain liberation.

14. The Origin of the Merit of Leaving Home (The Fourteenth Chapter on the Origin of the Merit of Leaving Home). When the Buddha was in the world, there was an elder in the city of Rājagṛha named Puṇyavardhana. He was over a hundred years old; his teeth had decayed and his strength was exhausted, such that everyone in his household, both young and old, could not help but feel weary of him.

Upon hearing the teaching on renunciation, one’s heart gives rise to joy; its merit is immeasurable and beyond the reach of analogy. The benefits of renunciation are higher than Mount Sumeru, deeper than the great ocean, and vaster than empty space.

Why is this so? It is because one attains Buddhahood precisely through leaving the household life; among all the Buddhas of the three periods of time, there has never been one who attained Buddhahood without first abandoning home and going forth as a renunciant.

At that time, the elder came to where the Buddha was with the desire to seek ordination. Encountering the Buddha while he was wandering and teaching, he went instead to Śāriputra; however, seeing that he was already advanced in age, Śāriputra did not accept him.
In this manner, he visited all five hundred arhats, yet none were willing to ordain him.

At that time, the elder went outside the monastery and wailed aloud. Thereupon, the World-Honored One followed after him and, through various exhortations and instructions, caused his heart to find joy; he then said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Admit him into the monastic order and confer the precepts upon him."
Because he was constantly harassed by the playful pranks of newly ordained junior bhikṣus, he threw himself into the water, intending to end his life.
Maudgalyāyana perceived this and, using his supernormal powers, immediately reached out to place him upon the bank.
When asked the reason for this, he explained it in full as stated above:
"This man is so dull-witted and prone to such anger that he cannot be tamed or transformed by the fear of retribution in the three miserable realms; there is no way for him to attain the Way."

At that time, Maudgalyāyana wished to travel through the air; he therefore instructed [the woman] to focus her mind and grasp the corner of his *kāṣāya*. Gradually they traveled until they reached the shore of the great ocean, where she saw a beautiful woman who had recently died. A worm then emerged from the woman's mouth and entered through her nose; it then emerged from her eye and entered through her ear. Having seen this, Maudgalyāyana abandoned her and departed.
The disciple asked,
"Who is this person? The Master replied:

"This was the wife of a great merchant in the city of Śrāvastī. Relying on her own beauty, she failed to cultivate meritorious deeds; harboring malice toward all whom her husband favored, she accompanied him here and perished by drowning. The sea did not accept her corpse, which washed ashore; yet, out of attachment to her former body, she has become this insect. Hereafter, she shall enter hell and undergo various retributive sufferings."

Proceeding gradually forward, he saw a woman who had taken off her clothes and entered a large cauldron filled with mud and water over a blazing fire; her skin and flesh separated from her bones, which she blew upon until they were restored to form, whereupon she took her own flesh and ate it.
Fuzeng asked the Master, "Who is this?
The Master replied:

"In the city of Śrāvastī, there was a lay follower who held the Triple Gem in high esteem and invited the Saṃgha for offerings. He would regularly prepare exquisite meals and send them via a maidservant; whenever she reached a secluded spot, she would select the finest portions to eat first."
Everyone questioned her:
"Did you not steal food?
The maidservant said:
"Monk, when you have finished eating, give me the leftovers so that I may eat them;
if I were to eat first, I vow that in a future life I shall eat my own flesh.
Because of these causes and conditions, he first received this "flower-retribution," while the actual "fruit" awaits him in hell.
Next, proceeding further, he saw a mountain of bones, seven hundred yojanas in height and breadth, which obstructed the sunlight and caused the sea to turn dark.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana ascended this mountain, where a great rib was moving back and forth as he walked up and down.
Puṇyavardhana said to his teacher,
"What mountain of bones is this?
[The teacher replied,] "If you wish to know, it is the skeletal remains of your own former body."
Upon hearing this, Puṇyavardhana’s body hair stood on end and he was overcome with such terror that sweat poured from him; he addressed his preceptor, saying:
“I have heard this, yet my heart has not yet been rent asunder; I pray you, teach me at once the full account of its origins and causes!”
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“The cycle of birth and death revolves without end, and the retribution for good and evil deeds follows like a shadow or an echo without fail.
Long ago, in a past life, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a village where the people and their wealth were abundant.”

At that time, there was an elder named Dharmavardhana, whose family lineage had long been devoted to the Triple Gem. He delighted in practicing benevolence and kindness, never harming living beings. The local people elected him as their magistrate; for several decades, the people and all things were peaceful and prosperous, and they all relied upon his virtue as if he were their own father.

At that time, the local magistrate, perhaps finding leisure, might take up games of chance; a wicked friend would then find an opportunity to draw near and assist him, imparting perverse doctrines and causing him to neglect his administrative duties.
Not long after, within the borders, the powerful and wicked became wanton and oppressive; lawsuits were brought forward one after another, yet punishments were not meted out with justice.

Suddenly, on one occasion, when the officials presented the full details of the cases, it happened that the magistrate was preoccupied with losing at dice and had no leisure to examine them; he ordered all of them to be executed.
The following day, he asked his military officers,
"Where is the criminal?
They replied that he had already been executed.
Upon hearing this, the magistrate fainted and fell to the ground; only after being sprinkled with water did he revive. Shedding tears, he said:
"All my loved ones and precious treasures remain here, while I alone must enter hell. I have now killed a man so recklessly that I must be considered of the *caṇḍāla* class."
Having formed this thought, he immediately passed away and was reborn in the great ocean as a makara fish, his body reaching a length of seven hundred yojanas.
The Buddha said, “Maudgalyāyana!

If various officials and subordinates, relying on their own power and prestige, oppress and plunder the people’s property and slaughter countless beings, they will at the end of their lives mostly fall into the form of the great makara fish. They will be surrounded and devoured by small insects; as their bodies itch, they rub against mountains, and the blood of the insects will pollute the sea, flowing for a hundred li until the water becomes entirely crimson.
That fish sleeps for a hundred years at a time; when it awakens, it draws in water as if pouring a great river.

At that moment, a group of merchants gathering treasures happened upon the fish with its mouth agape; their boat sped as if flying toward it, about to enter the fish’s belly, whereupon the merchants cried out in lamentation, all together in one voice: "Namo Buddha!"
Upon hearing the Buddha’s name, the fish closed its mouth and ceased its thirst; through the Buddha’s compassionate protection, the merchants were saved from death.
At that time, the Makara fish died of thirst, and various yakṣas, rākṣasas, and water deities vied with one another to drag the fish’s body out and place it upon the seashore.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, having completed his journey together with his disciple, the bhikṣu Puṇyavardhana, returned to the presence of the Buddha. Prostrating with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he was filled with immeasurable joy; he deeply realized the impermanence, suffering, and emptiness of birth and death, exhausted all fetters of existence, and attained the fruit of arhatship.
The Garland of the Previous Births of the Bodhisattva, Fascicle Four.
The Garland of the Previous Births of the Bodhisattva, Fascicle Five.
Composed by the Noble Vīrasena and others.

Translated by the Imperial Decree by Śāstrin Śīladeva Hui-xun, Dharma Master of Extraordinary Talent for Translating Scriptures, concurrently serving as Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial and Grand Master of the Song Dynasty: Just as the nature and function of the power of bondage are vast, so too the power of ultimate truth reaches the limit of the exhaustion of outflows;

the arising of roots of goodness distances one from those inversions, being tranquil according to reality and without diminution. The characteristics of the true cause and its benefits are pure and bright; through fervent and noble cultivation, one increases supreme offerings.
In this way, as villages are established and expanded in various places, they undergo successive changes; yet, at the limit of ultimate practice, they are harmonious and free from strife.

Bestowing gifts without inversion leads to awakening free from strife; thus, by remaining in the middle and distancing oneself from the two extremes, it is excellent that their intrinsic nature is thus harmonized.

The devas delight in his perfection of giving; through long nights of diligence, he has fulfilled the ultimate truth. The wisdom of sentient beings arises because of the World-Honored One; thus, his physical marks are supreme and perfectly complete.
The practice of giving through the movement of non-contention is vast and pure; the physical marks of the Tathāgata are truly supreme.
This concludes the eleventh section on the meaning of the Jātaka of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, concerning the Bodhisattva’s practice of giving as adornment.

The true marks of a great man are harmonious and unchanging; that is to say, they consist in following and hearing the bodhisattva practices, initiating a state of tranquility and immutability in accordance with the Dharma attained by oneself, and the perfect cultivation of the vast Brahma-conduct.

In that place, one further cultivates wholesome karma of non-arising, hears the profound and superior sublime practices, understands the matters of instruction and veneration, and hears the accomplishment of the fundamental self-nature.

Abiding in the supreme tranquility of the past, he tames sentient beings and bears their heavy burdens; his conduct is authentic and his speech is truthful, ensuring that even those sentient beings possessed of excessive anger do not give rise to such thoughts.

Furthermore, there is this situation: when the phenomena of ultimate reality give rise to anger, for such a person who possesses the moral virtue of a trainee (*śaikṣa*), the transformation of painful sensations will have no end.

Having thoroughly understood the nature and limits of saṃsāra, one practices generosity and respectful service without desiring results; relying upon the perfection of peaceful bliss, the cessation of conceptual signs and the fluctuations of change is mastered through supreme wisdom.

In this state, those in training emerge from afflictions; such a Dharma teacher is the true cause for the birth of mastery, possessing non-perverted meaning and truthful speech, with an intention free of signs that perfectly extinguishes evil, reaching the limitlessness where all perverted dharmas are exhausted.
At that time, those afflictive obstructions are stilled and brought to rest, far removed from verbal expression and consisting of true speech.
How does one go beyond the limit of suffering regarding a young girl?
By being unstirred by passion, the one in training remains far removed.

What is the root of defilement? It is the power of craving and desire, which is so intense that it cannot be stopped; it increases, undergoes transformation, and seeks out the exhaustion of defiled obstructions. Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) as non-erroneous, the suffering and bondage of a maiden are likewise [illusory]. By practicing the cause of tranquility, one understands non-contention; through supreme generosity, one understands non-binding; and by practicing in stillness, one remains free from erroneous speech.

The assembly of Brahmā engages in superior debate; their wisdom, which accords with the perfection of seeing the nature of reality, leaves nothing uncomprehended. Those in training (śaikṣa) distance themselves from worldly things and obtain a preceptor (upādhyāya); they possess the power to destroy the causes of such perversions and can compose treatises. They establish the protocols for instructors (śāstṛ), ācāryas, and ordination masters (karmavācanā-ācārya). Through these perfect actual causes, they engage in non-perverted discourse regarding those disputes. Being well-purified, they bring cessation and are able to sever the bonds of defilement. Thus, through the skillful means of emptiness, they understand that the nature of liberation is pure.
How does one thoroughly comprehend karmic activity?

Wisdom that understands the phenomena of non-transmigration is called supramundane. To understand in this way all stūpas, temples, and the causes of merit for Brahmā—hearing that this true cause increases the nature of the higher realms and results in the retribution of heaven, which is associated with non-anger—and thus seeking such purity in one's own state; this is how one comprehends.

This teaching is received and sheltered like a canopy; seeking to cultivate practice, one relies upon teachers and friends. Being thus instructed by such virtuous and excellent persons, one abandons the causes of violence and cultivates the practice of the ultimate truth. To understand such sincerity as this is difficult to attain.

The Bodhisattva dwells peacefully in this state, fully endowed with it; the Bodhisattva’s coarse tendencies are absent, their conduct is free from inversion, and their mind is untainted by bondage. They have departed from the path of the Pratyekabuddhas and emerged from darkness and pure arrogance.
How is it that the bonds of the mark of emptiness are as vast as clouds, making it difficult for ordinary beings to escape?

The profound Dharma is supreme and difficult to attain; it gives rise to conceptions beyond the reach of discursive thought, entering it only through the sincere words and instructions of the Bodhisattvas.

I was born among the assembly of Great Brahmās; far removed from the human realm, they are free from calamity and misfortune. Because of these sincere causes, such characteristics are established: being free from inverted seeking, practicing the ten virtuous actions, and being untainted by the bonds of sorrow and suffering. With a body naturally pure and bright, one attains the retribution of purity.

In this state, the Bodhisattva’s verbal instructions convey the meaning of the coolness of the precepts; they abide in tranquility with unerring, expansive, and empty modes of practice, receiving from the teacher the exposition of the characteristics of emptiness and stillness.
How do sentient beings obtain the causal conditions for the ten wholesome karmic paths through the instruction of a teacher?
How do they distance themselves from the four extremes of existence, emptiness, annihilation, and permanence?
And how is it that they distance themselves from causelessness?

There is a worldly cause called inverted karma; sentient beings, lacking knowledge, do not understand the root of inversion. They create the conceit of "I," their eyes failing to see clearly, as the torrential flow of inversion increases and they wander through saṃsāra. Through shifting and intensified cultivation, the view of self arises; lacking the intention for ultimate truth, they cultivate the inversion of self in emptiness, performing actions that are dull and obscured by the disputes of afflictions. To perceive those defilements clearly and thus bring them to natural stillness—this is the way it is.

One's own purity and lineage are free from pride; the *sattva* remains unchanging while craving and sensation increase; lacking the wisdom of cultivation, one dwells in sinful karma; thus, there is no cause for the non-cultivation of giving.

Having fully understood the pure intention of the bodhisattva’s practice, the preceptor speaks these words of instruction: "If one lacks the intent to cultivate [the path] and the habitual tendencies of self-grasping increase, there is no such principle and no distinct virtuous conduct; if one does not seek the fundamental teachings, it is improper. To regard the self as supreme and subject to transformation, to cultivate perverted perceptions, and for anger to remain unchecked—knowing that such things are entirely unreal and like an illusion—one should give rise to roots of goodness and distance oneself from false dharmas."
In this place there is a preceptor who has completely understood and mastered all inverted speech.
Excellent, son of good family!
The great brāhmaṇa, possessing exceptionally sublime physical marks, sought the practice of perfect tranquility.
How does one cultivate the path of the virtuous and peaceful Dharma?
One listens and understands that there is no characteristic to be cultivated, and proceeds toward the perfection of the side of pure meaning.
"O noble son! Being free from afflictions oneself, one may peacefully listen to and cultivate such tranquil and sublime benefits.

That sovereignty of the devas is the harmonious manifestation of a true mahāpuruṣa; it is obtained through stillness rather than through separate exertion. Such causal characteristics are perfected through the power of the Noble Ones, remaining far removed from the causal practices of the Śrāvaka vehicle of the Hīnayāna, while the worldly manifestations and modes of speech are predominant."
The twelfth section on the meaning of the *Jātaka* concerning the Bodhisattva’s Ornamentation through Generosity, when the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla was reborn as a Brahmā:

If his afflictions were truly bound, yet he possessed the sovereign power to cultivate the supramundane path—namely, by hearing in accordance with the true ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), understanding worldly benefits through wisdom, and remaining far removed from fundamental ego-conceit (*asmimāna*).

The Bodhisattva bestows the Dharma that is free from difficulty to rescue those afflicted by calamities; because he thoroughly understands the laws of kings and the flow of afflictions, he practices secret conduct and brings his egoism to rest.

The compassionate father of the world, this Great Man, nurtures his children with kindness; by his very nature, he impartially and fully understands the process of change and transformation. He accords with the meritorious dharmas of the vehicles of teaching, following the path that is free from cyclic flow. Adorned with an understanding of the causal practices of the world, the reality expounded by his teachings is the true single body.

This is the practice of transformation, analogous to the breaking down of phenomena; in this state, there is no wisdom that fails to perceive hunger and thirst, and it is difficult to understand the causal system of quiescence.

Cultivating in this manner, the nature of physical forms is free from bondage and inversion; there are no ten unwholesome paths, and one honors the practices of the Triple Gem in a state devoid of craving. Through wisdom, one realizes the actual reality of the past; regarding supreme virtue, there is nothing that is not clearly perceived.

One who practices the cultivation of tranquility and performs those acts of giving is called "the eye. In such a state, one is far removed from superior ignorance; yet, regarding the true Triple Gem, they are unable to know it. Such a place is truly obscure; not knowing that the root cause of defilement is thus, in this state, one understands the three characteristics within the Brahma-world.
What is the absence of goodness? It is the inability to cease the active manifestation of afflictions; it is the state far removed from those inverted practices.

I myself establish the speech of the Brahma-multitude, personally cultivating the noble and virtuous Brahma-conduct to perfection. In that pure place, dwelling in tranquility, one listens and hears; the assembly of Brahma-kings perfects their practice. In that place, that Brahma-multitude cultivates the practice of giving (*dāna*); everywhere they delight in the purity of their own nature, seeking the conduct of the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*) which is wholesome, pure, and immovable. It is tranquil, perfected, most supreme, and increases further and further toward the highest excellence.
The meaning of the Tathāgata-nature is free from notions of enemy or friend; possessing power and mastery, one cultivates the practice of tranquil abiding.

The assembly of Brahmās perceives this with their eyes fully open; through seeking it, they may attain vast physical marks. Their wisdom and understanding cultivate actions free from causal defilements of mind; having eliminated all desire-taints regarding the manifestation of signs and characteristics, they are like Arhats.
How do sentient beings become free from inverted calamities? Their minds are tranquil and devoid of the causes of material forms;

they initiate the practice of deeds according to the principles of Dharma and benefit, and through the non-arising of cyclic existence, they listen to the holy teachings. With a superior cause of aspiration, they rely upon the king; understanding peace and happiness as the distinct natures of each, this is due to the ten wholesome actions. Relying on the compassionate mother, they achieve the excellence of the essential nature. Abiding without thirst or lack, with no need for further bestowal and no power to arise [from elsewhere], by relying on the compassionate mother, they obtain peace and happiness.

The King possesses vast knowledge and vision that subdue [the mind]; he brings peace to the four directions. Like a mother who loves her children, he causes all disputes to cease; through harmony, he gives rise to auspicious matters. Free from the darkness of bondage, ego-clinging, and inversion, he is like an Arhat.
The three root afflictions—greed, hatred, and delusion—are absent within this preeminent lineage; like the moonlight, it is bright, unobstructed by clouds, serene, and lovely.
Such is the true benefit of hearing [the Dharma].

The King’s physical marks and countenance are lovely and of supreme excellence; yet, because he perceives no benefit therein, such recognition does not arise. His palace and women are beyond compare in their beauty, yet he remains pure, superior, untainted, and free from desire. It is in this state that he practices giving with a mind of true sincerity.

The King of Magadha has come to this abode; his power is most supreme, pure and unstained. Having abandoned darkness, pride, and fear, he is able to destroy craving and desire. He has attained the secret discourse of the Tathāgatagarbha and a mind of equanimity; he understands the limits of the cycles of the three worlds. Relying upon that which is like the earth—its color fresh and clean, its fragrance perfect—he accords with the majestic regulations of form and appearance, namely the Mahāyāna Mahāparinirvāṇa. It is replete with various perfections and endowed with merit; having heard and retained the sūtras, he understands them with blazing clarity. In this system, there is no inverted thought.
How can there arise, without cause and without distinction, the wisdom that produces the ten wholesome dharmas of meaningful benefit?
What is the characteristic of the cause?

It is the true tranquility free from prideful form; it is the harmonious union of pure, wondrous merit and virtuous purity; it is the cessation of defilement and the perfection of functional power. By cultivating the four foundations of mindfulness through the ten pure wholesome deeds, one reaches a state where the intense proliferation of ignorance and inversion ceases, and where the various bitter afflictions of this world—abiding in hunger, thirst, and the extremes of existence—are brought to harmony.
The king, having departed from desire, performs pure and wondrous acts of giving; yet he practices with autonomy according to the dharmas of affliction, craving, bondage, and dullness.

The bhikṣu, whose root is the most excellent vessel for sublime application, dwells at the limit of the three periods within the locus of the fundamental view of self. He obstructs the practice of the saṃbhogakāya and creates unwholesome karma; being the root of calamity, he lacks the conduct of noble sages. The celestial maidens exercise their sovereignty, remaining far removed from the human realm.
This is the practice of the non-cultivation of reality; not cultivating the ten wholesome actions is called ignorance.

In the locus of sincerity, one expounds the True Dharma, causing the mind to rejoice and wisdom to arise. When the mental consciousness is pure and subtle, it accords with the world; thus, through the mastery of this sincere mental consciousness, the inexhaustible meaning of its own nature is produced, accomplishing the unerring secret practice.
They are fully endowed with the hearing and retention of those excellent and wondrous dharmas; their fundamental discourse is the most sublime among gods and humans.

They cultivate the practice for reaching the other shore, that which is practiced by the noble ones. Bearing such heavy responsibilities, they advance in this way; through long-term causal practices, they remain far removed from alarm and fear. They preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma, which others hear and practice; their fundamental and supreme conduct is truly the causal practice of giving. They purely and excellently increase their cultivation without substitution over the long term; they receive and honor the teachings without giving rise to delusion. Exhausting the hindrances of affliction is called the conduct of the noble ones.

Regarding the limit of the practice of the most sublime and supreme generosity, it is a cause of purity free from defiled activity; its fundamental basis is a mind devoid of longing, and its manifestations lack reality, appearing only as they do to the mind. This ultimate truth is called pure conduct.

The torrential stream is long-lasting, fearful, and difficult to cultivate; its characteristics are inverted, its location cold and harsh. Dull, weak, and ignorant, one lacks self-cultivation; yet one honors tranquility, dwells in seclusion, maintains the precepts and disciplinary conduct, and stills the sound of anger—the mind is fundamentally without marks.

The sovereign’s mastery consists of the true practice of governance through correct methods; it is the fundamental cultivation of the functional power of the five aggregates. Its characteristics, nature, and realms—whether good or evil—are like the fundamental afflictions that bind; they rely everywhere upon a mind of hunger and thirst. When disputes and litigation have completely ceased and no longer arise, there is no further need for the cultivation of those constituent parts.

The supreme Dharma is terrifying and difficult to practice; its obstacles and afflictions are boundless. There is pure conduct that cuts the root of craving, yet it is difficult for such a state to arise amidst inverted appearances. Its power is difficult to restrain and no ignorance can subdue it. There is pure giving free from the mind of desire; its application is vast and honored by the devas. Possessing complete mastery, defiled inversion does not arise; its nature is inherently benevolent and virtuous, giving rise to sentient beings. Such is the purity, benefit, and sincerity of this meaning.
What is the manner in which their mental disposition is like the harmonious union of the devas?

It is the superior purpose of seeking the cause of liberation and attaining the fruit of *aśaikṣa*. In that place, there is a vast kingdom and realm, possessing its own methods for self-discipline and state governance; the people look up to it with unceasing longing, and their speech is autonomous and truthful.
What is the meaning of clearly understanding and knowing the intention associated with the absence of defilement and evil?

Through fervent cultivation, obstacles are exhausted and one is unbound; yet, due to the causes of afflictions, one performs worldly activities that constitute defiled and evil karma. That movement of transport arises dependent upon wisdom; cause and effect are not non-existent, as there is superior discourse. A compassionate mother speaks words from heaven that may be taken as a model; giving is the true cause, practiced in accordance with the Dharma. The nature of harmony is without the cause of dispute; one acts in reliance upon this.
