The royal system remains unmoved in remote regions; the Bodhisattva’s original cause is a rigorous seclusion. The four fruits and the stage of no-more-learning are the perfection of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The teachings of the supreme Dharma are cherished by the devas; their rarefied appearance brings joy and immovability. Tranquil and free from contention, they are as cool as the moon. Having constructed the truth, they remain far removed from the causes of dispute. Their corresponding aspirations possess merit and wisdom; the fundamental teachings are relied upon and followed by the devas. Out of compassion for sentient beings, they flow through saṃsāra without ceasing; in this state, desire and greed are the highest form of inversion.

Fully endowed with the noble dharmas, all causes of defilement are exhausted; fully endowed with hearing and retention, they diligently seek the true Dharma; through generosity and compliance, their renown is sovereign; this supreme secret cannot be destroyed by Māra.

The king cherishes the tranquility of distant realms; he exercises sovereign mastery over transformations and solemn compositions. The origins and consequences of calamities are strictly stilled; herein, wisdom remains far removed from the torrential flow of inverted attachments, defilements, and various types of pride.

The Bodhisattva practices the cultivation of the branches of tranquility; seeking the cause, they bring the unbroken mind to rest. Emptiness is inherently quiescent as they seek their own peace; bearing the burden of human existence, they take the compassionate mother as their foundation, until the name of sovereignty is attained and afflictions are brought to a final end.
The King is the one capable of subduing greed, hatred, delusion, and various forms of arrogance; he brings to rest the host of sentient beings afflicted by hunger and thirst.
The Bodhisattva, possessing a supreme and pure self-nature, attains a body that embodies the true reality of sentient beings.

When a king thus cultivates and honors his fundamental practice, he truly overcomes calamities, perversions, and fetters; he severs the ten root-floods of affliction through the performance of impartial giving; and he attains the majestic, powerful, non-contentious, and true nature of the pure realm.

That which is heard is the cause for the state of a learner (*śaikṣa*); the foundation of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is established as inexhaustible; it flows in accordance with the turning of existence, being unshakable and supreme; the root of the ten wholesome paths is supreme through its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); the afflictions of desire and greed are without bondage and undergo transition; at the proper time, one truly honors and cultivates the practice of giving; such is the case regarding disputes, for they possess no wisdom.
To subdue calamities and bring about tranquility, and to thoroughly understand the fundamental nature of heedlessness through insight—this is the unsurpassed instruction for Bodhisattvas.
Why is it that the afflictions of the mental ground are so difficult to sever?

Seeking the unreal, one performs boundless activities; like a mother nurturing her child, protection is the purpose. One realizes the dharma of the tranquility of sentient beings through the power of selflessness and the influence of virtuous friends. One accomplishes the perfection of fearlessness and tranquility—the ten types of wholesome dharmas at the limit of mastery—and by obstructing the meaning of impurity, one further gives rise to speech.

In boundless cultivation and veneration within the uninhabited realms, one seeks the invisible and boundless causal conduct; the true nature of past karma can be attained by following the cessation of pride. Through pure instruction, one rectifies the delusions of sentient beings; with wisdom, one understands the matter of threading the needle. When sentient beings hear this, the limits of defilement are exhausted; this is the cause for delighting in the flow of conditioned existence.

Fully understanding the faults and afflictions of sentient beings, in this place the king bestows gifts upon the people; while they dwell in tranquility, he seeks their transformation; with wisdom he understands and strives for liberation; and through meditative concentration and wisdom, he cultivates the marks of excellence.

In this way, the bodhisattva brings rest to their fetters and bestows the true benefit upon sentient beings; they practice giving with mastery, fulfill the retention of what has been heard, and cultivate the excellence of renunciation through detachment.

When the Bodhisattva initiates instruction and guidance, at that time the king and the people delight in giving and practice with wholehearted intent, relinquishing all secret treasures and precious jewels at once. Sentient beings in such a place are free from arrogance and indolence; therein lies tranquility, where afflictions have no cause and one dwells in ultimate peace. One thoroughly understands that giving has no fixed characteristics; it is quiescent and unmoving like the clarity of the moon. With the torrential flow of afflictions and the virtuous mind both far removed, there is no calamity for those of overweening pride. Since the fundamental state is eternally unborn, one observes the nature of inversion; the locus of transport is thus tranquil.

The true nature of that name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) is characterized by defilement, evil, and bondage; such sentient beings bear this physical form, yet they seek to bring about the cessation of the causes of defilement through pure tranquility, and the cessation of the appearances of pleasure and profit. Through the accomplishment of the fruits of retribution from worldly paths of action, there arise arrogance, food and drink, hunger and thirst, and inversion; being free from affliction, they seek to remain far removed from these.

In the past, during the time of inverted formations, the cessation of shifting appearances and fetters occurred; through pure giving, one sought excellence, cultivating the nature of compassion through corresponding virtuous causes, thereby guarding against the dust, defilements, and calamities of all quarters.

The seeker advances toward the cessation of afflictions; though dust and defilements do not shift, how could there be pure stability? Such limits give rise again to calamities; the cause of these limits is vast and fundamental. One seeks purity with joy and cultivates generosity, following and protecting the instructions for sentient beings.

The king constructed a vast dwelling place; for all sentient beings in the world, the three fundamental virtues—non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion—are the root of goodness. Their intrinsic nature is free from bondage, and thus the calamities of false views truly do not exist.

Compassion guides sentient beings from the afflictions of perversion; thus, one accords with the vast and profound silence, establishing a dwelling that follows and conforms to the Three Jewels. Free from the seeking of malice and the construction of ignorance, it is located where cities fall to the noble ones and where communities gather. It is the manifestation of pure causal practice, the abode of monasteries characterized by *dhyāna* and tranquility.

The self-nature of sentient beings is shifting and changeless; in the four dhyānas, the five desires are stilled. One equally accomplishes fundamental bliss, and at the limit of reality, one accords with the cessation of calamities. The appearances of dust and hunger and thirst are stilled; there is no place for the performance of the ten non-virtues. In every movement—bending, stretching, or rising—there is no darkness or pride. Secretly free from fear, one rests in profound stillness; seeking the unmoving, one perceives its original cause. Through the benefits of the ten virtues, all entanglements are brought to rest.
What is meant by not destroying the true appearance? It is to perform the karmic causes of pure giving;

to employ appropriate vessels according to the ultimate reality; to accomplish the sovereign truth of the secret treasury; and to recognize that the activities of self-nature involve inversion and contention. When the mind is directed toward Bodhi and the ultimate meaning is perfected, one seeks the practice of tranquility at the proper time, abiding peacefully in the root while seeking transformation for oneself.

The learner fulfills pure cultivation through giving; with all their heart, they manifest and honor sacred images. This is the fundamental limit of all acts of giving: past happiness increases and remains unshakable, while in the interim, there is purity and no cause for calamity—this is the singular power of hearing and retaining the teachings.
What are the characteristics and limits of the conceit of self (asmimāna)?

One hears of the various kinds of original intrinsic nature; one seeks pleasure through past karmas. Merit is non-erroneous and far removed from hunger and thirst; the root is without distinction, yet derivative karmas differ. Bound by the fetters of generosity, there is the perversion of craving; such is the reality of the torrential flow of afflictions.

By diminishing disputes and practicing generosity with mastery, one perfects wholesome karma and attains victory; free from dullness, weakness, and pride, one proceeds with vigor and repeatedly practices giving as one moves from place to place.

The world is peaceful, blissful, immovable, and truthful; thus, with such non-erroneous, clear, and lucid knowledge and vision, one is fully endowed with hearing and retention, exhausting all that is supreme, and possessing the true factors of the limbs in their proper extension and contraction.

The fundamental nature of the Buddha-dharma is thus signless; the true foundation of a king’s governance and transformation lies in the reality of its principles. Through the orderly execution of institutions, one attains cessation; pure hearing and disciplined self-mastery are supreme.

Advancing toward the cessation of inverted calamities, one transcends the torrential afflictions and their underlying tendencies; through the most supreme correspondence, wisdom arises, seeking the unerring, tranquil state of detachment.

The boundaries of the king’s realm are tranquil; having brought about the cessation of calamities and misfortunes through seeing and hearing, in this place the Bodhisattva understands them without error and is able to ward off all impure meanings.
Sentient beings perceive that supreme happiness; the King’s craving is truly boundless, yet the cause of their perversion suddenly ceases, as he seeks noble virtue to nurture all classes of beings.

The frontiers are tranquil and one can understand them according to the seasons; all created actions and performances originate from established systems. In this regard, the Bodhisattva acts like a compassionate mother, understanding the proper timing to cease inverted views and increasing superior observation to subdue various beings. Seeking to attain the pure ultimate meaning of hearing and retention, they realize that the root of truth is free from the causes of name-and-form, and thus they practice the nature of giving to subdue inverted views.

The root of immovability is solely the pursuit of giving; merit is ultimately sovereign, tranquil, and peaceful; it increases the delight in pure non-self. One thoroughly understands the nature of the fundamental torrent, as well as the characteristics of hunger, thirst, affliction, and dispute, along with the states of stillness, extremes, dullness, weakness, and pride.

Fully endowed with the nurturing power of a lion king, he possesses a fearless demeanor wherever he goes; his secret causal practice is the intrinsic nature of flexing and extending, and he performs sublime transformations and offerings without pride.
What is the truly superior cause of supremacy?
It is the sublime wisdom that is tranquil, disciplined, and pure, which accords with the speech used in various contexts and remains free from attachment.
What is the non-erroneous transformation of the ultimate truth?

The supreme cause of purity is that the nature of affliction does not arise; such is the sublime purity. The Bodhisattva teaches with mastery, seeking to bestow gifts, and speaks the true word, preaching the Dharma like falling rain.

How does the King exercise his governance? His methods are vast and extensive; he observes the self-nature of the non-contentious Dharma. His purpose is to nurture pure and wondrous causes. He is fully endowed with the root of correct principle and free from error. Through the harmony of his own nature, his person enjoys peace and happiness. In the places where he nurtures others, he engages in boundless cultivation. Hearing and seeing the truth, he seeks out the reality of things, thereby attaining the supreme limit of awakened wisdom.

Thus, the noble Dharma is pure and unbound; its root is complete, free from clamor and agitation. Its intrinsic nature is pure, with afflictions forever severed. The fundamental nature of the cycle of existence is a phenomenon of dullness, weakness, pride, arrogance, and transformation. The root of calamity is thus stilled in tranquility; the reflections of sentient beings are compliant yet devoid of reality.
How does a bodhisattva provide the most supreme instruction?
The nature of actual calamities such as hunger and thirst is a state of perversion.

In past times, sentient beings possessed vast and pure benefit; through the causal practice of giving, they attained sublime tranquility. Sentient beings understood the causal practices of the bodhisattva, initiating the ten wholesome paths and abiding immovably therein. The teachings endowed with virtue were originally non-existent, yet were provisionally established according to the capacities of beings. Such superior causes of the supreme secret are firm and unshakable.

What is the perfection and tranquility of the physical body? It is the accomplishment of true reality through practice, the sovereign limit of non-arising in the ultimate sense. Thus, the Bodhisattva Akṣobhya and the fruit of Arhatship attain purity; they bear the torrential flow of inverted afflictions, and the arising of calamities due to lack of causes is stilled. Observing the pure generosity of sentient beings, this is the power and function of liberation in ultimate tranquility; at that time, one freely cultivates and honors the teachings.

Thus, this view of self is vast and boundless, the source from which the torrential flow of afflictions arises; seeking further to bring about its cessation and distancing oneself from it, one achieves the stage of observation and thorough knowledge.
What is the nature of the taming of sentient beings?

It is the performance of deeds without attachment over vast periods of time; it is a fundamental nature as tranquil as space; and it is the observation that purity benefits both self and others—a state that is supreme, most excellent, and perfectly conformable.

One who possesses the power of practice achieves fearlessness; that is to say, the Mahāyāna understands the absence of bondage. Like a lotus emerging from the water, one carries out causal practices; through the fundamental ultimate truth, one is tamed and purified. By cultivating the karmic causes of giving, one attains wholesome benefits.

The fundamental nature of calamities is the non-practice of giving; one thoroughly understands that defilement and purity do not exist. With supreme subduing and the perfection of equanimity, the self-nature of the ultimate truth is devoid of "this" and "that."

The root of calamity is the practice of giving that is not true; one who follows pure wisdom seeks that which is thus. The nature of quiescence is free from the defilements and bonds of affliction; it is pure and nameless, beyond the transformations of form and mental data.

The power and function of stretching and contracting arise from the aspiration for giving; all sentient beings perceive this as inexhaustible. Following the nature of the supreme cause of such aspiration, those of dull faculties and prideful disposition are inherently incapable; through signless giving, they exhaust their conditioned practices and are able to sever craving by teaching the Dharma of reality.
How is it that the speech of the devas is true?

It is because they cultivate the supreme root cause of non-contention; they practice the fundamental rite of the boundless maṇḍala; they further cultivate the benefit of joy through renunciation; and they eliminate the root of darkness and pride, bringing the inversions to rest.

Seeking cultivation and progress, one fulfills hearing and retention; this fundamental, supreme cause is unerring for devas and humans. Increasing the cultivation of generosity accords with the ultimate truth; this cause of reality accomplishes the foundation.

Seeking the cause of generosity, one’s conduct becomes vast and pure; as the secret foundation, one bears the burden of sentient beings. Through the practice of giving, one cultivates the true secret mantra, wherein the cessation of desire leads to the supremacy of tranquility.

Fully endowed with the pure and supreme cause of hearing and retaining [the teachings], one thus seeks all causes with mastery; through the superior activity of ultimate reality, all calamities naturally cease.

Free from the defilements of bondage and attachment, and transcending the shifting realms of dull and dark afflictions, sentient beings in this state reach the limit of tranquility, possessing power and mastery in accordance with their fundamental nature.

When the causes of defilement and bondage are fully present as one, one understands that sentient beings cease their disputes; through virtuous and skillful practice, one realizes the ultimate truth regarding the calamities of conditioned existence, attaining the purity of generosity within the sovereignty of silent stillness.

The ultimate limit of the power of true intrinsic nature is such that wherever sentient beings may be, their various karmic actions cause them to wander through birth and death with ignorance as their defining characteristic. Upon realizing this ultimate limit, the view of a self is abandoned; the creation of calamities and their secondary afflictions ceases. The locus of harmony is unimpeded like space; one abandons all seeking even for the most sublime food and drink. Thus, the pure teaching possesses the meaning of being a vehicle for transport.

He expounds upon the cessation of the intrinsic nature of all afflictions; seeking the dharma of sovereign tranquility, he practices truthful giving and cultivates pure generosity, thereby perfecting non-contention and distancing himself from the root of perversion.

Seeking the secret meaning in such tranquility, one provides food and drink as verbal instruction; through the supreme burden of giving and tranquility, one truly understands the characteristics of space.

The fundamental mode of activity of the noble ones beyond training is such that the meaning of perfect liberation is equalized; the defilements are stilled and the root of contention is ended. The causal characteristics of contraction and extension give rise to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), while the limits of purity are the karma created in the past. Excessive pride and ignorance are brought to cessation, yet there is no tranquility in following the torrential flow.

The four types of karmic paths—those to be experienced in the present life, those to be experienced in subsequent lives, those to be experienced in future lives, and those of indefinite timing—are all fully mastered through past actions; such is the practice of the pure, ultimate perfection of generosity.

Encountering fire during the cold season carries a sublime significance; this state is the true, fundamental, and non-erroneous reality, wherein name-and-form (nāmarūpa) are integrated and past karma is transcended, serving as the supreme cause for cultivating the path of action.

The gods, seeking pure and wondrous peace and happiness, experience the causes of painful sensation as temporarily non-arising; their pleasure and sovereignty increase their dull arrogance, whereby they thus distance themselves from the functioning of past karma.

When the fetters of the pure and unerring sentient beings' giving naturally subside, the mental states produced by karma from previous lives do not arise; at that boundless time, the Victors receive [the fruit] first. Thus, the Arhats abide in vast purity and ultimate peace; their defilements and fetters are utterly extinguished in the past, and as their physical vessels are pure, there is no cause for affliction. With the intent to discipline sentient beings, they practice giving, thoroughly understanding the tranquility and purity of the world.
What is the manifold delusion of the conceit of "I"? It is the mind's desire to exhaust the fetters and hindrances;

it is the pure basis for the various classes of celestial beings; it is the thorough understanding that the practice of giving is perfectly pure and sublime; it is the realization through the path of the learned sages that there is no contention; it is the performance of disciplined conduct with rigorous regulations; it is the equality of high and low at the limit of happiness; such is the fruition that accords with the teaching, wherein the cause of generosity brings about purity of deportment.

Perfected in virtuous conduct, their activities are tranquil; those of dull faculties and pride are subdued so they do not arise. Having distanced themselves from seeking worldly power and its causes, they truly practice the giving of supreme aspiration. Their appearance is pure, beyond compare even among the devas, and they remain far removed from all calamities.
How is it that the supreme cause is entirely free from defilement?

By ceasing the tendencies of pride through the cultivation of generosity, one reaches the ultimate limit of sentient beings in the pursuit of the unsurpassed state, whereby the clear understanding of wisdom gives rise to instruction.
Regarding the period of purity, how is it truly so?

It is the realization of the perfection of benefit, tranquility, and insight; it accords with the supreme cause for the cessation of conceit; its self-nature is virtuous and its locus is pristine; and it is endowed with the excellence of the teachings, their hearing, and their retention.

Thoroughly understanding that non-perverted giving is inexhaustible, possessing the power of hearing and retaining [the teachings], and excelling in the mastery of both fortune and calamity; the cessation of pride, indulgence, and temporal fluctuations, as well as the establishment of systems for debate, knowledge, and vision.

The cause of practice associated with generosity is non-contention; the characteristics of the fruit of suffering are subdued and stilled. For pure sentient beings, hunger and thirst do not exist; such is the reality that remains far removed from fear.

When both parties are tranquil and free from calamity, and regarding the three categories of dharmas which are the ultimate truth of the world— wherein generosity is paramount and there is no conceit or stinginess—
how can one engage in debate to investigate their essential nature and characteristics?
The root of the desire for the accomplishment of the True Principle is the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), which serves as the basis for the body bound by defilements.
The faculties of inversion are dull and weak; since this dwelling of defilement is fundamentally non-existent, how could there be any transition or change?

The nature of the Tathāgata is the most honored and supreme; cow’s milk serves as a simile for being the foremost among all flavors; the cause of giving is pure and possesses unerring benefit; and the meaning of ethical discipline consists of wholesome and pure speech.

At that time, the king possessed sovereign power and great influence; his domain was vast, and he bestowed gifts even upon those in remote regions. His administration was disciplined and reverent, and his regulations were strict and severe; thus, his actions brought about genuine benefit.

The nature of secret speech is non-existent; the meaning of impermanence lies in the nature of flux and conditioned activity. The complete branches of the mother’s compassionate nurturing bring about the sublime tranquility of the ultimate truth through the discipline of language.

The practice of giving in the world is accomplished through its own nature; how excellent! Possessing wisdom, one brings an end to disputes and litigation. The King of the Frontier speaks of cessation: the cause that does not destroy is the distancing from base views, and the boundless correct principle has the purpose of transporting [beings] across.
What is the supreme, unerring state that is free from difficulty?
It is the fulfillment of extensive learning and the realization of the fundamental nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
*The Garland of the Bodhisattva’s Past Lives*, Fascicle Nine.
The Garland of the Previous Births of the Bodhisattva, Fascicle Ten.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Āryaśūra and others.
Translated during the Song Dynasty by the Imperial Commissioner for Ceremonials, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, [Wang] Xuance.

Translated by the Great Master Fancai (Bianji), Shao De, Hui Xun, and others, by imperial decree: The supreme cause of temporal divisions is the suchness of the primordial limit; the ten wholesome deeds, when cultivated with reverence, leave no further cyclic flow. Fundamental knowledge and vision are fully endowed with hearing and retention; pure wisdom is the true nature of reality. To hear the characteristics [of the teachings] and undertake their practice is to bear the burden of cultivation; to correctly understand their meaning and purpose is difficult to attain even through seeking, for throughout boundless regions, all is tranquil and still.

The bhikṣu remains far removed from fundamental fetters; his practice of giving is perfected and unwavering; his wisdom and understanding increase, leading to the realization of fearlessness; through pure and supreme causes, his giving never diminishes; and the power and function of the limit of tranquility can be attained.

In those still in training (*śaikṣa*), the afflictions (*kleśa*) have ceased; in noble ones who are beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the root and secondary afflictions are forever severed. Yet the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the four floods (*ogha*) remain. Worldly sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*); their fundamental fetters cause them to indulge in heedlessness. Lacking compassionate patience despite possessing power and mastery, they are difficult to liberate from the enveloping obscurations (*paryavasthāna-nīvaraṇa*) as the floods continue in succession. Thus do the fruits of merit and happiness persist in such a manner.
Knowing that those bonds and disputes are the root, one aspires for parinirvāṇa and seeks the meaning of liberation; such is the practice of listening without error.

When the calamities of water, fire, and wind arise in blazing intensity, one understands that they follow from anger, greed, and delusion, while the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally quiescent, profound, and unborn.

The nature of transformation is conditioned and subject to phenomena; the four types of karmic paths for sentient beings in the world—those ripening in the present life, the next life, subsequent lives, or indeterminately—are secret and profound, conforming to the signless, wherein the observance and violation of precepts give rise to reality.

The nature of the Tathāgata is devoid of the meaning of diminution; its self-nature is the purity and clarity of pure ethical discipline. Toward sentient beings in distress, one practices giving with a compassionate mind, such that realization arises spontaneously within the mental ground.

The Dharma of the other shore cannot be attained without cause; the practice of heedfulness can be cultivated by the devas. The root causes and conditions for happiness are the three virtues; when the nature of the realms is created through inversion, [rebirth] does not arise.

The rigorous discipline is pure, wondrous, and lovely; its ultimate limit is known through powerful insight. The manifestation of practicing generosity arises in full perfection; by reverently cultivating the honored image, the conditions for merit are forever firm.

Understanding that hearing is quiescent and as one wishes, because the Three Jewels abide without wavering; this fundamental ultimate truth is far removed from erroneous inversion, for the nature and categories of afflictions abide in stillness and are non-arising.

I see that the root of the predominant afflictions consists of the performance of boundless [non-virtues], which can be abandoned through the power of the Noble Ones; whereas the three roots of virtue—non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion—are incapable of producing the various types of prideful distortions.

For those in training who dwell in tranquility, active defilements do not arise; through the power of their mastery, their ethical discipline and virtue are pure. Their application to hearing the Dharma is superior and well-established, and they take the vast, peaceful Triple Gem as their ninefold object. With wisdom of nine grades, they seek the signless.

The devas, seeking joy, advance in their cultivation to pursue that [state]; they are able to sever craving and preach the Dharma of reality. They remain far removed from the fruits of retribution, where the seeds of causal action—whether existent or non-existent—do not arise. Through the power and function of such supreme dharmas and merits, the entanglements and inversions are entirely exhausted; thus, the shifting and changing of spatial limits and desires come to an end.

Just as those causes and practices for fulfilling virtuous deeds result in the manifestation of a hundredfold images—such as fields, houses, and villages that are exceptionally abundant—and bring about the benefit and peace of the pure teachings.

The self-nature of true suchness is primordially and eternally extinguished; it is without grasping or abandoning, profoundly still and tranquil. The sages of the Three Vehicles are all its virtuous friends, while the mind that is bound is truly inverted.

The nature of the pure realm is the sovereign cessation; one is far removed from the turbulent flows, inversions, and conventional constructs. Through the authentic performance of deeds, one subsequently cultivates and honors [the path], reaching the supreme limit where the fundamental mind is liberated.

Pure, secret, quiescent, and suchness itself, its characteristics do not arise and are difficult to fathom through thought; this ultimate meaning of reality is devoid of self, and such is the sovereign’s knowledge and vision in its creation.

Abiding securely in the True Dharma of equality and non-duality, the practice of the Path is perfected, tranquil and free from fear; sentient and non-sentient beings are by nature eternally quiescent, yet liberation is unborn and the conditioned is difficult to relinquish.
The conceit of "I" and disputes truly undergo transformation; one can sever the very limits where sensual desire resides. Thus, through such rigorous cultivation, one honors the truth.
That Great Being’s past was preeminent; his boundless karmic actions were accomplished through wholesome dharmas, and the wisdom and functional capacity of sentient beings are inexhaustible.
How is it that a compassionate mother’s nurturing is true?

The past, though inverted and defiled, is in truth pure; such is the ultimate reality of this secret treasury. For the awakened one, there is no inversion, and the supreme meaning is perfected; the *vinaya* discipline can thus be received by sentient beings.

The fundamental holy teaching on the perfection of the Buddha-ground states that such defiled wisdom born of wrong views does not arise; through abiding in tranquility and corresponding with the luminous nature of the mind, the ultimate truth emerges and wrong views do not occur, so that by seeking with equanimity, defiled wisdom ceases.

This concludes the section on the meaning of the Jātaka of the Venerable Protector of the Nation, the Bodhisattva practicing the perfection of giving; herein, the twenty-second and twenty-third meanings are combined.

I perceive that the suffering of sensation is a true inversion; its ultimate reality (*tathatā*) and supreme meaning consist in the cessation of activity, which is to say, the accords with hearing the beneficial truth.

That Bodhisattva’s practice of wisdom is preeminent; its various intrinsic natures are unbound and tranquil. He manifests the venerable image while seeking the fruit of fruition; dwelling in stillness, his mind is darkly absorbed and extinguished. In this austere abode, the afflictions are entirely exhausted. Regarding the meaning of the desire for wholesome dharmas among the twenty-two faculties, good and evil are as clear as a shadow following a form; this is a meaning that can be attained, and not one that cannot be attained.

The King’s undertaking is sovereign and expansive; he brings rest to evil and profoundly destroys its defilements. He carries forth living beings with superior characteristics; such a reality is difficult to encounter, for his regulations are most rigorous.

The afflictions have the meaning of being a torrential flood; they manifest as fully endowed karmic fruits and images. Since their self-nature is clearly understood, how could there be any adversaries?

Vast and subject to transformation, they are far removed from perversion. The power and function of giving are grounded in truth; through the perfect veneration of the noble words of mindfulness, one attains the inexhaustible marks of wisdom.

The Mahāyāna vehicle of the teaching of equality is supreme; the fetters of craving obstruct the practice of compassion, yet through the power of mastery there is no fixed transmigration, and one may follow the regulations of unviolated ethical discipline.

The name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is exquisite and translucent like jade; its features support one another with superior craftsmanship. The Bodhisattva is truthful and reliable in both movement and stillness; in this state, self and other are equalized in such a manner.

The power and function arise, and the fruition is accomplished; bound by the love of a compassionate mother, one accords with the remote regions. The various transformations of inverted pride manifest as the body of active bondage, capable of generating disputes. When the lifespan reaches its end, the internal and external are universally equal; in this state, the noble man remains far removed from clamor and contention. He is ultimately able to liberate sentient beings from their fetters, so that the torrential afflictions do not arise in accordance with conditions.

Advancing in the cultivation of the Noble Path, one’s merit becomes firm; by grasping the locus of the inversion of ego-clinging, the ultimate purity of cessation arises. Unified in the eternal and true, listening never ceases;

the mental ground is purified as the veils and obscurations are removed. Suffering, inversion, and slander cease; through that pure, wondrous, and sublime power, both self and other are empowered. The ten root afflictions do not arise, and the constraints of shifting bonds are correctly stilled.
What is meant by the mind being obscured and the power of form being destroyed?

When the true power of karmic retribution is exhausted of itself, the view of self through discrimination is eliminated upon entering the state of a noble one; the various types of conceit are truly ceased in accordance with such vision.

Darkness, dullness, and contentious disputes arise without cause; one follows worldly conventions to practice the ten wholesome deeds. Through the excessive attachment of pride regarding those limits, inverted discrimination determines the reception of karmic fruits.

The forest trees are damaged like the boundless void; having truly received the fruits of cherished branches, they are moistened; the body bears the conceit of "I," which is the root of increase; cause and effect support one another like form and shadow.

Just as space is boundless, tranquil, and unimpeded, so too do the fruits of craving arise from internal causes; without cultivating wholesome dharmas, one has no means of becoming a sage. Tranquility is like space, its locus vast and expansive, giving rise to wholesome causes and their fruits in accordance with reality.

The cessation of the inversion regarding intrinsic purity, the skillful establishment of buddha-activities through the characteristics of sound, the difficulty of being separated from the duration of one's lifespan, and the vast secret that carries both self and others.

Equanimity is a difficult practice when self-clinging is rampant; the pursuit of the perfection of ultimate truth is likewise so. Sentient beings cultivate virtuous conduct with gentleness and joy; such profound, serene purity is exceedingly rare to attain.
What is meant by the mind-factor having *tathatā* (suchness) as its nature?

At each respective moment, it abides in equanimity; ultimate reality is perfected and conditioned activity has subsided. The ten paths of action all arise from the mind; their dull and obtuse root, when examined in its essence, is solely ignorance (*moha*). Both the associated factors and the sovereign [mind] are likewise characterized by obscuration.

The seven and nine types of pride are distinguished; the Tathāgata has forever severed the floods, the roots, and the secondary afflictions. The meaning of the text on giving is what is called the Mahāyāna; the Jewels of the Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha are ultimately and irrevocably steadfast.

The two characteristics of good and evil stand in opposition to one another; one must realize that the time [to encounter them] is vast and difficult to find. To seek the causes for rebirth in the celestial realms, one relies solely on the power of virtue, guarding the locus [of practice] with vigilance and dwelling therein in tranquility.

The limits of transport are explained according to the three vehicles; through the increase of superior power, one thoroughly understands the spiritual friend. When the single type of concordant view of self is eliminated, bondage does not arise, and one dwells in the ultimate truth.

Fully endowed with the power of hearing and retaining the teachings, one bears the burden of the Tathāgata-nature, which may be known by its contact with all things; pure and wondrous name-and-form bring the mind to tranquil abiding, and perfect wisdom brings sublime awakening in peace.

In the ultimate meaning of *nirvāṇa*, both self and other are exhausted; through the power of unified wisdom, dullness and pride are all stilled. With rigorous wisdom, one clearly understands the long night; this great being realizes the true ultimate meaning, seeking the signless, sovereign stillness, and fully perfecting the practice of giving.

Because that cause of transport is free from the meaning of bondage, the accomplishment of that power is the state of equality; the conduct of the cause of vast perversion does not arise, and one respectfully serves and accords with the cultivation of perfected practice.

Thus, supreme and most excellent in the ultimate sense, with lush forest shade and far removed from calamities, possessing the marks of wisdom that understand the secret, they give rise to sovereign and boundless superior causes.

Practicing generosity in the world serves as the cause for the ten wholesome actions; with a mind of perfect sincerity, the Great Being brings them to fulfillment. Through the unerring cultivation of the causes of generosity on the ninth stage, those inverted practices are thoroughly eliminated.

The essential nature of dullness and self-conceit is reality; it fully gives rise to pure and wondrous forms. The vast power of desire and craving is inexhaustible; there is no cause for its removal, and thus birth and death are never ceased.

Following along with afflictions, one loses the resolve of a great man; lacking faith in the words of the Noble Ones, one acts as an ordinary person; at the limits of time, one makes perverted aspirations; thus bound and transmigrating, one brings about the accomplishment of evil karma.

The nature of the cause of purity is the relinquishment of and distancing from [defilements]; it is in this state that a great man extensively cultivates supreme deeds, remaining tranquil and unmoving in various locations, destroying the bonds of defilement so that their limits do not arise.

The sentient beings of the human realm possess vast meritorious karma; their five aggregates are indestructible and their transformations are inexhaustible. Receiving such sublime blessings has the practice of giving as its foundation; the essential regulations constitute the most superior grade. Their physical forms are magnificent and incomparably vast; their pure abodes are tranquil and unmoving; their renown increases, and their intrinsic nature is limpid and still.

When the essence of sentient beings is vast, obstacles do not arise; compassion guides living beings to initiate the ultimate truth. Unerring practice and generosity are the deeds of the Noble Ones, establishing the limit of reality in its indestructible nature. Hostile bonds are mutually dependent and can be overcome through compliance; the craving and seeking of desire are stilled by the Sages—a state from which the Bodhisattva’s compassionate vows are able to liberate.

The essence of pride is real and difficult to subdue; across each stage, its nine grades delude both principle and phenomena. Its self-nature is truly inverted and inexhaustible; the darkness of ignorance and folly makes the arising of tranquility difficult. Enveloped like a silkworm, how can one escape?

One who practices the cultivation of reality and honors the primordial limit, whose every mode of conduct seeks the full span of life, is a true Great Being who instructs sentient beings; such a person may rely upon the suchness of the equal nature.

The fundamental nature of consciousness, which is the support for name-and-form, is the supreme nature arising from the ultimate truth; it is the vehicle that corresponds to the deeds of the Great Being, and in the state of tranquility, it remains far removed from the conduct of desire.

The state of awakening throughout the ten directions is attained through complete purity; having entered the stages (*bhūmi*), one possesses specific capacities. Such superior causes have been cultivated over vast eons, and thus there is a distinction between the causal and resultant functions of noble wisdom.

This sublime practice delivers beings from suffering and brings them joy; it instructs all classes of beings to follow the noble teachings. Thus, with ignorance, arrogance, and the view of self as its root, one possesses the power to practice giving while dissolving all conceptual signs.

The self-nature seeks such transformation; it does not destroy the continuity of the physical remains of the transmigrating body. Within the limits of time, there exist both the pure and the impure, as well as the benefits and interests induced by causes that are virtuous and pure.

The system for seeking and hearing the truth is free from inversion, sovereign, and unshakable; yet in this state, where the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) increases and prevails, there is a corresponding tendency toward contention with no end in sight. There is nothing among the supreme causes for sentient beings that they do not abandon; while they create the causes for bestowing the Dharma as a source of benefit, the suffering of living beings destroys their very bodies, and they are unable to distance themselves from the limits of perversion.

The perfection of practice is like space, devoid of marks; the coolness of ethical virtue requires clarity regarding what is to be observed and what is to be transgressed. When the limits of evil are stilled and afflictions can be abandoned, this is the place where the Bodhisattva’s self-nature is pure.

He practices the cessation of activity and diligently cultivates the ultimate truth; he tames sentient beings through the conduct of a true hero, and skillfully purifies his cultivation through the means of generosity. The teachings bestowed by all Buddhas cannot be without cause; such is the reality of the Dharma’s manifestations as analogies. His dwelling is tranquil and equanimous like space; he severs craving and takes pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) as his cause, ultimately cultivating the practice of giving through the conditions of dependent origination.

The meaning of those torrents is an endless entanglement; the shifting appearances are guarded with mindfulness as if they were eyes. Cessation of evil views fulfills the ultimate truth, wherein the fundamental reality seeks its own inherent meaning.

The boundless and vast nature of a mother’s kindness is its essential meaning; therein, various true views arise and false views do not. This is the fundamental establishment of the Vinaya-piṭaka and its ritual protocols, wherein the nature of the realm of bliss is attained without craving.

The vast multitude of sentient beings protect themselves from strife and disputes; they are true men who have skillfully stilled their fetters. These great beings possess genuine power; with equalized characteristics, they cause the mind to abide in stillness. Fundamentally tranquil and free from inverted seeking, they point directly to what is called "silence."

The meaning and benefit of the images, from their origin to their end, are thus: when they are perfected and all disputes exhausted, how could there not be reality? Since that origin is inverted, how could it be otherwise?
Boundless grasping at a self cultivates defiled conduct.
What is the nature of suchness that is fundamentally free from fear?

One who delights in and is deluded by the inverted nature of form can relinquish their own body, skin, and flesh through giving; seeking out those locations for construction is considered supreme, and through such creative activity and transformation, they bear an inexhaustible burden.

Secret and profoundly deep, it is without signs to be perceived; those who are worthy vessels achieve complete mastery; the pure locations are pristine and supreme, extending even to the majestic and sublime purity of all transformations.

The pure teaching is well able to bring about stillness and tranquility; the causes for practicing the holy life increase in their manifestation, like the majestic and peerless lion king, with features exceptionally beautiful, bright white, and vast.

The mind is fundamentally clear and tranquil, naturally devoid of movement; its root delusion and darkness leave no cause for the arising of wisdom. With inverted dharmas, right knowledge does not arise, and although one possesses the capacity for hearing and retention, the mind of compassion is far removed.

Bound by attachment to the physical body since beginningless time, one eliminates the net of inverted views through pure and wondrous giving; by cultivating the most supreme and excellent causal practices, the essence of unmanifest form that upholds or transgresses [precepts] is called "morality" (śīla).

For sentient beings in whom craving blazes intensely, who are subject to boundless torrents of passion, arrogance, and wild dissipation, one must bring to rest their inverted karmic actions and establish them in the pure state where reality is realized.

This fundamental abiding in the mark of equality is free from any desire for hearing at any time; the realm and its directions are peaceful and tranquil; the forest shade of pure precepts is lush and flourishing; the virtue of the precepts is unimpaired and unified in purity; and the ultimate meaning of the system is fully accomplished.
What are those ten kinds of virtuous conduct that serve as its cause?

They are: the limit of excellence in superior marks; sovereign appearance of extraordinary and inexhaustible quality; radiant purity, majesty, and beauty; perfection in hearing and retention; and the non-erroneous fulfillment of both name and form through giving.

Afflictions do not arise, and the necklaces are fresh and pure; through the power of aspiration, one fulfills the practice of giving. In this state, there is vastness and mastery over the essential nature; the karmic merit of generosity is tranquil and majestic.

The intrinsic nature of wisdom is devoid of suffering; through reverent contemplation of the intrinsic nature of the three karmas, all inverted causes and practices are exhausted. The activities of dullness, ignorance, and pride, as well as disputes, are brought to rest through the perfection of compassionate guidance that seeks out and transforms them. The limits of wrathful states are pacified by instruction.

The husband’s distribution is even and impartial; he follows the instructions of his teacher regarding the limits of his robes; through his aspiration to hear and uphold [the Dharma], disputes cease of their own accord; and in his virtuous nature, there is no sense of transmigration.
How does one practice the gift of such sovereign mastery through the fulfillment of the awakening of reverence?

It is by benefiting and delivering others with an impartial and pure intrinsic nature, eternally severing the two kinds of heavy obstructions—the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*)—and forever cutting off the torrential floods, calamities, and afflictions that constitute the boundaries of vajra-continuity and defilement.

All that is with outflows (*sāsrava*) has the nature of being a vehicle; the wisdom that is the foundation of the Three Vehicles is difficult to attain. For worldly ordinary beings, who are defiled by impurities and engage in evil conduct, the power and function of inverted defilements arise; their branches and leaves flourish while they destroy the hindrances and coverings, yet their roots remain firm—this serves as a metaphor.
The Garland of the Previous Births of the Bodhisattva, Fascicle Ten;
The Garland of the Previous Births of the Bodhisattva, Fascicle Eleven.
Composed by the Noble Vīrasena and others.

Translated by the Great Master of Sanskrit Scholarship Shao De Hui Xun and others, including Song Dynasty Court Rank of the Fourth Class, Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, by Imperial Decree:

Self-nature is fundamental wisdom through which all is known; its superior characteristics abide in tranquility and freedom from affliction; it is profoundly serene, blissful, and realizes the meaning of liberation.

The evil realms, inverted views, and self-clinging are inexhaustible; sorrow and suffering increase ever more, while afflictions never cease. The manifestations of fundamental calamities are不定 (indeterminate), yet the Tathāgata has eternally severed the torrential floods of affliction.

The nature of that cause ceases its migration and transformation; it accords with and fulfills the root of meaningful benefit. Its power may be sought, and its capacity for transport is inexhaustible; through each successive stage of excellence, both movement and stillness are beneficial.

Fully comprehending that the mental ground exhausts all contention and seeking, the period of afflictions and inversions is brought to rest; the wholesome causes of the three vehicles restrain the various classes of beings, and the *dharmatā* of all Buddhas is profoundly serene and pure.

Through true knowledge and vision, pride and the like are rendered powerless; one thoroughly understands the tranquility of obstructive phenomena. The movement toward the extremes of fundamental pride is stilled, and the various fetters are restrained through instruction and admonition.

Sentient beings arise in accordance with their respective states; the bases of psychic power consist of desire, effort, mind, and investigation for the sake of purification. Repentance is called *chan* (confession), which purifies the vessel of the body; the Noble Path consists solely of wisdom that penetrates all three natures.
Ultimate reality does not transcend the wisdom of principle; suchness, the supreme ultimate, and wondrous awakening are perfectly complete. Truly pure hearing is the *mahāprajñā*.

The Buddha, the Great Being and Tamer of all beings, takes tranquility as his reliance and the mastery of movement as his purpose. The pure noble path exhausts the nature of the Tathāgata; through wisdom and understanding, one realizes the furthest limits of existence.

The assembly of evil destinies is wondrously difficult to escape; in the ultimate sense, there is no inversion, and pure karma is perfected. Free from bondage and detached from fetters, suffering and affliction have no cause. That which is truly sought as a fruit can bring liberation; the fundamental, vast, and great man’s inversions follow along with inverted limits and wrong conduct. Such is the bound nature of the learner (*śaikṣa*) regarding the roots of goodness; having reached the limit of entanglements, he fully understands his own fields and dwellings.

In this realm, the giving of sentient beings is substantial; the perverse operation of the retribution of evil karma ceases; the five hindrances and ten entanglements can be abandoned through the causes of Brahma-conduct; and there is the powerful nature of vast learning and retention.

With supreme and wondrous physical marks, one is far removed from calamity; the mind is formless, and nirvana is signless. Arrogance, bondage, and contention cease upon hearing the teaching; its fragrance is heard afar, for its constituent parts are true.

In remote regions, one gains superior knowledge; such are the various fields and locations. That true tenfold wholesome pure wisdom understands the characteristics of human conduct in their most excellent locations; the substance of form is supreme and indestructible. Sentient beings are well-instructed so that their cultivation of giving is perfected; the ground of the mind is supreme, unerring, and truthful. When afflictions, darkness, pride, and adversaries increase, one possesses the power to subdue and distance oneself from the hindrances and entanglements.

In this state, those who reverently serve and accord with the King have fundamentally cultivated supreme practices and abandoned the path of the ghost realm; they have perfected their burden-bearing until the infinite limit, as described according to the realization of the signless ninth stage.

One thoroughly understands the ten paths of action through wisdom; the nature of the realm is the reality of the exhaustion of all signs of equality. Because it is the supreme ultimate truth and the unconditioned dharma, one distances oneself from the darkness of arrogance through superior cultivation.
Karmic enmities and inversions number in the hundreds; the torrential streams of arising seeds and manifestations are inexhaustible.
How do sentient beings relinquish their retribution as hungry ghosts?

By severing the continuity of inverted pride and the fetters that shroud the mind, one abandons them through union with the root of tranquility. Seeking the true nature of non-conceptual generosity, one accords with the superior merit of equanimity; among the classes of beings in the human realm, the king is supreme.
What is that class of fundamental *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am")?

It is the attainment of affliction through successive bonds; it is the attachment to speech and the conceptual construction of wisdom; it is the cessation of the poison of medicine within the nature of quiescence; and it is the earnest seeking of truth through the cause of virtuous friends.

The place of excellence where affectionate care and nurturing prevail is far removed from various karmic activities and inversions; though retributive speech is filled with the poison of anger, the power of hearing and upholding the teachings through virtuous friends brings benefit and salvation.

Mastery and discipline seek the exhaustion of afflictions; one thoroughly understands the true fundamental nature of selfhood. Friends are dull and weak, subject to change and conditioned activity; such is the nature of the perfected, supreme cause.

The fundamental basis for the conveyance of the ultimate truth arises; within the afflictions, pride co-arises with desire. Through the virtuous instruction of a friend, the pure cause is initiated; proceeding as one should, one comes to rest the dust of defilement.

Through the sublime transference of pure and true generosity, one cultivates and honors the supreme cessation of fetters; from the flow of happiness, superior conduct arises, and through these excellent causes and conditions, virtuous deeds are fulfilled as desired.

Having abandoned the causes of defilement and delighting in dwelling in tranquility, one reaches the limit of the tenfold flow of wholesome signs; the nature of companionship and all inversions are exhausted, and through the perfection of one's own nature, reality is realized.

The untainted noble path realizes that suchness; the ultimate suchness is the perfection of reality. That celestial realm is free from suffering, the limit of things as they truly are, and the supreme limit that carries all living beings across.
The pure precepts are perfected and inexhaustible; the Tathāgata’s power of wisdom is vast and perfect; he proclaims the true Dharma, whose limits are inexhaustible.
How does he transport [beings]?
The Buddha acts as a virtuous friend, with the ten kinds of untainted wholesome karma fully perfected.
This is the twenty-fourth chapter in the sequential exposition of the meaning of the *Jātaka* of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, concerning the Bodhisattva’s practice of giving as an adornment.
The meaning of the unified, supreme Tathāgata-nature is such that its compassionate vows are cultivated exhaustlessly; this is what is meant by hearing the instructions of the Bodhisattvas.
What are the characteristics of seeking after tranquility?

The fundamental reality and ultimate truth of the human realm, the root of the various elements, natures, and categories, subdues the three karmas through the three secrets; its manifold manifestations are like the dense shade of a forest.

The constituent parts are pure and the cultivation of causes is sovereign; the noble path is impartial, resembling empty space. The power of its creative activity undergoes endless transformation, yet the poisons produced by the earth can be eliminated through the power of merit.

The causal practice for the perfect equality of sentient beings consists of performing the sublime and tranquil constituent parts; one should constantly act with compassionate guidance to benefit and rescue living beings, cultivating a pure mind and excelling in hearing and retaining the teachings.

The three kinds of non-erroneous reality are the root; through the instructions of the compassionate mother, one brings strife and litigation to rest; through the analytical understanding of wisdom, one realizes the nature of craving; thus, in such correspondence, there are no afflictive obscurations.

In whatever direction or place one cultivates the practice of subduing, it is difficult for sentient beings in the human realm to find the seeking mind; they follow along with inverted fetters, darkness, and dullness. At that time, the power of subduing and transformation is effective; one thoroughly understands the various corresponding aspects of dispute and contention. In this place, one cultivates generosity and establishes the means of subduing; those actual poisons and inverted views become harmless, for the Buddha-nature within each and every dust mote is non-dual.

True liberation is the unerring benefit; the power of hearing and retaining the Dharma results in the purity of wholesome qualities. Ego-clinging, craving, and bondage are unwholesome and obscured; the pure nature of name-and-form consists of the five aggregates.

He understands that the noble ones act without inversion; their minds are joyful and sovereign, their bodies are sublime, their realms are exquisitely beautiful and magnificently adorned, and they are as pure as celestial beings on a vast scale.

The supreme causes arise boundlessly with sovereign mastery; dwelling in tranquility, they subdue dullness, weakness, and the conceit of "I. While the physical marks are vast, the view of self persists; measuring victory and defeat, they bestow the superior, middling, and inferior.

In this place, the Bodhisattva practices with pure appearance and sovereign mastery; the purpose and benefit of the Supreme Vehicle are pure and unerring. Possessing the power of a king, his governance is exceptionally sublime and ever-unchanging; through the causal practice of tranquility, he bears the burden of the frontier regions.

Seeking the cessation of strife and dispute, one brings an end to clamor and confusion; one successively gives rise to pure and wondrous realms that are numinous, serene, stable, and unshakable. Like clouds universally covering all, they provide shelter for the people; the power and function of giving manifest in harmony, such that this state of equality is like a scale balancing its objects.

The sovereign power and function universally bestow a single canopy, stilling all defilements and realizing the power of full knowledge; it carries beings across all directions without fear or dread, and the unified appearance is solemnly accomplished.

Wisdom is vast and fully cultivated; therein lies sovereign purity of hearing and retention. Tranquility is supreme as inversion is abandoned; the power and function of the turbulent torrents are vast. Subduing the fetters and hindrances exhausts their increase, while one seeks tranquility and delights in the proper time.

When the mind-ground is free from arrogance and complacency, well-established in stillness and cessation, and the four marks of affliction no longer undergo successive transformations, it is like a sovereign ruler whose system of governance is perfect and complete; in such a state, the Bodhisattva is unimpeded like space.
What is the characteristic of sound? It possesses magnitude and obstruction.

Pure giving is the sincerity of the king; it arises through the movement of coarse and subtle investigation and analysis (*vitarka-vicāra*), yet in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), it is tranquil, serene, and immovable.

Regarding the ten types of wholesome and unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind, one discerns their respective times and locations; through awakening to the three natures, one is like a compassionate mother nurturing her child, skillfully knowing the child’s hunger, thirst, physical constitution, and temperament—this is when the king governs his realm well.
How does one bring an end to evil disputes and litigation within the mind-ground?

When the marks of form are fresh, pure, harmonious, and lovely, no actual calamities or destructions arise; they accord with the power and function of the original signlessness (*animitta*). This enables one to sever greed, hatred, and delusion, to preach the true Dharma, and to practice in accordance with it. One thereby comprehends the phenomena of birth and death across the nine stages of the three realms—how they undergo transformation, come and go, and possess no fixed superiority or inferiority—and realizes a state of tranquil equanimity free from the categories of darkness and arrogance.
What are the three roots of strife—greed, hatred, and delusion?

They are the causes of strife that result in the retribution of poverty. Through speech and conduct, one diligently seeks out and practices; bearing the burden of name-and-form with mastery, one clearly realizes the Mahāyāna through pure wisdom.

The ultimate Dharma is the perfection of wondrous enlightenment; over the vast expanse of time spanning three great kalpas, one cultivates mastery in giving, dwells peacefully within the field of the mind, and fully possesses the capacity for hearing, retaining, and practicing the teachings to overcome the afflictive hindrances.

In a tranquil dwelling, one practices giving with perfection; regarding kinsmen and their appearances, one’s mind constantly bestows kindness; free from the hindrances of entanglements, they are fundamentally unarisen; and one fashions a worthy vessel that is exquisite and lovely.

Perfectly fulfilling the sublime service of the noble ones, with the supreme wisdom of Śakra, Lord of Devas, he illuminates the mental activities of sentient beings; the Tathāgata’s power of movement is vast, his ultimate meaning is unerring, his secrets are pure, his physical marks are complete, and his lifespan is secure and firm.

The afflictions of desire and greed, along with sorrow and suffering, do not cease; while purity, excellence, and sublime cultivation distance one from darkness and pride, the limits of contention and strife result in the accomplishment of fetters and hindrances. Because the mind gives rise to intent toward the pits and traps below, it falls therein; seeing them suffering and tormented without end, the torrential stream of afflictions increases within the mental ground.

The physical marks are pure and wondrous, and their essential nature is fresh and clean; wherever they arise and reach their limits, the power of non-erroneous application fulfills the points of training, giving rise to the pursuit of the patience of non-arising.

Seeking the vast and sublime limit, carrying forth purity and perfect equanimity, practicing generosity with truth to bring rest to ego-clinging, one initiates the practice of giving through body, speech, and mind.

These ten paths of action reach the limit of mastery; they are supremely pure, fully endowed with the absence of conflict, and are known through the boundless noble wisdom that understands length, shortness, form, and the nature of obstruction.
The burden of giving is free from inverted pride; its operation consists of mastery over place and direction, fully endowed with the consciousness associated with *asmimāna* (the conceit "I am").

Its fundamental nature is that of bondage, characterized by pride and the like; it is fully possessed of dullness, weakness, and the inversion of self and other. Recollecting enemies and kin never ceases, and the afflictions and calamities of suffering are successively difficult to escape, giving rise to the superior states of rebirth through constant transformation.

The Tathāgata, through his intrinsically pure wisdom, understands and teaches the multitude of beings so that they may truly hear and uphold [the Dharma]; his pure and wondrous generosity is present everywhere, and he causes them to abandon the torrential flow of inversions and their lack of causal basis.

He possesses the majestic authority of a great king, inspiring awe; his appearance is exceptionally sublime, pure, and lovely. He acts with the mindful care of a mother nurturing her child, and through profound secrets, he realizes the ultimate truth.

Reverently following the conduct of the human realm, it is the cause for pure practice wherever one may be; the limit of anger is that which is cherished by the deluded mind. The three floods—greed, hatred, and delusion—are the root; the supreme state of no-more-learning does not part from the robe and alms bowl. The nature of practicing generosity is the most excellent path of action; it has the power to give rise to and accomplish suchness. The ultimate reality is present everywhere according to one's wish.

Seeking the Dharma of the mind, one understands that it is nothing but wisdom; in this state, the king’s noble virtue remains unshakable, and the realm is tranquil, free from the causes of strife and litigation. At this time, the meaning of excellence arises through the cause of giving; one destroys the haughty defilements and adversarial enmities of the place, contemplating the ultimate truth and seeking the practice of generosity. Through the commission of anger, fame and reputation perish; by abandoning the inverted views of "I" and "mine," one seeks only tranquility and self-mastery.
What time is it that one laments the sovereign who wields the blade of abundance, yet remains dull, weak, and arrogant in his actions amidst clamor and strife?

Such a torrent has the meaning of drifting and drowning; through the cause of giving, one rescues and benefits those in poverty and suffering. Through meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one brings to rest the defilements of inversion; by subduing self and other, one attains mastery over arrogance and indulgence. When the power of action is pure, clamor and strife ceaselessly end.

The pure teaching is supreme and free from enmity or poison; those in training advance with such aspirations. The nature of the Tathāgata is perfect in its instructional meaning, while the obscurations of affliction are by nature inverted.

Thus, throughout fundamental rootless kalpas from time immemorial, the nature of afflictions is ultimately like space; through pure instruction, one is tamed by what is seen and heard. When arrogance, indulgence, and pride are purified, consciousness does not arise; the limits of self-nature and the fluctuations of change cease, and the cycle of transmigration comes to a tranquil end.
How do those in the realm of ghosts seek out their way through ignorance?
Bound by superior fetters and conforming to defiled strife, the human realm is dull and weak, making it difficult for noble wisdom to arise.

When conduct is pure, one is carried across to excellence; through corresponding application, the fundamental practice is established. With sovereign power and function truly perfected, wisdom arises, free from fear and indestructible.

The precepts can restrain those who are inverted; through supreme self-discipline, one practices unbroken generosity. Vast physical form accords with beneficial purpose, and the nature of afflictions is entirely exhausted through their intensification.

The sovereign, supreme cause is fundamentally non-erroneous; yet when love and desire are involved in giving, one cannot eliminate signs. Because those afflictions serve as causes, their practice of giving involves attachment, like a great king whose governance and transformation are uneven.

True fear is the root of perversion and defilement; one who is sovereign and selfless practices giving with power. Through the cultivation of tranquility, past causes become profound, and that which is grasped as a physical body is found to be utterly unobtainable.

The flow of equality and reality is indestructible; it is that which belongs to the dharmas of the ground of sentient beings' entanglements and hindrances. The dust and filth of contention clog the realm of space, and from the root of affliction and calamity, craving arises.

In this place of calamity, there is nothing that does not arise; as ignorance shifts and changes, the passage of time increases. Yet, through the power of the Noble Path, one remains unstained and uninterrupted; it is here that the King’s sagely virtue flourishes.

The intrinsic nature of wisdom illuminates all without exception; like bees producing honey through collective effort to achieve success, the noble wisdom realizes perfect tranquility, giving rise to speech that is composed and free from confusion.

Sentient beings who are defiled and tranquilized are thus; those who grasp at a self as real give rise to fear. With the original intention of practicing the cause of giving, they are ultimately tamed at the furthest limit.
What is the predominance of the functions of its manifestations?

At the time of skillful means, it gives rise to excellence; its causal nature is boundless and its power is unimpeded. The self-nature of the mental ground is beyond the reach of language, while facial expressions shift and change according to joy and anger.

The causes for seeking such gifts in the past and future are as follows: the Bodhisattva practices the dharmas of the Vinaya-piṭaka with sovereign mastery, giving rise to the causal practice of instruction at its ultimate limit. There are five kinds, including the nature of the links of existence (*bhavāṅga*), the body, and consciousness; these are the nature of the immediate conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), and thus the seeds of retribution are not spoken of. Without destroying the nature of the corresponding causes (*sabhāga-hetu*) of the links of existence, one thoroughly understands that the true self-nature is thus; this is the meaning of the causal principle that accords with virtue and liberation from bondage.

The nature of darkness and dullness has an afflicted mind as its basis; the factors of purification are unobscured-neutral. This explains the essential nature of the sense-base of mind (*manāyatana*) in terms of its direct cause, taking the eight consciousnesses as its substance. Regarding the twelve bases, it is explained as "taming."
In what way are their aims and benefits desirable?

They consist of the natural arising of cultivation, the fundamental vehicle of wisdom and understanding, the overcoming of the turbid stream of dullness and mental obscurations, and the purification of the defilements of the view of self and contaminated speech.

Hearing, seeing, giving, and practicing bind the minds of sentient beings with pride; yet in reality, there is no self-view, no giving, and no practice—through the vehicles of the Three Vehicles, one moves with sovereign ease.
How is it that he thoroughly understands their exhaustion?

The secret cause is the complete cessation of suffering; the ultimate, unerring nature is the root of generosity. Since hatred is inexhaustible, wisdom is difficult to produce; the cause of bondage through illness can be abandoned through the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
What is the inverted practice that obstructs calamities?

It is to attain the supreme and wondrous self-nature of the world; to possess the power of pure and virtuous celestial meritorious karma; to be fully endowed with the hearing and retention of the five aggregates and name-and-form; and to manifest an inexhaustible excellence in one's physical appearance and conduct.

Subduing and purifying, you skillfully bestow meaningful benefit; excellent is your realization of the profound secret treasury. You truly subdue the characteristics of my own conduct and practice, such that through those supreme causes, the fruit of Buddhahood is accomplished.

Untainted merit is supreme as it transcends the world; the pure and wondrous nature-realm is the foundation of fearlessness. Through understanding and insight, one realizes the sublime and wondrous Buddha-dharma; with purity regarding name-and-form, one possesses the power of hearing and retaining.

The shifting and transforming of villages flows on without destruction; wisdom is vast, profoundly quiescent, and non-arising. Through repentance, all defilements are exhausted and tamed in this way; those realms of the gods are unified, pure, and wondrous, supreme, formidable, unerring, and truthful. Thus, the limits of these compassionate vows are inexhaustible, and their fundamental meaning is perfect and immutable.

The Tathāgata is vast, subtle, and perfectly complete; the śrāvaka who is beyond training attains liberation through the emptiness of phenomena, purifies the mental ground through the ten qualities of one beyond training, and gives rise to the ultimate pursuit of the supreme truth.

The secret and profound conduct of a bodhisattva concerns the sense in which sentient beings are fully possessed of afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*). For those who are dull-witted, arrogant, and of human disposition, one must truly and powerfully understand how to remain far removed from them. The essence of the afflictive obstructions—comprising the root afflictions, the secondary afflictions, and their seeds and manifestations—consists of twenty-six factors that are abandoned in common by the three vehicles.
The Twenty-fifth Chapter: The Meaning of the Jātaka of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, Entitled "The Bodhisattva’s Practice of Adornment.
The Garland of the Birth Stories of the Bodhisattva, Volume Eleven.
The Garland of the Birth Stories of the Bodhisattva, Volume Twelve.
Composed by the Bodhisattva Āryaśūra and others;
translated by Imperial Decree by the Great Master of Sanskrit Scholarship Shao De and Hui Xun, both serving as Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial during the Song Dynasty.
The limits of inverted defilements and the entanglements of suffering are like space; that is to say, they consist of following and hearing the causal practices of a bodhisattva.

What are its characteristics? Because there is still something further to be sought above the stages of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, they are said to be "wavering and shifting. The Mahāyāna, reaching the ultimate, is stable and firm, without movement; it is the cessation of Nirvāṇa, pure and silent. It is perfect and without counterpart, a wholesome nature free from defilement. While its power and function can be sought, its secret cause is non-action. Mind and object merge in profound harmony, yet the heavy afflictions remain boundless; through the vastness of its power and function, fundamental wisdom arises, severing [delusion] eternally and without interval.

When the nature of the noble arises, the nature of the ordinary is already abandoned; one relinquishes the meaning of fear through sublime hearing and retention, gathering and preserving the most supreme and vast words and meanings, while the limits of dispute and contention are stilled by the causes of the noble.

Guarding his aims and benefits like a lion-king, he is stainless and pure, seeking the blessings of gods and humans; in the true ultimate meaning, he is vast and free from contention, blazing with non-perversion, taming and pacifying; perfect, sublime, pure, and lovely, he reveres Śakra and honors his majestic appearance.
How does the activity of arising and transformation occur?

It is like clouds covering that which is pure and detached; it is the supreme appearance, stainless and tranquil; it is the fundamental basis of correct principle, as one desires, and of sovereign mastery; it is the power of the Great Being, the ultimate self-nature.

The realm is perfectly pure and free from the ten unwholesome actions; its physical forms are like jewels, manifesting supreme functions. Like the four bases of psychic power, its efficacy is most sublime, as it realizes the true nature of selfhood and nurtures all beings with reality.

Protecting with compassion the locus of craving, illuminating and understanding name-and-form to cease perversions, [observing] the modes of activity of the fetters that flow on without ceasing, this is the essential nature of wisdom regarding the sublime factors.
