My nature is sovereign, yet it is the limit of darkness and pride; there is a basis for inversion, and no practice of giving. The perfection of physical form has secret intent; such is the reality of non-inverted conduct.
What is the system of the virtuous mind that is like space?

It is like a king’s transition to tranquility; death and birth are constant affairs, as are afflictions and calamities. One practices giving with the aspiration for tranquility, cultivating it until the limits of time, and exalting its practice to vastness.

Those phenomena characterized by such signs take the appearance of form as their basis; through erroneous seeking, they posit a conventional ultimate truth, and by conforming to suffering while pursuing causeless pleasure, they obtain the retribution of long-term rebirth in the evil destinies.

Boundless forms and appearances can exhaust arrogance and indulgence; the various deities provide the causes for the retribution of kingship. Those various marks of birth are the root of the self; they produce dullness and ignorance, devoid of purity. They give rise to inverted views and the afflictions of impermanence; they bring forth suffering and all manner of disputes. At the moment of their arising, there is a nature of reverence; yet the various minds shift, change, and abandon [the truth]. Seeking bondage within those marks of renunciation, one distances oneself from the view of self and exhausts the practice of its very root.
What is the inexhaustible absence of pride and contention?
It is to seek the fundamental self-nature of purity; thus, by accordantly following equanimity and quiescence, one becomes fully endowed with hearing and retention, perfecting the stages of training.
Regarding the duration of the Avīci Hell, it is measured in kalpas; with its unceasing torment, when can one emerge from it?

That celestial realm is wondrous, pure, and real, with vast forms and inexhaustible merit. Its virtuous conduct reaches the pinnacle of perfection and excellence; in that sublime abode, one cultivates the practice of patience, seeks the benefit of generosity for the sake of higher stations, and is carried forward by the cultivation of superior and excellent giving.
What is the fundamental non-altering of craving?
To practice in this manner and seek the ultimate truth, one cultivates the mind through the practice of generosity and the ten paths of wholesome action.
This is the twenty-eighth chapter, "The Noble Birth Story of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla: The Ornament of Bodhisattva Conduct."

With right view, they practice giving that is ultimately undefiled and powerful; abiding in the stage of no-more-learning, they accord with right view and remain far removed from the hindrances and coverings—namely, by acceding to the authentic hearing of the Bodhisattva.
What are the characteristics and the limits of merit?

There is no burdening with inversion; when one upholds the precepts and cultivates practice, the retribution is pure. One who practices the Brahma-faring understands non-self; that which is the fundamental characteristic of inversion is itself reality.

The vast generosity accomplishes meditative concentration; it increases the welfare and benefit of the supreme holy life. It brings about the realization of pure and wondrous compassion and vows, cultivating the practice of transport and generating the ground of the mind. Its application in various spheres is joyful and unerring, reaching the limit of conduct free from the stains of negligence and hindrances.

The world is difficult to escape; yet there is the peace and bliss of meditative concentration, which is unerring, true, and possesses indestructible form and characteristics. It is the reliance for creative action and the sublime, wondrous cause, pursued through cultivation and the mental engagement of hearing and thought.

Vast ego-clinging entirely devoid of the guidance of compassion; the various afflictions at the limit of quiescence; restless and unceasing true darkness and pride; and the increasing greed, hatred, and defiled phenomena of the desire realm.

The ten fundamental causal practices of original seeking are the sovereign’s holy intention and fundamental virtuous friends; the causal limit consists of the mental ground that brings to perfection the karma of afflictions.

Those with wrong views give rise to the root of perversion; the view of self and the extremes of the world serve as their foundation. Through the superior performance of pure and wholesome karma, such results as those of the other shore are thus produced.

The power and function of the dharma of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) are ultimately quiescent and sublime; the roots of generosity (*dāna*) and ethical discipline (*śīla*) are preeminent. Cultivating the characteristics of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) removes hunger and thirst, yet those with the highest defilements fail to recognize the kindness of their teacher. Regarding unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*), they are deluded and ignorant; the pure dharma is the perfection of causal practice, the true mind, and the supreme ultimate truth of the world.
What is tranquility?

It is the state where the characteristics of the locus are upright and not deviant; it is the ultimate power and function that is manifoldly tranquil; it is the limit of purity where bliss is perfected; it is the peaceful and blissful activity of pure and wondrous practice.

Seeking individually through the most supreme power and function, one attains the superior cessation of non-erroneous reality; abiding here amidst fear, one hears the pure teaching, which brings to rest the darkness of pride, defilements, and evil conduct.
In this state, the celestial realm is vast and impartial; there is power, reality, discernment, and insight, yet there is affliction, pride, inversion, and no mind of seeking.
Why is this the cause of worldly lack of benefit?

The fabrication of a real self gives rise to bondage; by thoroughly understanding the various states that are free from conceit, one nurtures the darkness of pride until it blazes intensely, yet remains equal to the Brahma-world.

In this place there is a king adorned with merit, like a mass of fire blazing and radiant; his fundamental cause is the power of unbinding transformation, yet he possesses the reality of unbinding pride.
What are the boundless, pure assemblies?

They are free from the torrential flow of afflictions that bind and transform; they have transcended the pursuit of the signs of birth driven by pride and other dominant tendencies; they clearly understand and remain far removed from the quiescent, wondrous source; and they have reached the limit of the pursuit of the signs of birth born of inversion.

When disputes such as pride arise from their source, one instructs by means of speech to act toward them; through the perfect accumulation of the ultimate limit of reality, the speech of supreme arising reaches its consummation.

The root of calamity is bondage, the cause of defilement by afflictions; the appearance of radiance is named Vairocana. The speech of Bodhisattvas brings peace to the three karmas of superior sentient beings; hunger, thirst, and lack of strength reach a limit like space. The mind of greed and anger is equal and non-existent; sentient beings in the Brahma world dwell in the stage of the four dhyānas, and there are likewise those among the various devas who pursue through inverted views.

This speech is the self-abiding state of equality; this delight is the excellence of the sovereign. Furthermore, there is the singular union of practice at the limit, wherein causal conduct arises without time or place.

The mental ground is predominant, exhausting all taints and disputes; it gives rise to the tranquil appearance of speech. At the time of darkness and arrogance, its own nature is accomplished; the poisons of inverted defilements are difficult to stop. When the pride of self ceases and becomes tranquil, one seeks out one's own nature; yet the poison of afflictive defilement has the view of self as its root.
What is meant by "the eye"?

It refers to the speech of the Bodhisattva who seeks that prior path; it binds and colors one with signs and appearances, obstructing pure precepts. By cultivating the fundamental mark of self, one truly wraps and covers the purification of cessation. This creates the basis for the insubstantiality of the view of self, while the King’s excellent teaching brings that fruit to fruition and initiates the command of instruction.
What is the practice of giving sought in its true reality?
It is the teaching that purifies speech and fulfills the worldly Brahma-conduct; it is the supreme meaning by which a great king transforms and guides the world.
What further constitutes the limit?
The sovereign root is as spoken in the noble words: possessing sublime characteristics, one becomes a great king;
practicing universal generosity and the language of governance, the ten virtuous deeds transform his physical appearance, resulting in a perfect, inexhaustible, and supremely tranquil state.

When the bright moon arises, the host of stars all cease; when noble wisdom is activated, the multitude of defilements naturally perishes. Obstructions do not arise, and the world is brought to perfection. Thus, being fully endowed with the pursuit of the supreme cause, one understands the place of birth. Through the equality of the ultimate limit, one accords with meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), whereby the shifting transformations of the constituent parts bring both self and other to fulfillment.

including Song Chaosan Dafu and Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, for the purpose of propagating the True Vehicle, the transformation of aspirations, the perfection of the nature of wisdom, the subduing of the world, the holy cause of tranquility, the bearing of reality, and the ancient cultivation at the limit of the stage of enlightenment.

Seeking wisdom up to the point of transformation, one remains far removed from fundamental defilement; there is nothing that exists in stillness. Within the four aggregates, name and substance cannot be apprehended; the torrent of the world does not abide for even a moment.

The fundamental ultimate nature is boundless; it cannot be seen by the eye, yet can be attained through primordial wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). It is quiescent and effortless, yet undergoes occasional transformation; it is accomplished and arises within the temporal dimension of equality.

The knowledge and vision of the ultimate truth through the supremacy of intrinsic nature gives rise to the power of exertion and the full endowment of hearing and retention; among worldly locations, the form realm is supreme, and within the fourth dhyāna, one is free from the three calamities.

The conduct of the Sage is characterized by abiding in tranquility; he cultivates and honors virtuous deeds until they are purified and attained. Through the accomplishment of superior causes, the merit of the karmic fruit is realized, as he establishes the training rules and cultivates his practice of virtuous qualities.

The supreme and wondrous cultivation reaches the limits of the world; through perfect transport, one attains beneficial gain. This superior transformation is the fundamental reality, which subdues perversions and gives rise to the practice of giving.

Seeking out the accomplishment of the fundamental activity of hearing and retaining [the teachings], the torrential mental phenomena are fundamentally dark and dull; through the arising of correct understanding, perfect tranquility is produced, and one practices in accordance with the pure instructions.

The intrinsic nature of name-and-form has the five aggregates as its substance; it accords with the supreme practice of the ten wholesome paths. Conditioned by temporal factors, it is fully endowed with afflictions; its defiled appearance is the root of calamity. Yet, one further cultivates the state of liberation and tranquility; the twelve gates of birth encompass all hundredfold phenomena, like the sun illuminating colors so that they are fresh, pure, and lovely.

In that realm, the king is most virtuous; he guides and transforms with impartiality so that calamities are entirely ceased. He is able to remain tranquil and detached regarding karmic actions. In this place, the king is upright and free from depravity; his internal and external governance is as wondrous as divine wisdom, his enlightened nature is supreme, and his mind is free from inversion.

Seeking the supreme discourse through the world’s inquiries and challenges, one attains great learning and retention; the inverted perceptions and fetters of the world are brought to cessation without cause through the power of mastery, as one seeks the ultimate limit and remains far removed from the causes of fear.

In regions characterized by dullness, ignorance, and inverted practice, the great trichiliocosm is destroyed during the kalpa of wind-disasters; yet in this place, the Bodhisattva’s superior and profound realization brings about the perfect tranquility of the realm of subduing.

Eliminating the components of false views regarding reality and giving rise to the most supreme discourse through speech, such is the primordially present power of purity that leads one toward the ground of mind characterized by mastery in difficult practices.

The convergence of name-and-form constitutes the marks of merit; it advances toward the profound limit of practice. Such is the root of the ultimate tranquility, arising as the supreme, correct, and non-erroneous state.

The power of illness destroys superior practice; the fundamental disputes, torrential flows, and defiled evils, along with their established functions and even their limits, are the unconditioned nature of practicing tranquility.

Thus, this profound non-self is free from contention; its nature is fundamentally fearless and is not disturbed by sounds or forms. The pursuit of afflictions is not in accord with what is wholesome; it is rooted in defiled views that give rise to the causes of worldly toil.

The inverted aspirations of sovereign appearances arise from the mind as the fundamental activity of self-nature; from this root, a thousand kinds of defiled obstructions emerge, which are stilled through the practice of relinquishment and remain far removed from contention.

The pure full moon lacks radiance and does not shine universally; fundamental noble wisdom is untainted and uninterrupted; mastery is unbound and its regulations are supreme; afflictions are diminished as one advances in superior cultivation.

The ultimate truth is non-erroneous and can sever desire; it is the boundless purity of unconditioned union. Through the practice of tranquility based on that true cause, one eternally cuts off the afflictions created by cultivation.

When I perceive the limits of phenomena, greed and pride arise accordingly; the power of the unified name-and-form is able to perform cultivation and action. This diminishes the causes for practicing generosity and falling into poverty or illness; through the force of its own nature, it brings about the flux of calamities.

The places of practice increase disputes and litigation; sentient beings are unable to relinquish their physical forms and appearances; yet the Buddha-dharma and the holy life (brahmacarya) can eliminate obstructive defilements, like a blazing fire whose momentum cannot be stopped.

Fundamentally cultivating tranquility and freedom from the bonds of fear, one carries out the practice of transformation to its ultimate limit; through such tranquility and seclusion, one reaches the mark of exhaustion. Fully endowed with the retention of what has been heard, the regulations, and the instructions, one seeks the superior power and function that exhausts defilement and contention. By hearing and practicing, one removes fundamental pride, giving rise to the manifestation of all intrinsic natures, thereby becoming far removed from afflictions, sorrow, suffering, and terror.
What is the practice of transformative cultivation?

It is the ultimate limit of subduing, the true locus of reality; it is the pursuit of the supreme meaning, unimpeded like space; it is the blazing power and function of perfected wisdom; and it is the pure cause of giving that ultimately eliminates all afflictions.
Name-and-form blazes intensely like Kapila; thus, through sovereign and blazing cultivation, the assembly of noble ones attains the equality of ultimate truth.
Why is it that mental phenomena have no physical form?

The gathering and arising of all phenomena carries the sense of non-abandonment; the causal characteristics of the sensation of suffering are rooted in defilement; inverted attachments and mental afflictions are inexhaustible; and the activity of supreme transport is unerring.
What is the predominance of the floods of obstructive defilements?

They are like a fiercely blazing, violent torrent difficult to restrain; yet they are equal and boundless, truly without end, shifting and changing without movement, and ultimately subsiding in profound stillness.

The fundamental substance of contention and litigation is empty while its retribution is real; the limits of karmic activity possess a force difficult to arrest. Fully endowed with fear, and characterized by an increase in dullness and ignorance, such things arise from the extreme of perversion.

Tranquil and motionless, free from inversion, the power and function of the person blaze forth as they cultivate further; that inverted defilement and secret conduct come to rest, and the vast self-nature is excellently advanced. The sublime arises, taming the self-nature, and the pure retribution is perfect and powerful.
How does one seek the abandonment of evil and the cultivation of good?

One ardently exerts oneself toward the ultimate limit, practicing various forms of giving and advancing in superior conduct. One gives rise to the fundamental nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-svabhāva*), carrying out the practice of worldly norms. One seeks the state of tranquility where there is no further transmigration, attaining right liberation in the sense of being indestructible.
What is the stage of the wisdom that exhausts the root of contention?
It is the obtainability of the single integration of the factors of sentient beings.
Why is the characteristic of the mental division difficult to obtain?

The four aggregates called "name" are fundamentally devoid of material form; their basis is the tranquil abiding at the limit of patient practice. They are profoundly serene, pure, and stainless, for the self-nature of ultimate reality is fundamentally non-arising.

The bondage of giving is the distancing from beginninglessness; when appearances do not arise, its functional power accords [with reality]. That practice of affliction is cultivated toward cessation; destroying spatial locations, it is tranquil and detached.

The blazing and perfect appearance undergoes transformation; the causes of suffering possess no security that can be maintained. The power and function of arising are rare and marvelous; in the most excellent locations, there is stillness and tranquility. Joyful changes are cultivated according to one's inclination; the application of activities is sovereign and unerring.
How is it that the originally quiescent exhausts the characteristics of arising and ceasing?
How does one sever the defilements of delusion regarding phenomena and delusion regarding principle?
When primordial wisdom simultaneously severs the limits of inversion, the ultimate truth may find rest.
What is the nature of the realms (*dhātu*)?

The five aggregates of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa-skandha*) blaze with intensity; they may be fully perfected, pristine, and born through transformation (*upapāduka*). Through unerring cultivation, one attains clarity, tranquility, and stillness; their meaning consists of the ten powers (*daśabala*), which are pure, wondrous, and difficult to fathom.

The pure physical form is serene, limpid, and translucent; the substance of the form is distinct and as warm and smooth as jade. With such proportions, its bliss is beyond compare; through this supreme harmony, one may attain purity and wondrous excellence.

When the practice of giving is perfected through the relinquishment of both internal and external things, there is no inverted giving at the limit of sorrowful experience; for such a mind, strife and litigation are fundamental, and thus the name "miraculously born" does not exist.

With wisdom profound and far-reaching, all the devas look up to you in reverence; excellent is your practice of giving, for its merit blazes forth. In this state, you seek the power and function of tranquil abiding, fulfilling the ultimate limit of sovereign bearing.

Thus one knows and sees that these are obtained through the cultivation of giving: the five kinds of blazing objects—form, sound, fragrance, flavor, and the tactile qualities comprised of earth, water, fire, and wind—which bind through their power, causing such attachment that they are difficult to relinquish; yet for those bound by the pride of thinking "I am," there is no cause for such giving.

Compassion guides the arising of pure subduing; this is called attaining pure giving. Having universally attained the ultimate truth, the fruits of suffering are eliminated, and one may reach the final goal of the Mahāyāna. Even until the very limit of one's lifespan, there is nothing that does not yield the victory of giving.

Fundamentally tranquil, it is the limit of non-conceit; its purpose is to transport sublime sentient beings. Where primordial calamities exist, there is no place of tranquility; through the limit of pure and wondrous giving, one realizes the fruit of no-more-learning.

Among the minor derivative afflictions, harm coexists with the conceit of self-importance (*asmimāna*); in a dull-witted person, the defilement of conceit increases and flourishes. By its very nature and functional power, it lacks that dharma of conceit; it is fundamentally a contention of afflictions and a perverted practice.

Sentient beings are by nature disciplined and tranquil; though afflicted by illness, hardships, and bondage that impair their physical vigor, they give rise to supreme causes to discipline themselves and remain detached, dwelling in stillness and cultivating the practice of tranquility at its very root.

Pure giving abandons greed and delusion; in this regard, the king’s noble wisdom is all-pervasive. Through universal bestowing and transformative governance, calamities do not arise, and upon hearing the truth, the wicked and sycophants cease of their own accord.

In accordance with the instructions, they are indestructible; worldly fears can be subdued by the power of the Noble Ones. Through the supreme efficacy of the fundamental cessation, they perform superior cultivation to transport all classes of beings; their activity pervades everywhere so that there is no fear, and they aspire toward renunciation.
What is the fundamental fulfillment of hearing and retention?

It increases fearlessness and seeks common benefit; it employs superior causes for true cessation; it is the sovereign power of the ten wholesome roots; that giving is indestructible, a most excellent destination.

Bearing the burden of ensuring the peace and security of sentient beings in the borderlands, his sovereign power is conjoined with my vision; as sentient beings earnestly cultivate and practice their conduct, he establishes means to distance them from defilement, evil, and strife.

Through the power and function of the Noble Path, one practices discipline; having cultivated the supreme cause of wisdom over successive kalpas, the Bodhisattva’s mental ground thoroughly cultivates the knowledge and vision of the Buddha-dharma throughout beginningless, remote kalpas.

The ultimate fundamental vessel for enjoyment is gathered and stored within the self-nature of the original consciousness, as numerous as the atoms of the lands; thus one should train in this way, abiding well in cessation, and practice the tranquility of shifting images.

I see that disputes and contentions have been far removed from the beginningless past; I practice the conduct of giving with unerring purity, purify the three karmas through skillful repentance, and remain peacefully settled in the non-transmigrating dharma.

With far-reaching wisdom and understanding, one bears the burden of sentient beings; through the ultimate limit of tranquility, one achieves superior self-mastery; by generating virtuous causes, one becomes blazingly powerful; and one remains far removed from the fetters of fundamental inversions.

The ten kinds of wholesome states on the mental level are the reality; understanding their locus is the supreme practice. This is the essence of pure liberation and the fundamental meaning of correctly understanding that the afflictions are originally quiescent.

Sentient beings increase in the purity and excellence of the ten wholesome actions; free from the stains of hindrances and the fetters of entanglements, they abide in profound stillness and peace. For all devas, the foundation is a pure mind-ground, wherein physical forms are radiant and clean as they advance in the cultivation of the Path.

Through hearing and retention, one increases superior tranquility and ceases obstructive defilements; the nature of the realm is the indestructible bliss of the world, with the locus of discipline as its fundamental characteristic, wherein the power of reality functions without inverted causes.

The instructions of the ten wholesome paths are exceptionally sublime and pure; their marks of sovereign merit are inexhaustible. They increase the cultivation of wisdom and mental understanding for sentient beings, serving as the pure, wondrous, and supreme cause for the benefit of taming.

The sixth consciousness being serene is supreme; its self-nature is true reality, free from such states as pride. Thus, advancing in the cultivation of virtuous conduct is supreme; it is free from sudden violence and defilement, bringing the activities of affliction to rest.

Advancing upon the path before them, their meritorious deeds are serene; as the foundation of transport, they are free from the thoughts of affliction. Pure, limpid, and tranquil, no perversions arise; they listen to what is meaningful and beneficial for the sake of sentient beings.

The causes of inversion lead to conduct stained by evil entanglements; pure instruction brings one far from the defilements of worldly toil. One does not destroy the truth, practicing generosity with a benevolent mind; understanding folly, one tranquilly establishes cultivation. One does not corrupt speech, acting according to the teachings of sincerity and truth; the root of purity is the unimpaired mark of the tongue, seeking the sublime meaning of correct principle in serene stillness.
What is the skillful practice of giving that carries one across?

It is to practice in accordance with the most supreme purity, to masterfully subdue the limits of self-interest, and for the royal regulations to be strictly brought to rest; thus, the view of self is vast and boundless.

Truthfulness is the absence of ignorance, which is the root of afflictions; greed arises when conditions are favorable, while anger is provoked by what is contrary to one's wishes. Twenty-six delusions arise from the view of a self; if the root is severed, the secondary obstacles will be eliminated accordingly.

In this realm, the king brings forth supreme benefit; the peripheral regions of the world-system are peaceful both internally and externally; the ten paths of unwholesome action and their obscurations do not exist; and all misfortunes and errors are fully understood and brought to an end.

The devas’ state of perverted views and inverted characteristics is pacified through hearing and upholding [the Dharma] in accordance with it; their fundamental insight binds them to reality, such that these rules of conduct are perfected and free from contention.

Cessating perversions and initiating subduing, such is the dharma of hearing regarding the ultimate truth; through its equal arising, one becomes fully endowed with hearing and retention, attaining fearlessness and generating power and function.

Thus, practicing the pure and wondrous giving that is free from bondage is called the basis for the four original formless aggregates; through this sincere confession and repentance, it becomes pure and perfect, carrying the practitioners of the three vehicles to the shore they have attained.
Through the perfect practice of repentance for transgressions and abiding in tranquility, one may attain the pure happiness of the celestial realms; thus one pursues the truth with unerring purity.
This concludes the twenty-ninth chapter on the meaning of the Jātaka of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, concerning the Bodhisattva’s practice of giving as adornment.
The cause of perfect giving eliminates hunger and thirst; its superior nature is characterized by a pure and radiant appearance, namely, that which accords with hearing the conduct of a bodhisattva.

At this time, the power of the occasion nurtures the fundamental marks of merit; such are the limits of its activities, each according to their kind. Through its superior efficacy, whether advancing or halting, bending or stretching, every provisional arrangement is truly for the benefit of others, serving as the basis from which the three roots of goodness arise.

The supreme cause of giving adorns the physical marks; within the mental ground, it is truly thus—pure, wondrous, retentive, profound, and sincere. These physical marks are vast and majestic, serving as the basis for reliance.

The pure and wondrous realm is entirely pristine and immaculate; the four aggregates are manifest, their forms radiating brilliant light. With equanimity and fearlessness, one understands the proper course of action and withdrawal, as the fundamental consciousness self-realizes the accumulation of the supreme causes.

The physical forms and bodies of those various beings are thus; they possess the superior power to bear the ultimate limit [of practice]. In this regard, the purity of the mind of giving is fundamental, and this is what the great bodhisattvas delight in.

Understanding that the characteristic of sound possesses the power of hearing, that truly pure mind can destroy craving, and that through the power of purity one advances in sublime practice, one remains unmoved by location and undergoes no further transformation.
What is the tranquility of the meditative absorption of subduing? Such is the vast efficacy of the Noble Path;

through superior realization, one thoroughly understands this tranquility. When the ultimate limit is perfected, afflictions are far removed. Sentient beings do not transcend the limits of the six realms of existence; the achievement of silent stillness relies solely upon wisdom. Thus, the causes of conditioned change are stilled, and liberation is attained as conflict and defiling obstructions are distanced.
What is the meaning of hearing the characteristics of sound?

Through the immeasurable wisdom and noble power of seeking, the Mahāsattva is a great being; guided by compassion, they transport others through impartial hearing and retention, wherein tranquility and harmony cause dullness and defilement to cease.

True instruction eliminates both ignorance and pride; it subdues harsh suffering through the unerring ultimate truth. It gives rise to compassion with the characteristics of a sublime and wondrous voice, and its mental disposition aspires toward the great welfare of sentient beings.

Each of those who set out upon the path bears the burden to its ultimate limit; they do not destroy the supreme cause, the fundamental secret treasury, yet the root of ignorance causes sentient beings to fall into perversion, such that the villages and regions are distant lands difficult to reach.

Sentient beings of the ten wholesome paths flock to the seven assemblies; the purpose is to bring living beings to rest and to promote their spiritual advancement. Reaching the ultimate limit of hearing and practice, his fame is vast and his burden-bearing is never lacking.

The sublime benefit tames sentient beings; their practice of giving is pure and untainted by defilement. This supreme cause possesses power as unimpeded as space; this practice of pure causes is fundamentally free from bondage.

The power and function of the root of liberation are pure; the Brahma-faring is vast, and hunger and thirst are stilled. Knowledge and vision are disciplined and refined without fail; through the aspiration for pure giving, one gains the power of hearing and retaining the Dharma.

The mental ground accumulates unerring reality; the power of the cause of perfected hearing is vast; it carries sentient beings so that they are far removed from the stains of hindrances; and it bestows the perfection of the ultimate truth, free from all suffering.

In the state of tranquility, one abandons the causes of bondage through hearing; it is the pure vehicle of the unified secret. This is where Bodhisattvas exert themselves in pursuit; there, the pure assembly is fully endowed with mastery, retaining what they have heard without pride, and thus remains free from the fetters of change and transformation.
The supreme pursuit of the fundamental excellence, the cessation of disputes through pure instruction, and the practice of the ultimate meaning through the application of compassionate guidance—
how are these attained?
How does one seek it?

Through pure giving that accords with cessation, there is the perfect tranquility of being without self or dharmas; one is able to leave behind sorrow, suffering, and afflictions through thorough purification.
What is meant by the causeless destruction of pure dharmas?
It is when a person pursues reality, accords with names and signs, and subdues disputes, yet practices universal giving out of causeless desire.
What is meant by "transmigration and rebirth as supreme"?

It is pure, wondrous, and pristine because it is caused by generosity and ethical discipline (*dāna-śīla*). Through these, one attains the supreme state free from fear, the tranquility of cessation, and the ultimate peace that is without calamity or affliction for the multitude.

The secret of the primordially pure self-nature, the limit of tranquility through discipline on the stages of training, the fundamental cessation of the nature of virtuous causes, and the power of knowledge and vision in the application of correct principles.

The characteristics of contention and litigation are the fetters of the self in ordinary beings; they are inverted longings regarding the original self-nature. With afflictions as their cause, they are bound by the view of a self, and from this state, sentient beings give rise to speech.
In this place, how do sentient beings abandon [it]?
Their number reaches a thousand; fear knows no end. Through pure instruction, wisdom and understanding arise, yet the causes of bondage and the afflictions of suffering remain unbroken.

Generosity is all-pervasive and equal as space; by practicing with such excellence, one may attain the sublime. When afflictions are subdued, disputes cease; thus, the practice of fundamental wisdom gives rise to the boundless.

Sentient beings love, yearn for, and rely upon him in this way; he is a great sentient being whose shifting manifestations are like reflections. He feels compassionate attachment for sentient beings, never abandoning them in their sorrow and suffering, and he impartially accords with and tames them.

The instruction on the non-arising of confusion is thus: far removed from darkness and arrogance, it is a discourse of tranquility; its regulations are lovely, its provisions are for worthy vessels, and for sentient beings there is no neglect—how excellent, how fearless!

Subtle and supreme in its taming, transport, and discernment, it hears the truth as the Celestial Lord bestows his transformation; taking non-contention as its foundation, it employs the power of mastery for both contraction and extension. It reaches the limit of the heat and affliction of the torrential defiled dharmas, and through the forceful pacification of the causes of defilement, the increase of ego-conceit in the ultimate sense is brought to rest.

Abiding in harmonious practice, they dwell in immovability; seeking the supreme cause, they act with mastery. They cannot abandon the excellent and sublime place, which is the limit of giving—a realm free from contention.

In this place, he truly practices without inversion; as a Great Being, he guides sentient beings with compassion. Clearly abiding in contemplation, he bears the burden of bringing order to what is extremely difficult to manage. In such a locus where calamities prevail, his perfect power and function increase; yet, while delighting in transition, he has no desire for fixed abiding. His pure conduct requires no cultivation, for defilements have been replaced by their antidotes.
What is the sincerity regarding illness and calamity?
The power and function of the secret of tranquility can bring cessation.
What is the cause of deep inversion, darkness, and dullness?

How can the intensification of fetters, entanglements, and hindrances be halted? The root of afflictions has no means by which it may be shaken; the various forms of pride and delusion increase to such a degree that they are difficult to restrain; these bonds are hard to untie and must rely upon the power of the Sages.

The manifestations of defiled bondage have been incessantly suppressed; one should strive to cultivate tranquility and honor the teachings. The power of creating impurities is difficult to relinquish; when obstructions are heavy and merit is deep, it is extremely difficult to repent and atone.

Having thus accomplished these arduous and defiled deeds, he practiced with unerring cultivation, abiding in tranquility and stillness; turning his back on hunger and thirst, he perfected the ultimate truth and bore the burden of taming sentient beings throughout distant eons.

The power and function of the Noble Path are thus boundless; seeds and active manifestations arise upon the ground, one seeks and attains the pure teachings, and one abides perfectly in the ultimate truth, free from bondage.

The fundamental power and function are quiescent and subdued; they accord with the reality of shifting fluxes like a torrent. One clearly understands that the limbs of illness and suffering are without substance, and by bestowing [this insight] upon sentient beings, one attains peace and stillness.

With the physical form cast aside, one clearly discerns the purified mind; abiding in the state free from inversion, where meaningful benefit is to be esteemed, one dwells with mastery in accordance with wholesome dharmas, yet remains conjoined with the suffering of the predominance of the view of self.

It can destroy the activities of desire and purify them; at the proper time, hearing the correct principle gives rise to [insight], whereby one may avoid the conceptualizations of groundless fear; the fundamental burden is purified and becomes powerful.
Regarding sentient beings' afflictions, what dharma should they cultivate to abandon them?

In that state, the nature of merit is exceedingly great; such is the ultimate limit, the very basis of the ultimate truth. Taking this as the standard for compassion toward all living beings, this indestructible ultimate truth is that upon which sentient beings may rely.

The fundamental nature of the true appearance of the mental ground is to be impartially subdued wherever it resides; though the locations [of affliction] may be destroyed, they cannot be brought to a final cessation, for the mind remains unsettled within its dwelling.

Mastery gives rise to meditative concentration and wisdom which may be relied upon; while images shift and change, the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is immovable. The world is equal, and both ordinary beings and sages rely upon this; when one cultivates with reverence to the ultimate limit, not a single dharma can be apprehended.

The merit equal to the atoms of a buddha-field is boundless; though one may follow after sensual desires, there is no accord with the wholesome. How excellent are the various appearances of the directions and places! Pure, wondrous, and refined as fine silk, there is no thought regarding them.

Constantly contemplating the burden of bearing others and rescuing them from suffering without ceasing, and relying on the mutual support of bending and extending, one harbors only this intent; therein, one gives rise to vast compassion and guidance, with a mind that is sovereign, tranquil, and true, so that afflictions may cease and pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) may be established.

At the limit of his karmic activity, he was born into the Kṣatriya lineage; having cultivated such unerring power, the merit of the ten wholesome paths caused all living beings to look up to him with reverence. His provisions and offerings were exquisite and rare, while the bonds of affliction, defilements, and disputes were brought to rest.

Sincerity and the lovely nature of reality are its foundation; like a lotus emerging from the water, it is fresh, pure, subtle, and wondrous—tranquil, limpid, and crystalline, free from even the slightest speck of dust. Such is the magnificence of generosity when practiced with aspiration.

The various binding phenomena—perversions and calamities—and the obstructive defilements of the view of self are difficult to restrain; yet, through the truly superior causes that are virtuous, pure, and powerful, name-and-form are stilled and pacified, and only then are the dust and stains exhausted.

The reality of ego-grasping is a deluded defilement devoid of meaning; it truly causes the wisdom to be bound and undergoes constant transformation. The inverted characteristics of this defiling cause do not cease, and the fetters of autonomy increase contention and strife; through the instruction on the limits of action, they are brought to rest.

Regarding the sequence of the karmic fruits of past and future actions, when the Noble Path arises, evil karma is immediately severed; possessing the fullness of hearing and retention, one attains equality with sentient beings, and each respective location becomes pure and sublime.

The fundamental noble path brings to rest the defilements and hindrances; it gives rise to the causes of purity and brings about the realization of reality. Once the dust, stains, and disputes have been eliminated through diligent cultivation, one attains liberation from obstructive defilements and becomes supremely fearless. While the increase of perversions gives rise to further disputes, the instruction of the correct principle generates the ultimate truth.
What is the ocean-like assembly of vessels for pure giving?

It is the sovereign mastery of joy within the characteristics of the ultimate sense faculties; the non-arising of pride and the purity of the brahma-conduct; the increased cultivation of liberation and the ability to distance oneself from obstructive defilements; and the fact that the merit and retribution of sentient beings have pure giving as their cause.

The pure and wondrous deities clearly understand the excellence of causes; the ultimate reality of the secret treasury is eternally quiescent. While worldly phenomena possess the nature of dispersal and decay, such is the intrinsic nature of the Brahma-faring: translucent and still.

I perceive their vast attachments to be boundless; tormented by feverish afflictions and embroiled in disputes, they are stained by obstacles and difficult to subdue. Their bodies endure painful sensations and their conceptualizations never cease; clinging to defilements, they remain ignorant of the kindness of their teachers.

The sublime arising is sincere and non-erroneous; like clouds providing universal shade, the heat of affliction does not arise. Thus, through disciplined cultivation and seclusion, the reality of the Supreme Vehicle brings the cessation of defilement and inversion.

The factors of supreme benefit possess great power; by advancing in sublime practice, one removes defilements. Through pure, desireless, and wondrous tranquility, one subdues the mental ground and gives rise to generosity.

Having brought about the cessation of conditioned harmony, inversions have perished; one truly realizes the ultimate truth and intrinsic nature. Defilements and hindrances are temporarily stilled within the celestial realms, and at the limit of tranquility, the intrinsic nature is fearless.

Hearing the truth, one becomes free from defilements; through the power of superior application during the period of transport, the various past acts of giving—whether stained or pure—are carried forward, such that the fruits of practice are not received purely but in a state of intermingling.

The karmic fruition of the higher realms is the peaceful cultivation of practice; it is the perfection of true mastery and power. Cultivating virtue without error brings benefit in both contraction and expansion; it is the indestructible suchness, the cessation of stillness beyond cultivation.

Perverted aspirations are the root of calamity; the fetters and veils are fearsome, drowning one so that escape is difficult. Covetous greed blazes fiercely, with no end to enemies or kin; the characteristics of liberation are like a lotus flower that has withered and decayed.

Supreme, excellent, pure, and powerful; the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) has the meaning of supreme flux; the fragrance of ethical discipline is fragrant, virtuous, and lovely; the place of cultivation is supremely adorned and pure.

Moving and turning, one seeks pure instruction; yet self and other are bound by inverted practice. When union, sovereignty, and tranquility all cease, food and drink undergo transformation as the mind is purified through cultivation.

The power and function of cessation are tamed by virtuous causes; the fundamental nature of the perfectly pure dharma is its root; the excellence of the retribution nurtured over time is supreme; and it is fully endowed with the retention of what is heard and the fearlessness of ultimate meaning.

The realm of the nation is tranquil and the frontiers are at peace; the nature of generosity is such that stinginess and greed have been abandoned, and thus one may attain purity, excellence, and fearlessness.

Among the ten virtuous actions, generosity is the foundation; the nine *pāramitās* arise in succession. In this place, the noble man seeks to cease strife and litigation, and through the abandonment of fearful and evil conduct, he gives rise to reality.

The meaning of time and place is unified in a single locus; the characteristics of conditioned formations are thus quiescent. I perceive that the root of vast afflictions is the view of self, and the intrinsic nature of the body is ultimately insubstantial.

It is attained only at the stage of unsurpassed, ultimate awakening; the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is quiescent and utterly ungraspable. Bearing this burden without contradiction, one guides and attracts sentient beings through supreme, true, and most excellent instructions.

In that place, the limit of sovereign purity is perfected; its fearless form is vividly pure. It is the sublime Mañjuśrī, free from karmic activity, proceeding through the power of means with a dharmatā like space.
Regarding the ten paths of karmic action that are free from the signs of fear, how is it that one attains mastery and fearlessness therein?

The fundamental meritorious karma is unerring and true; as the authoritative word of the Sage declares, it is like the dharma of tranquil abiding, in the sense of being free from clamor and vexation. Defilement and contention take form as their basis; the dharma of tranquility has the sense of abandoning worldly toil.

With instruction that is unerring and well-purified as its cause, one exhausts all inverted defilements through stainless conduct; such is the benefit of pure giving, which carries beings across with equanimity, free from the notion of a unified self.

Truly performing acts of giving with aspiration, one employs sovereign power to establish and subdue; just as the duration of the celestial realms in that time is vast, the appearance of purity is as clear and translucent as the moon; diminishing perversion, the ultimate meaning is accomplished, remaining unchanging like space as all transformation ceases.

Thus, having subdued the limits of defiled wisdom, that deity undergoes transformation as the basis of purity and subtlety; it is perfectly tranquil, secret, free from signs such as pride, and its supreme reality remains unimpaired through hearing.

One should constantly practice the perfection of giving without error; it purifies the increasing poisons of strife and the terrifying states of inverted defilement, which are like licking honey from a blade.

The root of transformation and change increases contention and strife; that which harms the realm of the nation dwells securely in wondrous goodness; endowed with the characteristics of hearing and retention as a unified whole, the pure stillness and tranquility increase in their physical manifestation.

In the ultimate sense, it is free from error and temporal limitations; one understands the signs of calamity in the past; though oppressed by famine, food and drink are entirely lacking; yet the virtuous causes of sentient beings increase with sublime purity, and the practice of giving is established in a state of non-distraction and tranquility.

The supreme and wondrous power of transformation is extraordinary; though illness is sincere and real, it subsides only to increase again. Perverted views, fear, and sorrowful suffering multiply ever more; afflictions and calamities arise without ceasing, never finding rest. As the torrential flow of afflictions arises, ceases, and is born again, one should exert the power of giving with a wholehearted lack of stinginess.
What is the instruction on the regulations for the stage of training?

It involves bearing the burden of power and function while extinguishing fear; it entails the further increase of the root afflictions of defiled inversion; it involves insatiable greed and longing for the marks of form; and it concerns the noble cultivation of virtuous conduct, which is a precious supreme cause.

The unalterable self-nature is far removed from the three arrows; generosity gives rise to the ten perfections (*pāramitās*); the pure instruction is the noble benefit; the fetters and obscurations are like flowing currents, their characteristics equal to space.

I see that the increase of views is the root of afflictions; yet when one performs karmic actions through skillful cultivation of generosity, these pure and powerful superior causal practices give rise to fundamental tranquility and the ultimate truth.

True freedom from hunger and thirst is not attained through the practice of giving; it is only through the superior observance of ethical discipline that one gains such nobility. This sublime fruition is accomplished by compassion for sentient beings, who at all times offer worship and veneration.

Truly performing the cultivation of secret practices, this state is the ultimate limit, pure, wondrous, and powerful; thus, the torrential floods are stilled in accordance with reality, and the fetters, obscurations, and disputes are cleared away through hearing.

Arrogance, conceit, and haughty negligence are increased; disputes, litigations, and calamities are subdued and stilled; the mental ground gives rise to the increase of tranquility; one cultivates and practices giving while eliminating all signs of phenomena; and the true power and function of reality eradicates afflictions.

The distinct retributions and meritorious qualities of sentient beings' name-and-form are free from the inversion of defilement regarding self and dharmas, and are characterized by quiescence and detachment; they are able to destroy greedy desire so that all inversions and defilements are exhausted, representing the pure power and function at the ultimate limit of the body.

Seeking that which removes the darkness of self and other views and pride, one delights in equality and ultimately accords with it; the village is abundant, supreme, and pure, increasing fearlessness and giving rise to transport.

Bestowing the cause of tranquility halts the characteristics of saṃsāra; it possesses the sublime benefit of being without a place of rebirth. The body’s marks and the desire-greed for cultivation constitute reality; the power and function of the surging torrent undergo transformation. Through the provision of transport, one repents and atones for prior transgressions.

Such instruction lacks the power of transport; though one seeks to cultivate the practice of giving and prepares the requisites for offerings, even if one possesses the hearing and retention of the true secret treasury, the torrential floods of fear and agitation will shift and change in this manner.

In this state, one seeks the limit of sentient beings; amidst the defilements of reality, there is contention in the borderlands. Fearing change, one swiftly cultivates the practice of giving; in accordance with what is cherished, one truly engages in cultivation, so that the stains of inversion and the terrors of existence are brought to an end.

Sentient beings transmigrate without exceeding the six realms; their bondage and flux are designated as their characteristics. By cultivating the causes of the ten wholesome actions, they receive the retribution of humans and devas; at the limit of that period, their transport comes to rest.

That celestial realm possesses the characteristic of the ultimate truth, which is indestructible; yet, afflictions arise from the intrinsic nature of sorrow and suffering, and various fetters and hindrances ensnare one through the fundamental bond of the view of self. To understand this is to achieve purification and subduing.

The Tathāgata possesses perfect and peerless power and function; through hearing, reflecting, and practicing, he has cultivated virtuous merit; his generosity is perfected to the ultimate limit of the absolute truth; thus, he perfectly understands this virtuous nature.

The pursuit of the sublime within this system is such that one fears perversity; through pure discipline and tranquility, one practices giving and proceeds in this manner, for the secret treasury of the Tathāgata has peerlessness as its meaning.

The perfected meaning is non-erroneous and free from images; relying on the authoritative scripture of the noble ones, one traverses the torrent of transmigration. Through discernment, the vehicle is set in motion and equanimity arises; by advancing in practice, fearlessness increases and activity becomes supreme.

Those who possess dullness and cultivate perversions, yet practice sincere conduct in that state of purity, will freely advance toward the ten kinds of benefits; thus, through these superior, pure, and wondrous bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda*), they attain the purity of the fragrance of indestructible wisdom.
