The Garland of the Previous Lives of the Bodhisattva, Fascicle Fifteen.
Composed by the Noble Vīrasena and others.

Translated by Imperial Decree by the *Sō-sansai-dai* (Court Rank of Sagely Virtue), Acting Assistant Director of the Court of State Ceremonial, and Great Master of Sanskrit Learning for the Translation of Scriptures, Shōtoku Eikon and others: The Thirtieth Chapter of the Meaning of the *Jātaka of the Venerable Protector of the Nation Adorned with the Practice of a Bodhisattva*.

The arising of the supreme cause for the perfection of giving and bodhicitta; the pure wisdom that is capable of detachment through silent stillness; the fundamental cultivation of the system of patient conduct, tranquility, and the disciplined holy life; the departure from the three calamities through the vehicle of the ten wholesome paths; the arising of auspicious and supreme meditative concentration toward the goal; and the thorough knowledge of the timing, the equality and excellence of the settlements, and the hearing of what is to be known—namely, the hearing of the true reality of the Bodhisattva, their fundamental characteristics, their limits, and their merit.

The ultimate power and function are inherently unborn; moral virtue is perfected and pure instruction is revealed. Through the view of self, karma is created and craving arises accordingly; through wisdom and auspiciousness, all are universally rescued in equanimity.

When defilements do not arise, there is liberation and purity; when that true path of practice causes fear to cease, the root stains of contention and attachment become difficult to relinquish. As the ten paths of action of body, speech, and mind arise accordingly, superior tranquility exhausts all inverted defilements, like the full moon, cool and serene, reflecting all things as they are.

The activity of the limits of ego-clinging (*asmimāna*) never occurs; through perfect tranquility and the full possession of hearing and retention, the faculty of the ultimate eye arises to perform the function of seeing. The nature of worldly appearances is not solid; pride and its roots are entirely without reality. The arising of the ultimate truth can exhaust famine and scarcity; the causes and conditions of illness and affliction, as well as their appearances of terror and fear, and even all rare or shifting phenomena, do not exist.

Precepts are pure when one hears the truth; the causal conditions for the class of pride arise accordingly; the flow of defiled causes brings about calamities; yet the fundamental practice of the Supreme Vehicle can bring liberation from them.

Seeking out the superior generosity of hearing and retaining [the teachings], one is bound by the power of defilements and perversion; yet purity is difficult to find, and only in a place of tranquility is it attained—like the full moon in the sky, there is no hidden corner it does not illuminate.

Mastery brings the cessation of defilements and detachment; the world is illusory and ultimately lacks solidity. The noble and virtuous Dharma tames sentient beings; its place of arising is truthful and tranquil.

The movement and transition of the root of the fetters and hindrances is such that the nature of delight is supreme non-contention; without destroying the nature of defilement, one reveres with solemnity, increasing the burden to give rise to the extraordinary.
In this state, how can there be the "I" and the "mine" as predominant?

The self-nature, the entanglements, and the mental factors associated with them are all stilled; the true power and characteristics [of phenomena] cease to arise. On the level of the mental ground, the superior cause of wisdom does not emerge, and the calamities of inverted defilements blaze fiercely.

The nature of affliction is the root of contention; the characteristics of desire and greed bring about calamity and distress. Shifting and grasping at things, one's lineage is unstable; by advancing with honey to seize material objects, one's life comes to an end. Such inverted pursuits are the cause of bondage and fear.

The excellence of superior tranquility and bliss purifies the mental continuum so that inverted defilements do not arise; through skillfully cultivating the subduing of the fetters of affliction, one possesses the power to carry out the practice of superior generosity.

I see that the Noble Path can eliminate the causes and conditions [of suffering]; it honors and cultivates righteous benefit, being pure, wondrous, and stainless. It is the ultimate limit of truth, wherein one honors and cultivates generosity, giving rise to supreme causes within the mind and bearing the fundamental burden.

Transformation and subjugation, hearing and retention without error; the mental factors are preeminent, and attachment is unceasing. Karmic actions bring about various calamities, misfortunes, and obstacles; even the slightest taints of obstruction are subtle and difficult to sever. The ninth stage, the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-Perception, is adjacent to the state of the Sages; it is only at the ultimate locus that the causes of the Sages are finally severed.

The characteristics, power, and momentum of transmigration are all exhausted; yet the functioning and cultivation of that name-and-form (nāmarūpa) increase. At the limit of sovereign mastery, one is never free from alarm and fear; amidst the vastness of clamor and stillness, the holy life (brahmacarya) comes to rest.

The activities of afflictions arise as fluctuations; the torrential floods of defilement, evil, and inversion emerge simultaneously. True entanglements seek cessation, and the great classes of sentient beings follow accordingly in their cultivation, whereby merit and truth give rise to the ultimate meaning.

I view karmic actions and calamities as having the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as their cause; on the mental plane, various forms of pride increase. At such a time, the holy life (*brahmacarya*) ceases; yet through hearing the Dharma and practicing generosity, there is the benefit of pure fruit.

The sovereign arising of the truly supreme cause obscures and obstructs the ultimate nature; one must understand the locus of the truthful ultimate cause, understand the vast limits of negligence, and understand the characteristics of painful affliction. Thus, the limit of tranquil wisdom arises, and through pure generosity, defilements are distanced and eliminated.

The past shifts and changes, and wherever villages may be located, this place is truly one of bitter poison to be abandoned; the four aggregates, including both the named and the nameless, encompass all that is defiled and pure, while the power of superior aspiration performs its functions.

Sentient beings in the celestial realms cultivate pure and wondrous generosity; they ultimately realize the truth and remain far removed from defiled obstructions. They create filth and engage in intense strife and litigation, yet through perfect cultivation they advance in the purity of practice. Their wisdom and understanding increase, conforming to the power of its application; through diligent generosity, they possess the strength to bear burdens. This transport of merit, which eliminates all deficiencies, reaches its ultimate consummation here. Thus, this is the limit.

Fearing the entanglements and hindrances, one advances in cultivation and subdues them; the seals of the secret truth are perfectly complete, and its unimpeded application remains indestructible across boundless locations; through the power of these auspicious signs, fear is cast far away.

The celestial retribution obtained for a vast duration of time possesses the limit of power and the purity of intrinsic nature; in this state, where the surging torrent of afflictions is destroyed, one practices the ultimate application of giving in accordance with disciplined subduing.
What is the aspiration for the pure and sublime celestial realms?

It is the place where the bonds of generosity are predominant; it is the unceasing purification of defilements through authentic transport; it is the nature of non-erroneousness, preeminent in hearing and retention; it is the state of purity, tranquility, and profound stillness.

The power and function of sentient beings who practice giving without inversion are unified in the fundamental excellence of the Youth; he is fully endowed with purity, subtlety, equanimity, and immutability. The cause for this Youth’s pure and non-inverted giving is profound.

Sentient beings cultivate the excellence of generosity as their inherent nature; they tame their inverted fears according to reality. They practice the cultivation of supreme tranquility, bringing to rest the afflictions of evil, bitterness, and dullness. Thus, they bestow gifts with impartiality.

The nature of beings in the human realm is subject to constant flux and transformation; sentient beings are so numerous that their burdens are endless. In this place of ultimate quiescence and immovability, it is best to resolutely cultivate the sublime vehicle with vigor.

The practice of sovereign generosity is difficult for the four aggregates to comprehend; its power and function are supreme, giving rise to purity. Without destroying the temporal sequence, one reverently cultivates the benefits of the fruit; the King is most excellent, tranquil, and true. Wisdom arises through hearing and retention, carrying one across; through the causal practice of truthful sincerity, one tames all longing. The King’s sublime merit is preeminent; the extremes of affliction are abandoned by both devas and humans.

Sentient beings hear that the celestial realms are thus; the Bodhisattva, whose nature is pure, offers consolation. Just as in the past, Śilpa was peaceful; from the ground of afflictions, he gave rise to compassion. Through superior discipline, he shattered the causes of bondage; through the purity of wisdom, pride and the like were stilled. The shifting images of conceptual forms cause alarm and fear, yet his delight in pure giving is likewise supreme.

Ultimate reality is fundamentally quiescent and free from inverted conduct; it conveys those beings and gives rise to speech. It transports and shifts away the fetters of defilement; it lacks the practice of giving and acts as the cause for the conceit of "I. Its intrinsic nature is the causal factor of phenomena, appearing in the form of apprehension and fear.
What is the lack of tranquil conduct due to the obscuration of afflictions?

It is the clamor and contention produced by the power and function of the view of a self; such secret tranquility does not exist there. In that place, sentient beings cultivate pure conduct, reverently honoring the causes and karmic actions of the supreme and unerring.

Sentient beings accord with the limit of purity, exercising mastery in their practice so as to give rise to non-erroneousness; yet their speech is arrogant and unrestrained, increasing their conduct of flattery and deception, while they seek out the nature of things and distance themselves from the conduct of saṃsāra.

That which is called the causal practice of pure formation binds and defiles its own nature with such dread; it is truly far removed from the supremacy of verbal expression, and the cessation of painful afflictions, darkness, dullness, and inversion occurs.

The superior characteristics are free from the defilement of self; the noble path nurtures the meaning of removing the defilement of obstructions; it is pure, wondrous, and true, accomplished over distant eons; it gives rise to the ultimate limit of sincerity and the cessation of dispute.

Endowed with the mastery of sentient beings through perfect hearing and retention, the fetters and obscurations are subdued and their constraints brought to rest; the ultimate limit is perfected, vast and unerring, as the aspiration for that state gives rise to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Its characteristics are tranquil, and its grasping is stilled; the power of destructive actions no longer arises. Although the dullness of defiled extremes and the body of bondage still persist, the principle of liberation emerges.

The fundamental limit of the excellence of abiding in stillness is the secret nature of the fundamental power; herein, there is no cause for the seeking of self-view, as the bondage of this and that limit is the root.
How do inverted disputes arise?
How are the constituent parts equal and tranquil?

Without destroying the power of the phonetic expressions of sounds, such is the basis for the tranquility of causal characteristics; only when the fundamental wisdom arises can the root of obstructive defilements be severed—the ten types of evil conduct that constitute the root of karmic creation.

The Bodhisattva subdues vast perversion; when such calamities arise for sentient beings, they constitute the ultimate limit of the supreme causes of the temporal process. This is the purity of suchness, devoid of the meaning of accumulation.

The torrential stream of the superior [nature] binds one to the marks of form; sentient beings exercise mastery over their own nature of indulgent desire. The characteristics of reality are supreme and not false; the power of kings brings an end to all disputes.

The causal power of the three natures can be cultivated through practice; when one pursues desires and follows the stages of training, such temporal conditions give rise to inverted defilements. When the torrential flow increases, the cessation of what is meaningful occurs; the power of bearing burdens gives rise to generosity, while the power of equanimity leads toward cessation. The fearless appearance of a great man is supreme, yet the increase of defiled evil is ultimately inexhaustible.

The ultimate truth arises from the limits of those characteristics; the cause for the vast bestowal of generosity arises from their movement and transport; the limits of the defilements of self-nature are brought to cessation; and inverted appearances can no longer be found.

Perfect in physical form and free from defilement, having long been spared the sudden calamities that befall others, he perceives with clarity the tranquility of ultimate benefit and truth; through the power of equanimity, this Bodhisattva brings all beings to subdual.

The non-arising of the conceit of ultimate reality and so forth occurs; through correct reasoning, suchness is realized and afflictions are stilled. It is in this place that the Bodhisattva provides instruction with skillful words, a pure conveyance of the supreme secret.

The holy life is tranquil and true, free from fear; through its fundamental power and function, all afflictions and hardships are exhausted. Generosity carries one forward in accordance with right mindfulness, so that the fundamental reality brings an end to darkness and arrogance.

Excellent speech and instruction, pure, wondrous, and silent; through the hearing of the sublime cause of universal purity, how does one create a place where clouds of purity are spread to provide shelter for all living beings?

The stains, obscurations, defilements, disputes, and inversions are stilled during the stage of training; one tames the fundamental inversions of one's own nature and seeks tranquility. Thus, the shifting states of sentient beings—sorrow, suffering, calamity, and the feverish afflictions—are brought far away.

With a dignified and upright appearance, one listens to the non-contentious; in this state, one practices giving, hears and upholds the truth, and as a Bodhisattva who bears the burden of sentient beings, one’s speech in teaching is free from bondage and calamity.

Thus, the heavy residues (*dausthulya*) of afflictions that delude one regarding emptiness, the sovereign power over the meritorious conduct of the predominant causes, and the sentient beings therein who are fully integrated—all these increase in darkness and pride, shifting and changing like space.

The non-erroneous arising brings forth the benefit of hearing and retaining; such superior causal conduct is free from fear. One delights in the locus of inverted disputes, yet the limit of thirst diminishes one's own nature. Following along with tranquility leads to the purity of subduing; the limit of hunger and thirst consists of inverted attachments. For sentient beings, the recollection of dwelling in stillness arises; such are the virtuous words of the Bodhisattva.

The non-perverted Dharma ceases disputes and litigation; it is pure, disciplined, and abides in mastery. Mindfulness can clearly record and maintain the nature of what is heard, serving as the foundation for the sublime and wondrous stillness of the established order.

Sentient beings listen to and receive the instructions with tranquility; sentient beings mindfully recollect the supreme cause of giving; the root of my view gives rise to defilement; and through the accomplishment of supreme power, one practices stillness.

The supreme and wondrous causal practices arise in equality; during the period of complete and perfect cultivation, there is no fear in speech nor any defilement or diminution; in the ultimate sense, there is no inversion and no arising of dispute.

At the time of the ultimate limit, the torrential flow arises; because this cause is secret and free from the defilement of contention, it is pure, unmixed, and all calamities have ceased, as one practices non-erroneous conduct in tranquil suchness.

The power and characteristics of clamor and affliction are characterized by arrogance and self-indulgence; the causal nature of saṃsāra is pure and non-erroneous. Sentient beings understand this and achieve superior detachment; through the words of instruction, the sattva practices giving, and cultivates with superior reverence a pure aspiration.
How does the meaning of selflessness arise as benefit?

Through the fundamental speech-instructions on the practice of giving, one initiates tranquility at the ultimate limit; in the state of peace and happiness, calamities are far removed. How does one seek the nature of auspicious wisdom so that defilements are exhausted and there is rigorous purity?
The Bodhisattva Infinite Inversion provides this instruction: How is it that such great giving brings forth such vast merit?

By establishing a superior function within the tranquility of the village, one seeks the fruit of Buddhahood and guides all living beings. Their fearful conduct reaches the limit of emptiness; they understand the supreme joy of transport. Delighting in forms and appearances, they give rise to harmony and compliance. Having truly practiced giving, they have already eliminated contention; therein lies the nature of reality, which is without the sense of shifting or change.

The root of bondage and the limit of fear consist of name-and-form and the five aggregates; the aggregate of form can be accumulated, while sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are without substance and difficult to comprehend. With fundamental bondage as the cause, the meaning of true arising occurs.

The place of practice is tranquil and subdued; pride and the mastery over dharmas are purified and stilled. The fundamental provision is the fulfillment of hearing and retention; one remains far removed from the three arrows, and all defilements are extinguished.
What is the fundamental limit of conditioned activity?

That essence of verbal expression is ultimately thus: true hunger and thirst are the compassionate vow for universal salvation; the power of the mental ground is the root of diligent cultivation; and only when the superior causes of calamities and defilements are exhausted can they be ended.

The torrential flood of contention gives rise to dullness; when sentient beings are thus transported and accomplished, the characteristics of true arising and the appearance of karmic fruition become the supreme cause and dominant influence for abiding in tranquility.
What is the fundamental nature of time?

Its location is as terrifying and perilous as a mountain pass; herein the Bodhisattva practices truthfulness, while sentient beings shrouded in the darkness of ignorance know nothing else. This is the ultimate limit of time and the true power of its function.
What is the ultimate tranquility of the nature of phenomena?
It is the practice of generosity that accords with the dharma of aspiration and joy.
What is the cultivation of the power of purification?

Free from the obscurations of ignorance and pride, and devoid of inverted dharmas, one offers worship with diligence; the ten wholesome paths increase a hundredfold, the royal lineage flourishes, virtuous deeds are highly esteemed, the mental states are true and real, and wisdom and understanding are pure.

The Bodhisattva’s instruction on the root of calamities: the causes of action for both self and other shift with sovereign ease; the teachings of wisdom are pure and subduing; the secret nature gives rise to sentient beings.

With a pure and harmonious mind, liberated through purity, the Bodhisattva guides and receives sentient beings in this state; by hearing the nature of reality, they attain detachment and realize the tranquility of the dharma of non-arrogance.

The holy life is free from contention and fear; it acts with generosity, subdues the increase of darkness and pride, and brings tranquility. It consists of virtuous speech toward sentient beings and the superior practice of giving; it is the power of delighting in the causes and karma of sublime conduct.

The practice of the ultimate cause for the activity of subduing, the superior benefit for sentient beings of great learning, and the manifestation of offerings through the pure conduct free from contention—this is the unerring reality of intrinsic nature.

The root of purity and excellence is the cultivation of wisdom through giving; the cessation of inverted defilements follows accordingly; it is the supreme instruction of tranquil fearlessness—how excellent is cow’s milk, the foremost among all flavors!

The limit of time for vast wisdom is excellent; the characteristics of the borderlands are exceptionally sublime; seeking tranquility brings boundless offerings; and pure, wondrous speech is the excellence of cessation.

When fear arises, one practices repentance to attain tranquility; through fundamental subduing, there is natural purity. Since the fundamental self-nature cannot be apprehended, its equal benefit is the reality of quiescence.

Through the cultivation of the limit of intrinsic nature, one attains cessation; through the pure pursuit of sublime tranquility, the causes of affliction and inversion are forever stilled, and all seeking for karmic retribution is brought to an end.

The Bodhisattva teaches so that afflictions do not arise; he brings to rest disputes, defilements, and evil deeds; he bears the burden of seeking the supreme transcendence; poverty, illness, and all stains do not arise; and regarding dull-witted activities, he is fearless in each and every instance.

Sentient beings who hear this are exceptionally powerful; through the purity of giving, they accord with reality. It is unchanging, vast, and pure, its fundamental nature being the non-arising of suchness.

Pure and wondrous, the practice of giving is sovereign and unerring; because its causal conduct is sublime, its locus is indestructible. Through the unerring cultivation of causes for pure giving, afflictions are extinguished, resulting in profound stillness and tranquility.

Possessing a pure and harmonious capacity for hearing and retaining the teachings, one abides in the fundamental ultimate truth that is free from inversion and is sincere and real; through the conditions of virtuous friends, one reverently practices without cessation, so that its power and function are vast and no defilements arise.

The root of purity, wondrousness, excellence, and tranquility; the true power and function that sustains all living beings; the most supreme and distinguished capacity of wisdom and understanding; it thoroughly purifies greed, hatred, and delusion, and through ultimate wisdom, it is truly free from bondage.

Extensively practicing generosity without expectation, advancing toward perfection with mastery over all movements, possessing the unerring characteristics of the causal practice of hearing and retaining the teachings, and having a nature free from the stains of bondage that is like space.

The vehicle carries one toward the abiding in the exalted self-nature; sentient beings take the practice of generosity as their foundation; the exchange of debate refines the merit of wisdom; and the shifting flow of the aggregate of formations illustrates the meaning of impermanence.

The heavy obstacles of afflictions pervert the truth; various calamities blaze forth without ceasing. The causal practices that lead to transmigration must be stilled through the clarification of the mind; through the power of the established system, hearing and retention become perfected.

The sublime benefit of mutual correspondence consists in the removal of the obscurations of dullness, defilement, and verbal conceptualization through the modes of activity of the Noble Path. Taking purity as the foundation for conforming to superior characteristics, one realizes that shifting reflections lack substantial reality. Through the aspiration for the practice of the Path, one attains fearless hearing; the cause of pure excellence can be fully realized, and its power and limit remain as immovable as a mountain.

The power of making offerings arises from the aspiration for harmony; the foundation of instruction lies in truthful conduct and practice. When calamities, defilements, and perversions arise, the flow of pure and wondrous causal actions brings them to cessation.

The intrinsic nature of virtuous deeds is unshakable and does not shift; defilements do not arise as they follow along with the progressive advance; the causes and conditions for instruction give rise to non-erroneousness; and in speech free from faults, no entity can be apprehended.

In the nature of suchness, both emptiness and existence are extinguished; yet its sovereign power and function bear the burden of generating and evolving. As it advances and retreats, the three realms of existence are thus produced; at the limit of darkness and dullness, pure subtlety does not arise.

In this place, non-erroneous fundamental wisdom arises simultaneously; the torrential flow of afflictions is ultimately severed; the indestructible supernormal powers are extensively cultivated and increased; the supreme causes for practicing fearlessness are eternally tranquil; there is no inversion as sovereignty is perfected; respect for teachers and elders brings peace and benefit; and the locations are vast and distinct in this manner.

Pure, wondrous, and indestructible, one seeks the absence of contention; in this state, although various phenomena of greed and desire are perceived, the fundamental fetters and hindrances have ceased and do not exist, for through the liberation of wisdom, all transformations, defilements, and bonds are utterly exhausted.

One truly practices giving with excellent and wondrous characteristics; its benefit is unerring and as tranquil as a mountain. One seeks the fundamental power and function through the cultivation of the Brahma-faring life, and pursues the foundational practice free from the dharma of dullness and darkness.

The function of fundamental wisdom is a sublime and pure merging; when wisdom merges with True Suchness, the principle accords and the spirit attains union. For sentient beings, the meaning lies in the arising of generosity; through understanding language, one seeks the self-nature with precision.

With a preeminent physical form and pure name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), he is one who has brought to rest the activities of a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*); through the vast cultivation of equanimous wisdom and understanding, he brings to perfection the power and function of harmonizing the peripheral regions.

The fetters and hindrances of merit and power are stilled; being far removed from defiled obstructions, conceit does not arise. Through the power of aspiration, one understands with wisdom and insight, skillfully cultivating the bases of supernormal power to effect transformation and bring cessation.

The Bodhisattva provides skillful instruction and admonition; all devas together receive the ultimate limit of the supreme truth; afflictions are brought to rest and hunger and thirst are forever abandoned; through the presence of superior causes, they thoroughly understand discrimination.

Endowed with the excellence of meaningful benefit, one possesses the power of hearing and retention; through unerring cultivation and practice, one thoroughly eliminates obstructive defilements. These two types of transformation belong to the true Mahāsattva: the original defilement is itself non-defiled, giving rise to the sublime purity of wondrous manifestation.

Distant from signs, one cultivates the practice of the ultimate limit; through well-purified, superior, and well-established cultivation, disputes are stilled, and the activities of the ultimate limit bring about distance from the torrential floods.

The true physical forms of the celestial realms are majestic and beautiful; through the power of pure and superior causes, they are further enhanced, such that no causes for the miserable realms exist therein.

In accordance with such vast knowledge and vision, one is able to sever the bonds of the root afflictive hindrances. By following and understanding their respective functions, one seeks the transformative power of those physical forms.

In accordance with the root causes of worldly calamities, one practices the benefit of giving without seeking reward or retribution; truly seeking the cessation of enmity, one prioritizes the performance of deeds that create the causes for rebirth in the celestial realms.

Through wisdom, one understands that these are great sentient beings whose pride has increased and whose holy life has ceased; having purified their cultivation, they understand the signless, and regarding various mental activities, they harbor no desires or aspirations. They cultivate tranquility and honor the cessation of non-contention; while the nature of the view of self is explained based on defiled wisdom, the characteristic of sentient beings practicing generosity does not perish.

The occurrence of the torrential floods is the nature of bondage; such is the limit of fundamental calamities. The veils and perversions are, in truth, excellent; the pure locus is timeless and boundless.

Practicing truthfulness, tranquility, and cessation, he thus accords with the benefit of non-contention; in this state, the Bodhisattva impartially and freely delivers all beings with universal equanimity.

Having realized the teaching on the equality of intrinsic nature, remaining constant from beginning to end without love or hatred, making offerings with supreme excellence, and providing relief to living beings without momentary lapse.

When I perceive the temporal divisions, both self and other vanish; I clearly understand that arrogance and indulgence are solemnly brought to an end. There is nothing but the Sublime One’s teaching, a pure pursuit free from all signs and characteristics. Sentient beings suffer diminution and are born only in evil realms; as the former body perishes, the subsequent body arises again, attaining realization simultaneously with the Buddhas of antiquity.
The Bodhisattva’s instruction and discourse is that the creation of true benefit consists in making the cessation of evil the foremost priority.

The fundamental defiled phenomena begin with the view of a self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*); through this, attachment arises toward agreeable objects, aversion arises toward disagreeable objects, and delusion arises toward neutral objects. Subsequently, the remaining twenty-six afflictions arise; because of these, there is the creation of defiled obstructions and the pursuit of perversions.

There are no afflictive defilements that are not ultimately real; that which is real possesses seeds, while that which is provisional is established through function. In this regard, the fundamental power of giving arises as a source of instruction.

What is birth by transformation (*upapāduka*)? Those with superior wholesome karma are born by transformation as gods; those with predominant unwholesome karma are born by transformation in the hells. To exist suddenly where there was none—this applies equally to the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the state of birth (*upapattibhava*). There is no difference between the nature of the state of existence prior to birth (*pūrvakālabhava*) and the state of death (*maraṇabhava*). Both the state of birth and the state of death are established based on the foundational consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); that birth and death occur in a single moment is according to the words of the Noble Ones.

The Dharma possesses the quality of sustaining its own nature, and the locus of phenomena contains both defilement and purity. Through wisdom, one seeks understanding; through hearing, one achieves retention. When the view of self does not arise, afflictions subsequently cease; when one seeks the virtuous path, pure dharmas then emerge.

The ground where the cause of excellence arises is that which originally lacks a mind of giving, resulting in meager rewards; it is the root of the ultimate truth of unconditioned tranquility, wherein the Bodhisattva as a virtuous friend guides one toward fearlessness.

The nature of the fundamental essence is one of supreme bearing; thus one should practice with ease and without pride, relying upon a strict discipline and tranquil abiding, wherein there is no increase in the arrogance of speech or the Dharma.

One seeks to attain the non-contentious, equanimous, and tranquil state; the king’s sincere and truthful commands are impartial; the passionate conduct of sentient beings subsequently constitutes the path of karma; and the Bodhisattva guides them toward the coolness of virtuous karma.

Practicing generosity with sovereign mastery and a mind free from obstruction, one experiences retribution that is favorable to the present life, favorable to the next birth, favorable to subsequent lives, or of indefinite timing; these are called the four types of sequential retribution. This carries one across to the respective shores of the Three Vehicles: while the shore of humans and devas is temporarily attained and then abandoned, the ultimate and eternal attainment of the Three Vehicles is not like this; through diligent seeking and progress toward it, success is achieved only when the day is full.

Ultimate completion is what is called the "other shore" (*pāra*); the meaning of being indestructible, the meaning of being non-flowing, and the meaning of being without repetition—this is named the "other shore.

Wholesome phenomena of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-kuśala-dharma*) are exclusively mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), while wholesome phenomena of association (*samprayukta-kuśala-dharma*) pertain to both the primary mind and its concomitants. These are the causes for the limit of mutual predominance; through wisdom, one understands and realizes these ultimate expressions.

It is taught in the Noble Teachings that the desire for hearing is by nature a delight and leads to understanding; it directs sentient beings toward their lords and performs its functions; through hearing and cultivation, it brings joy and tranquility; it is the root of craving for the phenomena of desire; it coexists with diligence at the time of wholesome dharmas; and it pervades all three natures, whether defiled or non-defiled.

The various kinds of virtuous conduct are none other than benefiting all beings; the merit of hearing and learning gives rise solely to wisdom; their adorned appearances are exceptionally beautiful, fresh, and pure; all intrinsic natures are truly subject to transformation; merit and wisdom are pure, wondrous, and lovely; and the places where they are established are pure, wondrous, and free from defilement.
What is meant by liberation through the simultaneous exhaustion of both [afflictions and their traces]?

When the Noble Path arises, darkness does not appear; it carries one toward tranquility and shifts one toward excellence. The defilements and stains of affliction are unable to cause harm; in this state, wisdom arises and all obscurations of darkness are utterly exhausted.

The pure pursuit of non-erroneousness is difficult to attain; the calamities of strife and contention are stilled by the teachings of the Vehicle; there is no entanglement with the filth of illness; and the poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion are the root of all inversion.

True wisdom is difficult for sentient beings to give rise to, because they seek tranquility and remain unshakable; through the vast sphere of the Bodhisattva’s instruction, they cultivate power and dwell in equanimity where calamities do not arise.
What is fearlessness?

It is the fulfillment of the purpose of practicing pure conduct; the accomplishment of non-perverted actions in the world; the diligent cultivation of generosity so that the conduct of egoism ceases; the successful completion of superior deeds such that the system is purified and craving is stilled.

Flexibility and extension, advancing and retreating, represent the meaning of harmony and tranquility; liberation from birth and death represents the meaning of severing afflictions; the King represents the meaning of protecting the nation and bringing peace to all living beings; supreme truth represents the meaning of increasing profound stillness; the original arising without inversion represents the elimination of active functions; and the constellations represent the meaning of being serene and free from change.

Accomplishing the superior matters of non-loss and increase; the matter of illuminating the true foundation; the matter of distancing oneself from the calamities of the stars; and the conduct of great wisdom that subdues various forms of deception.

Fully understanding the affliction of ignorance that leads to exhaustion and transmigration, one establishes the fundamental prosperity of sentient beings; bearing their defilements, one practices giving universally.

Though the suffering and transformations of sentient beings are difficult to relinquish, one accomplishes the truly secret and wondrous speech, harmonizing in both advancing and retreating, and reverently upholding it upon the crown of the head.

The five kinds of resultant fruits, such as consciousness and so forth, constitute existence; setting aside the immediate consideration of wholesome and unwholesome karma, the force of inverted defilements arises, and one single-mindedly seeks the constellations to establish oneself in their original positions.

The nature of that power of transport is not empty; through the diligent cultivation of the designation of darkness and dullness, it becomes well-purified. It instructs on the root, causing goodness to arise, and further possesses the sublime dharma of tranquil abiding and self-realization.

As one’s stages of practice advance and one gradually ascends to the ranks of the sages, one clearly realizes the various secrets of one’s own nature; the power and function of its radiance become exceptionally sublime and pure, and one attains the fearless self-nature that is the original cause.

Mutually enhancing the perfection of the faculties, one establishes the primordial, non-erroneous purity; realizing that the nature of self-grasping is illusory, one cultivates pure and sublime practices as the cause for the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Knowing that which is fundamentally unarisen is liberation; seeking the holy life, one abides in tranquil stillness; with no resentment or retribution to oppose, one remains solemnly detached; and one reverently honors the profound and subtle treasury of the Dharma.

The function of this sublime teaching as a vehicle for transport is such that the king’s edicts are as dense as a forest; thus, the people all come to rely upon and admire them. His laws and decrees are stern, yet he treats all living beings with impartiality. His holy achievements in governance and transformation are so abundant that they are unsurpassed; though enemies and adversaries exist, they ultimately pose no threat. He transports all things without a single failure, and all regions everywhere rely upon and receive his instruction.
How is it that that land is so solemn and tranquil?
Why are the words spoken by the Bodhisattvas so profound and awe-inspiring?
How is it that they dwell in a state of non-erroneousness?

Wherever the laws of change and transformation prevail, they bring increasing relief; when one reverently cultivates righteous conduct entirely free from deceit, all shall universally attain peace and security without distinction, and as governance and transformation flourish, joy shall be boundless.

Ultimate tranquility is as peaceful as the realm of the gods; practicing pure generosity, one provides relief equally to all. Cultivating the equality of all phenomena in each instance, one brings the performance of deeds to perfection in daily life.

Various obstacles and difficulties return to their former state; one realizes that defilements and disputes are entirely of the same nature. The fetters of the mind have no correspondence with reality, yet once evil karma is formed, it is difficult to alter.

Friends abound like a forest, from which one cannot distance oneself; afflictions and strife are so powerful that they cannot be halted. Ceasing the creation of karma and again cultivating superior practices, one cultivates the teachings of the Noble Ones and practices the conduct of cessation.

Distant from the hindrance of afflictions and relying upon the truly pure Dharma, its self-nature, characteristics, essence, and meaning are like space; as vast as space are the heavy burdens of worldly toil, for the Dharma is fundamentally without self, quiescent, and pure.

The arising of profound teachings and practices at the ultimate limit, the performance of the dharmas of tranquility belonging to those in training—such a place is peaceful and fearless, yet it possesses the characteristics of inverted cultivation, defilement, and contention.

Furthermore, one cultivates pure reality, listens in accordance with the meaning that is like space, and accords with the vast and sublime equality, thereby performing the three types of activities that accord with primordial wisdom (*jñāna*).

The king repents for the accidental destruction of things; through the superior hearing and study, there arises a mind of seeking; the self-natures of both are equally beyond verbal expression; and through dullness, the limits of the world are nurtured.

The Brahma-faring is pure and unbroken in the world; he seeks the giving that is dear to kings, yet lacks the meaning of hearing and the meaning of the secret treasury; though capable of reality, he does not practice the perfection of worldly conduct.

Having fully relinquished the conceptualization of the suffering of death, one thus pursues the excellent state of serene stillness; swiftly attaining liberation from afflictions and calamities, one accords with mindfulness as the land becomes abundant.
How does one give rise to conduct that accords with suchness (*tathatā*)?

In all places, defilements are purified; the dust and grime of all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and the cessation of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) occur. Movement is thus the root of tranquility; for such a person, clamor and contention are entirely stilled.
The world is at peace and the people are harmonious and joyful; likewise, the dharmas of bondage are tranquil, blissful, and free from anxiety. Such is the ultimate limit and the fundamental basis.
This is the thirty-second chapter on the meaning of the Jātaka of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, concerning the Bodhisattva’s practice of adornment through giving.

The supreme burden of the ultimate limit of reality, the fundamental purity of the nature of phenomena, and the various causal practices that constitute the functional power of the fruit—these are what are known as the aspects of the bodhisattva’s conduct in accordance with hearing.

The boundaries of this sublime place are unerring; it gives rise to the power and function of perfection without bondage. Its fundamental practice is giving, a conduct free from transition or change; the arising of the signs of pure causes is difficult to attain.
The phenomena of conceptualization are truly afflictions; the arising causes and conditions are ultimately ceased through the cessation of obstacles.

The nature of consciousness accords with the pure teachings, and wisdom realizes the self-nature of its functional power. With the fundamental transformation of generosity as the foremost, the mental activity of compassion guides the sublime self-nature. This sovereign power of pure karmic action is what is called the reality of functional power.

In accordance with the nature of reality, one does not give rise to [deluded] cultivation, but practices virtuous conduct; bound by afflictions, one contemplates wholesome karma; through the superior power of karmic fruition, one engages in the discourse of the holy teachings, and through knowledge and vision, one thoroughly understands the sublime practices of both self and others.

One should contemplate the pure activities of the noble Dharma; these are the very dharmas that bind one to the true nature of reality. Evil karma truly exists and its ugly fruits are not non-existent; one must contemplate how to abandon them as taught by the Noble Ones.
The pure, wondrous, and true proceeds without non-existence; when no place arises, the correct principle is revealed. Like a mountain unmoving, it is the aspect of purity.

When the fruit of suffering arises, the *manas* arises simultaneously; following its support, there is the sense of mutual interaction. The nature of the torrential defilements coexists with the sixth consciousness, arising sequentially with both collective and individual retributions.

Seeking the fundamental cause, one engages in ceaseless activity; the ten virtues support one another to complete the hundredfold. Through the practice of giving, one carries across the distant and long kalpas; by the power of pure goodness, one remains far removed from the bonds of defilement.

Birth is fundamentally a fabrication that does not arise without cause; wherever it exists, it is the suchness (*tathatā*) of supreme reality. The characteristics of the body are pure and subtle, and mindfulness extends to the furthest reaches; as one perceives this tranquility, the cessation of thought continues without end.

Mastery in the cessation of meditative absorption (*dhyāna*) is pure; through the practice of giving with an impartial mind toward the great multitude of sentient beings, one cultivates the superior power of one's own fundamental nature, whereby the reliance upon signs increases mastery.

Perfectly fulfilling the ultimate truth of fearless tranquility, the faculty of hearing functions without obstruction wherever it may be; dwelling in stillness at remote borders, one clarifies the mind and brings it to rest, exhausting all fundamental fears through pure and skillful action.

The Noble Path is unbound and free from dullness and pride; its activity is indestructible and its practice becomes ever firmer. Through harmonious mindfulness, it possesses power and is never forgotten, giving rise to the supreme conduct of the pure path.

The sublime and supreme causes of shifting reflections transport beings with impartiality, unerring, and eternally tranquil; pure and wondrous generosity brings peace and security to every place, and the meritorious practices of these supreme causes exist everywhere.

Practicing the conduct of a bodhisattva in accordance with the Dharma, one extensively bestows boundless practices upon sentient beings; being clear-sighted, sharp, reverent, and conscientious, one is fearless, sublime, and wondrous; abiding in selflessness and the middle way, one is tranquil, serene, and full of loving-kindness.

The nature possesses power and conduct is unerring; there is boundless listening and detachment. The fruit of suffering is indestructible and arises as reality; originally devoid of characteristics, it is tranquil and immovable.

The perfected nature possesses the fruit; its self-nature is limpid and tranquil. Primordial wisdom is impartial and not void of principle or phenomenon; nirvāṇa is attainable through superior clarity and sharpness. Ego-clinging does not arise, and the limit is indestructible.

Tranquility accords with the path of primordial and subsequent wisdom; through the fulfillment of the activity of pure power, the locus is without diminution, and the source of non-inversion arises; there is no time for distribution, as giving and cultivation are performed simultaneously.

The power and function are supremely excellent, and its self-nature is pure and wondrous; it is the retribution of the celestial realm and the cause for cultivating the Brahma-conduct. It is a pure, wondrous, and victorious army that opposes the afflictions; like indestructible vajra, it can shatter their very nature.

Purifying the practice of giving, one seeks the cessation of dullness; thus cultivating the ultimate conduct, one dwells in the state of reality, which is impartial and untainted. With the full complement of powers, one remains far removed from arrogance, performing sublime practices that are ultimately perfected by their very nature.
What is it that is obtained from that which is fundamentally real, pure, and wondrous?
My dwelling, power, function, and practice do not increase; they are sovereign, pure, and untainted by evil giving.
Why is it that the construction of houses and buildings is deemed inadequate?

The retribution of lack of refinement results in poverty; wandering through saṃsāra is unstable, subject to change and downfall. By diligently seeking virtuous conduct, happiness follows accordingly, and one's physical faculties remain unimpaired, the body as it was before.

The fruition of accomplishment brings forth inexhaustible merit; herein, the Bodhisattva’s instruction is serene and tranquil. Its true nature is sovereign and free from seeking; the Lord is fearless, supreme, and infinite.

The unalterable self-nature possesses the power to give rise [to practice]; through the fulfillment of the effortful cultivation of the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*), all such practices of the bodhisattva path are established within the fundamental Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*) that is free from cultivation.

When the bonds of calamity and misfortune are stilled and the mind is settled in peace, one seeks the sublime and advances toward the great fruit; with the power to arouse such a mind of diligence, one attains the perfection of the limit of detachment.

Virtuous conduct is free from inversion and far removed from fetters and hindrances; by contemplating and demonstrating their characteristics, one diligently cultivates supreme power. When the timing is inverted, the practice of the Path is entirely deficient; yet when one delights in the truth, nothing is established in vain.

There is the great rain of the Dharma, which is beyond verbal expression, ultimate, supreme, and characterized by the complete transcendence of all phenomena; it is excellent, free from contention, and accords with what is sought, yet it lacks the root of giving and consists only of its branches.

The teachings bestowed by the Sages are not established in vain; the conduct defiled by worldly dust and the entanglements of afflictions are both subject to change and corruption, such that neither can be found [in their true nature]. The conduct of a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa), however, is of preeminent lineage.

Immovable and eternally quiescent, it is beyond all speech; indestructible like a precious jewel, its mind is ever-guarded; entirely devoid of activity and lacking the nature of transmigration, wisdom understands and realizes the nature of suchness.

The influence of karmic retribution and cultivation is thus; the compassion of the Bodhisattva exhausts all that can be said; such is the distinction of the true and the guidance provided; through the power of purity, defilement finds no end.

The state of bliss is beyond all comparison; that nature of giving is supremely pure in its ultimate sense. Having accomplished confession, one is as stainless as the heavens; ultimate defilement is free from the characteristics of verbal expression.

It cannot be said that there is a fundamental, superior function, nor can it be said that there is a self-nature of the self; the meaning of the original birth is eternally real, and its activity follows accordingly.

To seek out views is a perverted practice; it is the co-arising of torrential defilements and views, as well as conceptual discrimination. To be silent regarding such speech, to bear the burden of truth, and to act for the benefit of sentient beings—this is the practice of pure giving.

It conveys the meaning of crossing over birth and death through various means; how excellent is the practice of giving that removes the suffering of poverty! Its secret efficacy is beyond words, and its joyful discourse is ever-increasing.

In the state of tranquility, there is no end to longing; in supreme generosity, the mind is universally impartial; in the body, there is no inversion and the physical form is pure and bright; in the ultimate truth, there is no bondage, and through the power of the noble ones, there is fearlessness.

This matter is stainless and its nature is pure; through the power of hearing and retaining the teachings on the laws of transformation, one diminishes the self-nature and abandons uneven conduct. When defilements are exhausted, the virtue of precepts can be realized.
Among the practices of the heavens, one must value truthfulness; likewise, the retributions of the evil realms are never in vain, for the efficacy of wholesome and unwholesome karma is equal.
How can one practice patience with such diligent effort and without retreat?

Should one encounter adversity or harm, their resolve remains firm and difficult to bend; they endure with equanimity the oppression of cold and heat. The conduct of ordinary beings consists truly only of giving; through pure wisdom, they manifest various forms of activity, yet they must still fully experience the retributions of the evil realms.
The thirty-third chapter: The Meaning of the Jātaka of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, Adorned by the Bodhisattva’s Practice of Giving.
The torrential flow of perversions gives rise to the conceit of self, which is the very root of what is called the sixth consciousness.
The Bodhisattva considers the duration of time to be vast and long.

To realize the Great Fruit, a small cause is insufficient; one must cultivate the causes of the ten thousand practices to obtain the boundless fruit. Since both bodhi and nirvana transcend words and thought, one cultivates the practice of diligence until great compassion is perfected.
What is the timing?

Just as it is difficult to emerge from the coarse heaviness and obstructions of space, so too must one first eliminate them through the three fundamental wisdoms and the eight subsequently attained wisdoms; only then can one attain mastery over the retributive fruit, becoming fully endowed with the hearing and retention of the Dharma-body, Reward-body, and Transformation-body.

The fundamental power and function of the teachings are pure; they are the ultimate reality and the fruit of the śrāvaka. Those of fixed nature attain nirvana without remainder, their physical bodies consumed and their wisdom extinguished; those of indeterminate nature turn their minds toward enlightenment and enter the body of transformation. Following the Mahāyāna until the attainment of Buddhahood, they are fully carried across by the Buddha-dharma and the sublime conduct.

This great sentient being benefits both self and others; that sentient being’s body possesses all the seeds of the Buddha. Whether obstructed or unobstructed, whether ordinary or noble, this single intrinsic nature remains constant throughout vast eons.

In this state, the mental factors are wholesome and indestructible; among great beings, they accord with what is desirable, even unto equality, providing benefit to all. They bear a preeminent burden, seeking the practice of diligence.

The nature of the fetters and hindrances arises fundamentally from self-clinging; they are the clamor and strife desired by worldly villages. These are truly defilements, devoid of pure conduct; yet in the state of equality, one is drawn forth by compassionate vows.

His intentions were perfectly fulfilled, and he benefited all beings without exception; the king of that land was renowned for transforming others through his virtuous speech, and at that time, the people followed him as readily as the wind, while the sovereign exercised his supreme power in accordance with their needs.

Utterly pure and sovereign at the limit of sincerity, the place of its manifestation is incomparably magnificent; endowed with the power of hearing and retention, the body and mind are tranquil, establishing the supreme cause of the exalted self-nature.

Because the afflictions of the celestial realms involve harm, one may be received through the power and function of the virtuous friends of the Three Vehicles; the true nature is ultimately blissful, like a lion king who dwells without fear or dread.

Seeking to hear, receive, and maintain [the teachings] to fulfillment; the meaning of liberation arising from the purity of self-nature; the power and function of the characteristics of the primordially superior nature; silent stillness, signlessness, and a tranquil mind unmoved.

When karmic creditors from the past confront one in the present, it is difficult to escape them suddenly; therefore, cultivate the most supreme goodness to atone for former transgressions. Whether the retribution of sin or merit is light or heavy, the creditors will naturally withdraw their hold upon the constituent parts of sentient beings. To realize one's own nature and bring afflictions to rest depends entirely upon noble conduct.

The concoction of poisons and the incitement of disputes are based on the fundamental elements of existence and the proliferation of discursive speech; yet, within the sovereign power of their functional scope, nothing can be apprehended, for in true suchness there is no sense of volitional construction.
When a Bodhisattva practices generosity, they do not contemplate its reward; they perform acts of equal giving without inverted characteristics, a fundamental practice that is tranquil and sublime.

Where there are bonds, clamor, and disputes, they find themselves in a state of sovereignty within a peaceful location; their fundamental mode of being is a superior movement toward seeking tranquility and practicing in secluded places.

In each and every instance of reality, there is no pain or malice; reality is the fundamental basis for the cessation of disputes and the dullness of ignorance. Thus, through this non-erroneous cause for the increase of supreme merit, one abides in tranquility wherever one may be and extends the practice of giving universally.

In every place of rebirth, one accords with pure causes; having accomplished equanimity, one realizes cessation. Practicing the supreme generosity, it is conjoined with non-attachment and the like; as painful sensations shift and change, wisdom increases.

The nature of loving-kindness is peaceful stillness; the karmic retribution for acts of giving is never in vain; the selfless nature is understood according to its true meaning; and pure, truthful reality is ultimately like space.

In the tranquility of meditative concentration, suffering and affliction do not arise; by remaining unmoved regarding name-and-form, one realizes their intrinsic nature. With sublime joy and delight, one seeks superior karma; through pure happiness, one hears and retains the teachings therein.

The essence of great sentient beings is warm, moist, harmonious, and joyful; the supreme ultimate truth is tranquil and equanimous; the power of the secret mantra language is difficult to fathom; and its nature is such that it is truthful, authentic, and worthy of veneration. By cultivating and honoring this in this place, through its sovereign power, there arises the perfect excellence of overturning [delusion].
What is meant by the state of the primordial nature being supremely honored?

From the very moment of birth, one possesses qualities unlike others; because the essence has degrees of excellence and inferiority, it possesses a real nature that can be truly understood through its causes.

Those of superior and wondrous nature, who are preeminent, are always settled in their composure and advancement, increasing and flourishing in radiance; through the fundamental practice of impartial application, they give rise to the ten kinds of conduct, such as the precepts and patience.

The intention of true practice is quiescent; giving without abiding in stillness involves conduct that is inverted and defiled. The meaning of the characteristics of cessation is that birth cannot be apprehended; the bodily marks accord with the nature of the elements and can be attained.

Unchanging conduct is peaceful and provides a refuge; being and non-being are immutable and both transcended. The visualization and recitation of the mantra-practice are far removed from conceptual deliberation; the merit of upholding the precepts is the cause of the most sublime greatness. Through the power of meditative concentration, one enters the path of the sages; when actions are performed in accordance with equanimity, they are detached from worldly involvement, and even bondage is eliminated.

In this state, the Bodhisattva’s praise increases; they carry out what is supreme and understand pure conduct. Since neither the root nor the limit can be apprehended, wisdom understands the true characteristics of that practice.

The power and function of where merit resides undergoes transformation; the power and function of the ultimate truth is the achievement of the Lord of Devas. In this place, one practices the cultivation of equal images, whereby the nature of fortune and prosperity increases and one advances toward the higher realms.

The purity of the Brahma-faring is the foundation of the mental ground; it is ultimately supreme, perfect, and unerring. The mind of giving gives rise to the ultimate truth; its characteristics are pure, subtle, and rare throughout the world.

Those who behold it never tire of practicing the bodhisattva path; the compassionate mother manifests through the mastery of signs, and her giving is like space—fundamentally quiescent. Such is the truth.

When calamities arise, there is the power to remedy them; each is truly pure and pleasing. By cultivating wisdom, one attains genuine liberation; in this state, the suffering of the bodhisattva has truly ceased.

Just as there is no analogy that can reach the exhaustion of the defilements of affliction, one cultivates pure conduct while bound by the five aggregates; thus, name-and-form and the five aggregates are all subsumed therein, wherein the torrential floods, defilements, and disputes exhaust the hindrance of affliction.

The cultivation of tranquil conduct gives rise to its own nature; in this state, superior generosity carries one forward. That creative nature is profoundly systematic, giving rise to wisdom and the superior pursuit of the goal.

The time of non-erroneous, fundamental exhaustion of bonds and defilements is the tranquil activity of the celestial realm, the reality of which is pure, wondrous, stainless, and the functional power of the root.

Self-grasping, sharp delusions, dull defilements, greed, and ignorance—though one diligently seeks mastery, these fetters are difficult to exhaust. Through the characteristics of possessing power, one seeks the giving that results in superior rebirth and the arising of ultimate truth.

The characteristics of stillness and tranquility are pure in their locus; this is the meaning of hearing and upholding the true and supreme cause. In this state, the bodhisattva is free from dull and obstructed karma, and follows along with the cycle of birth and death to guide and receive all classes of beings.

Sentient beings in the celestial realms possess the meaning of the unerring cause; they perform noble practices and revere the ten wholesome karmas. Their activity is signless, seeking the meaning of harmony; their sublime cultivation is free from the cycle of transmigration.

The arising of the sublime from tranquil non-diminution; the sovereign excellence of the marks of self-grasping; the nature of the veils of perversion and reality; the profound union of suchness and the noble nature of primordial wisdom.

The subsequently attained wisdom (prsthalabdha-jñāna) can only arise when it takes suchness as its object through the transformation of images; thus, the causal and resultant stages differ in terms of being direct or indirect, and so forth. The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is thus complete from beginning to end: while enshrouded [by afflictions], it is called the *garbha* (womb/storehouse), and when free from enshrouding, it is the *dharmakāya*.

To cultivate the ultimate limit and seek the essence of the Dharma, one accords with cessation and repeatedly distances oneself from [delusion]; thereby generating benefit and practicing fearlessness, one gives rise to the primordial appearance of all formations.

One need not rely on a superior mind for the practice of giving; the field of merit that is signless is truly supreme. The essential nature of giving can destroy signs, and that which is based on the absence of nature is inherently free from longing.

Pure and supreme, it is far removed from craving; its ultimate limit in the practice of the path is auspicious and wondrously sublime. That which seeks its suchness is ultimately unattainable; when one is led into the gateway of reality, there is neither "is" nor "is not."

The nature of verbal expression relies upon names, phrases, and syllables; names, phrases, and syllables are conventional designations that establish reality. Their root is non-arising; through hearing and retention they are nurtured. In this state, there is no destruction—only profound stillness and eternal quiescence.

The purity of devas and humans is likewise free from alarm or fear; excellent is this non-empty, superior self-nature, the supreme, unerring, and true cessation, whose perfect appearance is the pure nature of non-contention.

Generosity is the power that is the root of merit; it is the cause for a compassionate mother and the foremost basis for noble lineage. By aspiring for tranquility, afflictions do not arise; thus, when each honors the other, they become mutually superior.

Within that celestial realm, through the causal conditions of merit, the nature of excellence is supreme and unerring; the realization of the aggregate-nature arises from the manifestation of true characteristics, and as the marks of transmigration are exhausted, the ultimate truth is brought forth.

Thus, through such confession and repentance, one exhausts all faults and afflictions—the various delusions regarding both principle and phenomena—and comes to fully understand that the categories of faculties, whether sharp or dull, are without equal; such are the primary and secondary afflictions, as well as the discriminative and co-emergent [ignorances].

The locus of the time of abandonment is as explained in other treatises. One seeks the superior power through the sequence of the categories of phenomena; when the practice of the virtuous and excellent is truly perfected, such cultivation of the fundamental by the virtuous and excellent is called "fundamental conduct" (mūlacaryā), profound and secret.
The thirty-fourth chapter on the meaning of the Jātaka of the Venerable Rāṣṭrapāla, titled "The Bodhisattva’s Ornamentation through the Practice of Giving.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s practice of supreme conduct.
*Bodhisattvajātakamālā*, Fascicle Sixteen.
